mr. president, ladies and gentlemen, decision time is now upon us. we have had more candidates, we have had more debate, and we have had more openness. it represents a change in the method, in the way we have done our business. it is a good change and i hope it is a signal of an appetite throughout this house to engage in the years which come and the balance of this mandate in a culture of transformation of how we do our business. the campaign reveals many perspectives, not least about the strengths and weaknesses of the candidates – and i have my share of both. i read about myself in polite journals that i am loquacious. i live in ireland, where we are all loquacious, near blarney where there is a stone and a castle. when visitors come there and kiss that stone, they say in hibernian english that they leave with the gift of the gab, meaning loquacious in polite journals. i may be that, but the more important part of this campaign is that it has offered the opportunity to listen and to learn. i have listened and i have learned that there is an appetite for change, that there is a great feeling in this house that we need to do more politics in the best and visionary sense of that word. i have learned that we want less voting and less technicalities and more capacity to be politicians and to bring our influence to bear. in other words, we want more vitality in how we manage our affairs. we need to bring closure to many of the issues of reform that have been before us for so long. the complex members' statute is difficult and the hard work led by nicole fontaine is testament to that. but we must continue to try. i tell this to members: i will, in a hands-on way, try to achieve that reform, but never over the heads of the members of this house. it will be done in the fullest, most transparent and open shared consultation. (applause) i have learned here how good we are at legislating on and talking about equal opportunity and gender equality, but how bad we are sometimes as an institution at putting it into practice. i pledge today before this house that, should i have the privilege to lead at the end of the day, i will promote the equality of gender in various ways, but most visibly and at the outset by it being apparent in the construction of the cabinet. since 1998 i have had the privilege to lead the liberal democrat group and together, i believe, with my colleagues, we have established a capacity for doing politics, which is the business of this institution. we are 626 members, we are a parliament. i am not seeking, mr bonde or other colleagues who share your fears, to be the sixteenth president or prime minister of the sixteenth state. i am proud to be a parliamentarian and we must bring our parliamentary and democratic vision to bear on the great issues of the day in europe. we must make europe fit for a future on a continental scale and we must make the democracy in this house fit to offer a real leadership and act as a counterweight and check and balance against the excesses of technocracy or bureaucracy. i want to say to hans-gert poettering and to the ppe-de group how greatly i appreciate his and their unswerving commitment to be full and faithful partners to an agreement which we made. but i want to say this also: i have had the privilege to visit many groups, many committees, many intergroups. i want, if i can, to lead a presidency which is a stakeholder presidency, open to build on the talents of those who will contribute. i ask you for your support. finally, mr president, smaller groups in this house do not find themselves with the credible possibility that my liberal democrat group finds it has today. i do not know what the final result will be, but i know this much: i cannot see how those who say that they value more openness, a change in the system, who would like to see a fairer share for all, can reconcile this with voting for a large-group candidate, not because of any fault with the candidate, but because of the nature of the system we have. if you wish to transform the system, today's vote will be the first mark of whether we are dedicated to transformation and change. that is my appeal; i ask for your support. i should love to have the privilege to lead; but the choice now rests with you.

mr president, in setting out the presidency's programme with regard to key policy issues, which will be addressed over the next six months by the european union, the spanish prime minister has stated that his priority of priorities during spain's six-months' presidency of the eu will be the global fight against terrorism. i strongly support this political objective. the european union has certainly adopted a series of measures to combat international terrorism in recent months as an immediate response to the horrific terrorist attacks in the united states last september. the prevention of the use of the european financial system as a money-laundering route for terrorism must continue to be a priority for our union. the fifteen governments of the union should also be in a position to freeze the assets of terrorists and those involved in organised and international crime. i very much welcome the spanish government's objective of promoting more police cooperation across the borders of the union. this is very important because intelligence agencies within the union, together with europol, have to work much more closely together in terms of exchanging and sharing information if the terror networks operating in europe are to be broken. the enlargement negotiations with the applicant countries will be entering a new phase during the spanish presidency. this presidency is being entrusted with two very difficult chapters in the negotiations on enlargement, namely agricultural policy and regional aid. the union and the applicant countries must sit down and hammer out an agreement on the difficult chapters of the discussions because otherwise enlargement of the union cannot take place quickly and will not be a success. countries in eastern and central europe are presently receiving eu structural funds so as to make their economies more competitive. this is an important policy objective because it will ensure that on entry these countries can participate within the union in a competitive climate. if the economies of eastern and central europe are not competitive, then they will not be able to participate within the internal market in any real, effective sense. equally, promoting market economies in eastern and central europe is good news for businesses within the union, which can also expand their goods and services into new markets. the spanish government is also going to set up the convention in march this year to look at the development of the future of eu policies within the union in the context of the next intergovernmental conference in 2004. it is important that the terms of reference of this convention are clear and decisive and that its conclusions in due course do not turn out to be an unattainable wish list. amendments to the treaties have to be agreed by european union leaders and any proposals emanating from this convention must be balanced, progressive and achievable. i also welcome the commitment of the spanish government to promote the implementation of eu regulations and directives, which should expand the use of new information technologies into all parts of the union. this is exceptionally important if the union is to remain competitive in the years to come. finally, one of the great disappointments of laeken was the failure to reach agreement on the siting of up to 12 new important eu agencies. i hope that the spanish government can reach agreement quickly on the location of these important agencies, in particular the european food authority and the european maritime safety agency.

acting president of the council. - thank you very much, mr president, ladies and gentlemen. i am grateful for all the speeches which have taken place during this sitting, which i have listened to with the greatest attention. i would like to say to you, ladies and gentlemen, that i certainly share many of the ambitions that have been expressed here. i also share many of the concerns and it should not surprise anyone that there are some things i have heard that i do not directly share. but i must admit that, from a general point of view, i have the feeling that the basic elements of the issues, the objectives, the ambitions that we can share today, the different institutions and european citizens in general, when we put our ideas and projects into practice, are or can reasonably be driven for the future. i would first like to stress the importance of the institutional dialogue and, within the institutional dialogue, to stress once again my commitment. we shall have occasion to speak of this european impulse and also of the work of the spanish presidency, both in the month of march after the european council in barcelona and in the month of june after the european council in seville. and this, of course, without prejudice to the presence of the various members of the spanish government in the various parliamentary bodies of this institution. i would like to say that as president i see no problem with the establishment of what some of your honourable members have asked for and requested: the creation of a working party for interinstitutional dialogue involving the council, parliament and the commission, which will clearly show how our work can be carried out. i think the commission has no objection to this. so, from that point of view, i am aware and share some of the concerns that you have, such as the handling of second and third pillar documents, which must be resolved with all the guarantees that the circumstances, the facts themselves and the sensitivity of the matter require, as is done in so many national parliaments, with guarantees of security and with guarantees of reserve. it is clear that we can make progress on many of these issues and therefore the presidency will have no problem in setting up this interinstitutional working party. i should like to concentrate, if i may, on the objectives and programme of the presidency and not on any other circumstances. i believe, ladies and gentlemen, that we are facing a very important occasion for the european union, a historic moment, a truly relevant one. i think we have an opportunity here that we should not miss. that occasion manifests itself, at least, in several circumstances. the reality of the world after 9/11 has changed and it has changed in a dramatic way. the priority in the world today is the fight against terrorism and security. the same change after 11 september is causing fundamental strategic changes in the world which will define the world of the future, on which the european institutions must reflect, must dialogue and on which they must take a position for the future. the european union as such, in its various institutions, cannot remain on the sidelines of what reflection and participation in the profound strategic changes that are about to take place in the world mean. secondly, it is a very important occasion from an economic point of view. and for several reasons. firstly, because we have the euro, our single currency, for the first time, which is a guarantee of stability and has been a great success. secondly, because for structural reasons, to which i shall refer later, our economies need to continue to commit themselves to strong reforms. thirdly, because we are currently experiencing a period of economic slowdown and if we are not able to take advantage of the introduction of the euro, giving a boost to economic reforms, we will lose an opportunity for recovery for our economies which is undoubtedly very important. the third point to be made is that we are about to complete an operation of undoubtedly extraordinary scope, which we can call enlargement, enlargement or whatever we like; but which, in the end, is the great political operation of the reunification of europe and this is a goal which would in itself fulfil the ambitions of a political generation which is able to look back on european history and which is concerned with preventing and rationally organizing our future. finally, we are aware that we must make institutional reform, and to that end we have proposed the convention and an intergovernmental conference. all of these ambitions present us with a decisive opportunity. i would like to convey to this european parliament the commitment of the spanish presidency to share our ambition and, at the same time, to work consistently to achieve our objectives more effectively. that is why we have set out some priorities which, in the light of what the honourable members have said, i should like to mention very briefly. firstly, the fight against terrorism is no longer a problem of some but of all, to which some may devote more effort, but it is the responsibility of all. i certainly appreciate, as i have said, the work and efforts of the european parliament in this respect. we must certainly consider the fight against terrorism not only in itself but also in relation to the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice and the commitments of tampere which are part of that reality of a more integrated europe which we wish to build for the future. the european union has a duty to help the victims of terrorism. it's true, you know. the question is whether the european union has generally been able to rise to the occasion at this historic moment. i think that the european arrest and surrender order - which is supported by the 15 member states of the union - the fight against the financing of terrorist organisations and the drawing up of a list of groups of organisations and individuals who support terrorism are extraordinary steps. i hope and hope that at its meeting on 5 february the european parliament will also take a definitive step in this direction. how do you do that? we must do so from the standpoint of the rule of law. the honourable members are quite right when they say that the rule of law and our freedoms must be fully guaranteed. and it is true, and it is right that we should not forget at that time that this is what democracies guarantee and that this is precisely what those who practise or support terrorism want to ruin and put an end to. (applause) the maintenance of democracy based on the rule of law is undoubtedly our best guarantee. there can be no middle ground in the fight against terrorism, because there is no middle ground between life and death, between legality and illegality, between respect for the law and complicity with terrorism. what we have is a clear defence, when it is necessary from an international point of view through the international coalition, and when it is necessary with the internal commitment or international cooperation of all, so that our freedoms and our rule of law win. and to achieve this we must develop operatively the questions of security, intelligence, cooperation between forces, joint investigation teams and also common judicial issues which are part of the european integration process in a decisive way. and if we are consistent in seeing terrorism as one of the greatest threats to our civilization at the moment, we will have to introduce terrorism as an objective in the definition of the european union's security and defence policy. i think this is a very important aspect and deserves to be dealt with as a very special point, at least in two chapters of relations which are very relevant for the european union: one, with the united states, with which we also have to talk about criminal law. of course, we respect our extraditions and we remain firmly opposed to the death penalty, or in favour of the legality of the courts and all the trials that can be made on any person. but we need to talk about it. and we must also talk about drawing some conclusions from some of the concerns of the honourable members about the meaning of cooperation in the fight against terrorism with russia.
- i'm sorry to interrupt you, mr prime minister. i must urge you to sit down in silence. i would ask the bailiffs to invite members who are having conversations to sit down or leave the chamber. (applause) we cannot work under conditions that are intolerable for a parliament in such circumstances.
acting president of the council. - mr president, i would like to say that in this context we can make progress in setting up the international criminal court and in improving the instruments of international legal certainty. but in this chapter of the fight against terrorism i would like to end by saying one thing clearly: let us never forget - i know that the vast majority of this house do not forget - the moral lesson of the victims and let us never forget what our fundamental obligations are. not condemning terrorism and talking about dialogue, supporting terrorism and talking about dialogue, killing and talking about dialogue is not only wrong but also an insult to common sense and to the memory of those who have given their lives or put their lives at risk precisely for defending human rights, freedoms, the rule of law and democracies, especially in certain countries. a process which must be maintained and continued - we can achieve the ambition of the lisbon strategy, which is a europe of full employment, more competitive and with more possibilities to look at our future prospects in the world from the point of view of welfare. obviously, that's what we have to do. that is why linking the introduction of the euro to the process of economic reform and placing that on the horizon of the barcelona european council is absolutely vital for europe. i will only briefly remind the honourable members of a few facts. during the 1990s the united states of america grew every year except one above 3%. during the 1990s, the european union grew by less than 3% in all but one year. as i said in my speech, the european union has lost six points of income to the united states. as i have said, the capacity for technological innovation in the united states and european investment in north america, which have found in that country more conditions than in european countries, has caused a profound crisis effect in the european economies. i think we would be making a mistake if we did not realise that there are structural factors, in addition to those of the current economic crisis, which are impinging on our attention. that is why barcelona, at this moment, once the euro has been introduced, is an absolutely fundamental challenge. what's the point? to make the goal of full employment possible. if i may say so, i am one of those who still believe that the best social policy, the best policy of solidarity and also the policy of common sense is that which creates jobs and stimulates economic growth and which therefore makes societies prosper and more just, more supportive and more equitable. (laughter) that's exactly what this is about. that's why we're talking about transportation, energy, the financial plan. i hope that the commission and parliament can actually resolve their last differences and establish the financial action plan. that's why we talk about education, about jobs. that is the way to work towards a more competitive and progressive europe. and if we do not - and i want to give you my own impression - there will be an economic recovery in the united states which will once again give europe a competitive advantage in terms of employment and the economy. and that should not be confused with what it means to not maintain or question the european social model. the only way we can preserve the european social model is to make it sustainable, viable and financially viable, and that is done with growth and employment, which are the recipes, without a doubt, that we must support. - the agenda calls for the debate on the introduction of the euro, which has been in our pockets for a few weeks now and is the realization of a long-cherished dream within the european community. it is a magnificent tribute to the capabilities of the european central bank and the european system of central banks, a magnificent tribute to the banking, financial and commercial system and the retail system and, above all, a magnificent tribute to the european citizens, who have accepted it with such rapidity that it has now virtually replaced the currencies of the member states concerned.
the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been involved in the negotiations on the euro for a number of years. the operations for the introduction of the euro in these first two weeks have worked out extraordinarily well. our most optimistic forecasts have been overwhelmed. europeans have shown enthusiasm and responsibility, and all those involved in the change have shown dedication and rigour. the introduction of the euro on 1 january 2002 is the culmination of a project we have been working on for many years. our fellow citizens feel that the construction of europe is moving slowly. in historical perspective, however, it is perceived as moving forward at great speed. it took the member states ten centuries to achieve monetary unification in their territories and the community achieved it in just over 40 years. i would like to begin by paying tribute to the men and women who have made this project a success. there are many of them, and some of them were mentioned this morning. i will not repeat their names, which are on everyone's minds, but the project - if i may say so - has not only fathers but also mothers, and i would like to single them out in one particular person: christa randzio-plath, who personifies the involvement and commitment of this parliament and its committee on economic and monetary affairs to the euro. (applause) but it would be unfair not to mention two other members: karl von wogau, who in his role as chairman of the committee on economic and monetary affairs also played a relevant role, and the former president of the european commission, jacques santer. i would also like to make a reference to my predecessor, yves-thibault de silguy, who played a key role in the previous period. we have worked together with parliament effectively and i hope we can continue to do so to take further steps in the task before us. i would therefore like to say that the introduction of euro coins and banknotes is not just the culmination of a project. it is also the beginning of a new era in the history of european construction. the physical reality of the euro offers us the opportunity to make further progress in our integration process. i shall refer to that later. i want to focus now on the most decisive aspects of these first days of change. first of all, i would like to point out the enthusiasm of the europeans for their new currency. it was, without a doubt, an essential factor in the success of the operation. european citizens have quickly integrated it into their daily lives. by 1 january, the sale of coin kits had already been a success. from 1 january, consumers began to use the notes en masse. atm withdrawals have been higher than expected since the early days. bank counters were so crowded during the first week of january that in some countries the volume of withdrawals or exchanges at the counters was greater than the volume of transactions at atms. another indicator of the success of the single currency among citizens has been the rapid advance of payment in euro. it rose to 20% on 2 january, the first working day. today - and this is less than nine days apart - nine out of ten payments are made in euro. this is a success in that more than 90% of transactions are carried out in euro within two weeks. the second comment on the adaptation of atms is that it has also been rapid and has taken place throughout the euro area. for two years now, the commission and the european central bank have been asking banks to change their plans and adapt atms almost immediately. this action has been a success. on average, 80% of atms were adapted on 1 january. the percentage rose to 90% on 2 january and to 97% on 3 january. on 4 january, virtually all cash machines were supplying only euros. a comment on trade: most citizens have sought first of all to get rid of their national currencies and to obtain rebates in euro, thus showing their desire to use the euro exclusively as soon as possible. traders mostly respected the commitment to make returns in euro, which allowed the stocks of old coins to be drained quickly. the acceleration of euro payments coupled with the exceptional measures taken by most merchants prevented long queues at shops. saturday, january 5, was the key day in this regard. the test was conclusive and in all participating states the queues were normal. this situation did not change from the following monday, when sales began in many european countries. however, the first week of january was extremely difficult in trade. on the one hand, the pre-feeding of shops was insufficient or encountered some logistical problems in some member states. in addition, many consumers used the purchases to dispose of national high denomination banknotes, which quickly led to problems with the supply of small banknotes in a number of the participating states, a situation which was resolved in one way or another. a comment on the price behaviour, a subject on which the commission has had the pleasure of drawing the attention of the member states and all the actors of change in the months before 1 january. i can tell you that, according to the reports which have been sent to us by the responsible national authorities, there is no significant upward change in the prices of goods and services as a result of the changeover to the euro, save for a few isolated incidents. in some cases, moreover, there have been downward adjustments, although it is fair to say that in other cases and on a specific occasion, the opposite may have been the case. overall, there is no sign of a significant rise in prices and we do not therefore expect a negative reflection in inflation in january. in conclusion, the commission considers that the balance of these first two weeks is very positive. the largest swap operation in history has gone off virtually without a hitch. it is a huge victory for the union and a demonstration of the high quality of meticulous preparations. the efforts of all the actors involved in the euro transition - the eurosystem, national governments, the commission, private operators and all citizens - have borne fruit. the success of the introduction of the euro is the end of a chapter - as i said earlier - but not the end of the work. we must now reap the fruits of this success by strengthening and deepening the coordination of economic policies and by making the structural reforms necessary to increase growth and employment in our union. the same energy and ambition that guided the creation of the euro must now be applied to coordinating economic policies that can boost growth and employment. in the short term, the euro area stability framework has made it possible to provide a balanced and timely response to the economic slowdown we are experiencing. the clear improvement in budget balances has created a margin to cushion the impact of the small deterioration in budget deficits that has occurred as a result of the overall slowdown. in 2002 we expect to be able to resume satisfactory growth, which will contribute to the overall economic recovery. the successful introduction of euro banknotes and coins, removing uncertainties, will help this recovery by boosting consumer and business confidence. in the medium term, the european union set clear objectives in lisbon for strengthening growth potential and job creation. to achieve these objectives it is important to maintain the momentum that will enable us to carry out the necessary reforms to increase the employment rate and productivity. the commission proposes three priority areas for this year: first, employment policies and in particular active labour market policies; second, economic reforms to strengthen competition, integration and investment in network industries; and third, investing in knowledge to increase competitiveness and employment. i shall not dwell further on these points, which were the subject of the president of the commission's remarks yesterday. the increased interdependence of the economies of the member states, and in particular of the euro area, calls for stronger and more effective coordination of economic policies. in this context, i believe that coordination should be strengthened on the basis of a better analysis of the economic situation and policy mix of the euro area: greater openness in the development of consensus on appropriate policies and the provision of information to the member states and the commission on the main economic policy measures that each country is going to adopt in the future, so that the peer review we have at community level can work effectively. progress means meeting our commitments: those of the treaty and those of the stability and growth pact. moving forward also means taking on new challenges. we are going to devote our efforts and work to this as the commission, and we hope to have the cooperation of parliament, which we have always been prepared to give up until now, and with which we hope to continue working in the same efficient and consensual way as in the past.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. i would like to begin by thanking in particular karl von wogau for his 22 years of involvement in this process. we regret that he is leaving us in the committee on economic and monetary affairs, but we know that his good work will continue to help parliament and the process of european integration in the committee on foreign affairs. karl von wogau said, referring to jacques delors, that one cannot fall in love with the euro, and christa randzio-plath said, however, that the people are happy. both issues are probably related to a fundamental question: the euro is the first element of european identity that affects all citizens of the member states of the monetary union. apart from being very important - as was the abolition of frontiers or the internal market, which however only affects goods, only affects citizens who cross the border at a given moment - the euro is also a part of our european identity which we use every day from morning to night, in all the countries of the monetary union and under exactly the same conditions. it is an element which must be highlighted as very positive among our common elements, which have nothing to do, however, with unification, since it is clear that we also have clear differential elements. from now on, the euro will give us coins and notes and a slight increase in economic growth, as a result of the removal of uncertainties. but it is true, and i agree with some of those who have spoken, that the fundamental elements will be derived from our capacity for potential growth or, in other words, to launch the lisbon process more ambitiously than we have done so far. we can disassociate ourselves from the united states, as mr ruffolo wants, we would like. however, experience in 2001 has shown us that being relatively independent in commercial terms does not prevent us from being affected by a crisis in the united states as a result of the channels of transmission of the economic effects arising from the interrelations between companies and financial markets. the exchange rate is going to be the real test of the euro. i have always said that the exchange rate was never an objective of the union's policy. our monetary policy objective is to keep inflation low and we are convinced that a currency with low inflation over the long term is a stable currency, it is a beloved currency, it is a safe-haven currency and it is a currency that will have an important role to play in the economic world. but apart from the economic aspects themselves, what about our institutional structure? is the euro the beginning of economic governance? i believe that we have designed a model in maastricht based on a single monetary policy and coordinated national economic policies. i think that's our model. and we have to work to make the euro a success on that basis. i do not want to prejudge whether we should make more or less progress in the process of political integration. i might perhaps be in the camp of those who are in favour of greater political integration, but i also understand that this is a decision by the quince that will have to be taken in other areas, in other forums and as a result of another debate. i am convinced, however, that we can move forward in the process of greater coordination of economic policies, which in no way means unification of our economic policies, because our situations are different and therefore they must be applied consistently. today, as in so many other times, we sometimes confuse stability pacts with economic policy guidelines. is the stability pact a problem for the economic policy of the union? it is a debate we have had a few times in this house. i would like to reiterate what i have always said: the stability pact is nothing more or less than the necessary element to enable us to have a policy mix between budgetary policy and monetary policy that facilitates a monetary policy of low interest rates. the structural changes in our economies and the drive for growth, the congruence between our national economic policies and the policy as a whole with monetary policy will have to be managed through the broad economic policy guidelines. we have the instruments, we have to perfect them, we have to improve them, but i think the system works. the policy mix will be one of the key elements of the spanish presidency, as the president of ecofin has stressed, and i am sure that we will have occasion to debate this fundamental point in this house. of course, structural reforms, as i said earlier, are still the key to the future. a comment on the enlargements of the euro area. in the pre-in countries we have seen a greater interest in what is happening in our experience in the euro area. i would rather say that the three pre-in meetings have aroused considerable additional interest, reflected in some of the political elements communicated or perceived in recent days. it is true that there are still those who are critical of the euro, and it is true that in the eurosceptic world, given that short-term problems are not raised, what is feared at the moment is what will happen in ten or fifteen years' time. of course, we can't say anything about that. i think it is difficult to manage what will happen in ten or fifteen years, but i am personally convinced that in ten or fifteen years we will have far fewer problems than we have at the moment in that respect. what are the conditions for pre-in countries to enter? exactly the same as everyone else's, no more, no less. the maastricht conditions are met with the additional opt-out to which denmark and the united kingdom are entitled. there will be no change for pre-in or candidate countries. we believe that equal treatment for all the member states of the union is a fundamental principle which we must not under any circumstances correct. a final comment on a minor subject but one which, to some extent, was the one that concerned us today: the practical problems of the introduction of the euro. has commerce played the role of the bankers? i'm not sure. trade has served as an incentive for the rapid adoption of the single currency through the feed-in system. it is true that some practical problems have arisen, but rather from the pressure of some citizens to use commerce as banking, when they have sought to exchange high denominations of national currencies in commerce and not in banks, as should have been expected. are there serious counterfeiting problems? not serious, not less serious. at the moment we have no evidence of counterfeits which could technically be called 'counterfeit euro notes'. there are photocopies. there are scanned euros, but they are very different from the real euro and therefore the kind of concerns that sometimes arise should not exist today. i believe that the euro has a very high safety factor, very different from other national currencies in wide circulation in the world, and that it should give us the guarantee that this type of situation is not going to occur. i also think that some of the statements that have been made about the operation of machines are not correct. there are practical problems. anyone who approaches even toll booths not far from here will see that some tolls do not work with all the currencies of each of the countries of the union. these are practical problems which are being raised, and we should not overestimate them: they are anecdotes within a process of great importance and great complexity. i do not think that the price problems are significant, nor do i think that the price reductions will influence the prices in january, as they have not in the past, since they have never been taken into account. last week, when we spoke to the former president of ecofin, mr reynders, we said that the clear lesson we have learned from this process is that the next time we change our currency we should not do it on 1 january. but since i'm sure this situation will not arise, i think even that experience can be dispensed with. ladies and gentlemen, thank you very much for your enormous cooperation during this period. it has been essential to help the member states to do their job well, to make the public better informed and also to give the commission an incentive to work.

mr president, i too join my colleagues in congratulating you on your re-election as vice-president. i also wish to congratulate the rapporteur and all the draftsmen on their work on what may appear to be a very simple topic but, when you get into the detail and analysis of it, proves extremely difficult. rather than repeating what has been said already, i would like to deal with three particular selection criteria. of course we must have protections in place to ensure that those who are guilty of wrongdoing, fraud, racketeering and of interfering with community assets and finances should be excluded from public contracts. however, i have one concern with regard to the question of a judgment that is not yet final: we are acting as judge and jury in denying somebody a right to be an applicant for a tender without having a final decision or analysis made as to whether that person is guilty of a crime or not. this is something we must be very careful of. in conclusion, it is about time that these directives were brought together, that the texts were clarified and that greater certainty was put into the legislative framework under which people have to operate. but, most importantly of all, it must be seen as a move towards guaranteeing better public services for all people.
mr president, not for the first time in this house i have the opportunity to express concern with regard to the safety of nuclear installations, and in particular those with an established record of poor management, since they put the lives and health of millions of citizens at risk. such is the case with the british government's nuclear installation at sellafield. this is not just my view: the litany of management blunders and serious technical defects is a matter of public record, which has been exposed, despite efforts to keep it secret. it is inconceivable that the british government should set out to justify not only the continuity of sellafield in its present dangerous condition, but also wish to add further to its operations by commissioning the mox processing facility. because of its closer proximity to ireland than to most parts of the british mainland, the irish government has again raised serious objections to the continued operation of this dangerous plant. records in this house will show that on a previous occasion i called on the commission to exercise its powers under article 35 of the euratom treaty in relation to verification of nuclear installations at sellafield. in reply to queries from my political group, the commission recently confirmed that the last time it undertook such an audit was in 1993, nearly a decade ago. bearing in mind the number of times that this matter has been raised in the house by all political groups, how can the commission possibly justify its silence and inactivity on a matter of such serious public concern? i call on the commission to immediately initiate an examination of all activities on the cumbria site and ask the commissioner to give assurance to that effect in his reply.
mr president, it is obvious to everyone that the fishing industry needs fish. without fish there can be no fishing industry. one of the biggest problems with the common fisheries policy over the past 20 years has been that several objectives have not been prioritised. this has created conflicts. the only way to ensure that the fishing industry has any kind of future is to put conservation at the top of the agenda. this is a prerequisite for the industry, not an obstacle that has to be overcome. unless conservation is the number one priority, compromises with other objectives of the common fisheries policy, such as economic ones, will always lead to further erosion of stocks. we have tabled an amendment which would set as a prime objective the need to ensure that fish stocks and other marine species remain abundant. both the fishing industry and the committee on fisheries claim that they agree with the need to conserve stocks and protect the marine environment. the recent cuts in quotas for several stocks in the eu last month provide ample illustration of the need to make conservation of stocks the main priority.

set up by the marine minister and included stakeholders. it is vitally important that they should be included at all times. no common fisheries policy or other policy can be successful unless the stakeholders play an important role in it. no doubt the discussions this year in council will be difficult. important decisions have to be made in key areas, particularly the social and economic dimension of the common fisheries policy. it is my view, and one that i know is shared by many members representing coastal regions, that the green paper does not address these aspects adequately. it takes little account of the importance of the fisheries sector in coastal regions where there is no alternative source of employment, be they in ireland or elsewhere in the community. there must be integration; with my country in mind, consideration must be given to fisheries policy, regional development policy, rural development policy and objective 1 areas. i welcome the frankness with which the commission has spelled out the current state of european fisheries and many proposed changes, if implemented, would help to solve some of the current difficulties. a number of additional critical changes must be made to further strengthen the common fisheries policy. greater involvement of fishermen and stakeholders in the management process is long overdue. involving fishermen will do a great deal to improve the credibility of any future policy. genuine regionalisation of management and control will greatly benefit the sector. i would urge the commission to underpin the decentralisation process by creating a europe-wide network of regional advisory committees. unless practical and feasible changes are made to the control system, fisheries policy will not have the confidence of fishermen and will certainly fail. my country has benefited greatly from membership of the european union over the years. however, the fishing industry has paid too high a price in having to share its abundant fishing grounds off the west coast of ireland with greedy neighbours. if there is a depletion of stocks it is not irish fishermen but some greedy neighbours in other member states who are responsible for it.
mr president, as regards the miguélez ramos report the verts/ale group considers that the conservation of fish stocks and the protection of the marine environment are of fundamental importance to the common fisheries policy. the alternative will inevitably be overfishing and problems for the industry in the long term. given the importance of conservation this report falls very far short of what is really required. among other things, it seeks to relieve the fishing sector of responsibility for depleted fish stocks by saying that it is the fault of pollution, habitat destruction etc. while these factors play a role, there is no doubt whatsoever that the major cause of depleted fish stocks is the excessive amount of fishing carried out by the fishing fleets of the european union. it is time we stopped this state of denial and faced reality. we also object to the calls for alternatives to the decommissioning of fishing vessels, which is the single most important step towards allowing stocks to recover. we also need to look at the fact that vessels are being transported to other parts of the world, thereby simply passing the problem on. considering the desperate need to incorporate the concept of environmental protection into fisheries, this report falls far short of what is required. the verts/ale group cannot support it.

commission. - mr president, i shall quickly make a few comments which the debate has suggested to me. first of all, i would like to thank parliament for the initiative of a debate on the annual activities of the european investment bank. you are aware, and some of you have pointed out, of the bank's important role in channelling savings into investment in key sectors within the european union and also outside it. they have highlighted the bank's fundamental objective of contributing to our aims in close cooperation with the commission. the bank has already launched the lisbon initiatives. the 2000 initiative is now fully operational and is continuing to increase its involvement in financing small and medium-sized enterprises. president maystadt will make some further comments, but i would like to congratulate the bank on the good work being done in this particular sector and, above all, on the transformation that has occurred by giving greater attention to venture capital. in this sense, the european investment fund is becoming an important community venture capital institution as a complement to the market forces governing supply and demand. some of you have suggested the need for the bank to pay more attention to environmental elements. i think we must be aware that each institution has its own role and the bank's role is basically financial. environmental issues are of course fundamental, but each institution must play its part. i would like to make two additional comments. the first concerns the bank's expansion into other areas. i think that point 7 of the report mentions this matter. however, we must not forget the expansion of the bank's activities in recent years. it is sufficient to recall that croatia was included in the ceec allocation in 2000 and the special option for customs union with turkey was included in 2000, and the federal republic of yugoslavia was included in november 2001. some of you have expressed concern about the prudential supervision of the bank's activities. it is true that the statute of the european central bank allows for this, but it is also true that the european central bank has no authority. even if it did, we would have to ask ourselves whether the idea of supervision of the european investment bank is consistent. the european investment bank is not a commercial bank, it is a multilateral bank owned by the member states and established as a community institution by the treaty. i therefore think that it is not right for another community institution to supervise one community institution in addition to the other. the bank's activities are also closely linked to the activities of the european investment bank, which is the main source of finance for the bank. the court of auditors is already carrying out audits of its activities when they involve european union funding. so i think this issue deserves a deeper analysis. we do not think that there is a need to create other supervisory functions or institutions. finally, on the subject of barcelona and the possibility of financing cooperation with the mediterranean, raised by mr gasòliba, mr maystadt will comment on the activities of the european investment bank. i will simply say that the commission is working on the laeken mandate to have a report as soon as possible. we would all like it to be finished for barcelona, but logically we will have to follow the normal procedures.
president of the eib. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me begin by saying how honoured i am to have the opportunity for the second time to answer questions from your house, as mrs van den burg has requested; this could become an annual tradition. even if the european investment bank is not formally accountable to the european parliament, it seems to me normal in a democracy that all public institutions, including financial institutions, should answer questions and take account of the priorities expressed by the elected representatives of the citizens. i shall therefore be very happy to try to answer the questions that have been put, although i am aware that in five minutes we cannot of course give a thorough answer; but we will have the opportunity to continue the dialogue, particularly in the economic and monetary affairs committee, under the dynamic chairmanship of mrs randzio-plath and on the basis of the excellent report by mr olle schmidt. i would like to limit myself today to giving some answers to four categories of questions. first, those relating to the eib's activities; secondly, the questions of control; thirdly, the questions of information policy and transparency; finally, fourthly, i would like to say a word about equal opportunities, an area which mrs randzio-plath is particularly keen on. first, as regards the eib's activities, mrs randzio-plath rightly pointed out that regional development remained the european investment bank's primary mission. in collaboration with commissioner barnier's services, we have developed a set of indicators and are working to assess more systematically the impact of the projects we finance on regional development. the growing importance of the eib's activities in the applicant countries was also mentioned - and the rapporteur, mr olle schmidt, rightly emphasized this point. enlargement is a huge challenge for all of us, for those who are already in the european union and for those who are about to join it. it is clear that the european investment bank must step up its operations in these countries to help them to meet the conditions of accession as quickly as possible. to date, the eib has already a portfolio of over eur 16 billion, mainly in infrastructure (transport, communication and energy infrastructure) but also in the environment and, increasingly, directly in the promotion of the private sector. the environment, another area which has particularly attracted the attention of your rapporteur and of several speakers, i think must be approached from two angles. the first is the volume of environmental projects we finance, projects which directly contribute to the protection or improvement of the environment. i can give you a preview of the figures i will make public next thursday. last year, we funded environmental projects for six billion in the form of individual loans and two billion through what we call global loans, which are loans to intermediary banks, which in turn lend to local communities. so six billion euros for environmental projects in the european union and half a billion in the candidate countries. this means that we are now allocating about one fifth of our lending directly to environmental improvement. we hope to gradually increase this proportion to a quarter of our total lending. this is the first aspect, but there is obviously a second aspect, and your committee has rightly paid a great deal of attention to it: that is that other projects, those not directly aimed at improving the environment, must also take account of the impact on the environment. we must therefore put in place the means to assess more systematically the impact of these projects on the environment. that is why, following a suggestion made in the report of the previous year by mr lipietz, we have changed our internal organisation and have set up an environmental unit within the project management, whose task is precisely to verify that environmental aspects have been taken into account in the analysis of projects. and we intend to improve our methods in this respect. the mediterranean is another area of eib activity. without going into details, i simply want to say that we have noted the objectives announced by the spanish presidency and that the eib is at the disposal of the council and the commission if it is felt, given the importance of our activities in the mediterranean, that the eib can make a contribution to the achievement of these objectives. finally, i would like to echo the concern expressed by many of you, in particular mr olle schmidt and mrs randzio-plath, with regard to support for small and mediumsized enterprises. i can say that we are continuing to do so not only through global loans but also through the european investment fund, which last year provided €800 million of venture capital to small and mediumsized enterprises. as regards control, it may be recalled, as commissioner solbes has pointed out, that the eib is already controlled in various ways. i would simply say that we are trying to apply the prudential rules of the banking sector. if it were considered desirable to add the control of a body specialised in banking supervision, the eib would obviously have no objection. we would be very happy if an external authority specialised in banking supervision would check that we are applying prudential rules correctly. as regards information and transparency policy, firstly, we now publish all our strategy papers; secondly, we publish a statement of our evaluation methods; third, we publish, with a few exceptions, the list of all projects under consideration so that the public can react and comment; fourthly, we are now publishing in full all the evaluation reports produced by the independent ex post evaluation unit which was set up a few years ago. a word to finish on equal opportunities. on several occasions mrs randzio-plath had drawn our attention to an undeniable imbalance in the bank's senior management. there's always only one woman on the executive committee. i regret that, but that is a matter for the member states. as far as the actual framework is concerned, i can tell you that we have just decided, last year, to appoint four women to the senior management, which is therefore a start of rebalancing. in conclusion, mr president, we want to ensure that the eib remains an institution at the service of the european union, which necessarily implies closer cooperation with the commission and continued dialogue with parliament.

commission. – mr president, both mr goebbels and mrs randzio-plath are well aware of the answer. they know that when the comitology procedure was decided on in mid-1999, the commission issued a unilateral declaration, which has become known as the "aerosol" declaration, which was given in exchange for something called the contre-filet, another procedural device. the commission and council accepted that the contre-filet procedure would disappear, and in its place came this unilateral declaration, which referred to a much earlier case in connection with veterinary matters. that is why in the unilateral commission declaration mention was made of particularly sensitive cases, because the veterinary situation back in the early 1980s concerned human health. the declaration stated – again by way of replacement of the contre-filet procedure – that the commission would not go against a majority opinion of the council, thereby basically maintaining the status quo, while bringing things into sharper focus. therefore the stockholm resolution adds nothing beyond what was already in place under the comitology procedure, because the same words – the ipsissima verba – that appeared in the declaration by the commission in june 1991 reappear in the resolution of the european council. so matters have basically remained the same. if mr goebbels is asking on which article this is based, then the reply is on articles 202 and 211.

high representative for the common foreign and security policy. – mr president, i will try to be brief and to start by thanking you all – those who are here, those who have left – very much for your support for our efforts to bring peace to an area which, as i said at the very beginning, is geographically close to us and also very close to our hearts, minds and values. i would stress once again that the difficulty of the problem is not the absence of a mechanism to provide a solution to the crisis. we already have the mitchell report, which contains the steps to be followed, and it has been accepted by both sides. the problem is not that we do not have rails on which the train should be travelling but that we have not been able to get the train out of the station. the train cannot leave the station until the requirement of a seven-day period of complete calm has been fulfilled. but what happens? when you set seven days of complete calm as a precondition, you can always find somebody who is not for the peace process and who, at the last minute, can engineer a catastrophe. therefore, you are back to square one. that has happened on a couple of occasions. this manner of doing things hands the initiative to the most radical people and takes it away from the moderates. that is the problem we have at this point in time. let us hope that the modest beginnings of conversations – i would not call them negotiations between the two sides – held right now, yesterday, tomorrow, maybe the day after tomorrow, maybe at the beginning of the week, will produce at least a change in the disappeared, but it has been reduced. the same thing has happened on the other side. frustration has created a sentiment that the peace camp cannot bring about peace in a reasonable period of time. that lack of trust and of confidence between both sides was not present before. i remember very well the relative friendship in oslo between arafat and peres and between rabin and arafat. that has disappeared. we have to do something to reconstruct society vis-à-vis society and we, as europeans, have a tremendous amount of work to do there, to bring these societies together, because they will have to live together. whatever we can do through this parliament, through the institutions, through the ngos, we must do. i would like to tell you two little anecdotes, one from a very good friend of mine who was in the peace camp in jerusalem. the other day he told me that he would not dare send his daughter and his son to school in the same bus. that is a dramatic and profound change in the heart and in the mind of somebody who would otherwise be a fighter for peace. on the other side, on the palestinian side, you go to a hospital, you talk to a paediatrician and he tells you how a little boy has been killed. this is a terrible blow to trust and confidence among people. therefore we have to work also with societies. we have to engage societies, universities, schools, doctors, etc. to impress upon them that they have to live together and that europe will be behind that sentiment of reconciliation. that is something we have to do. i will conclude by recalling a beautiful phrase from yitzhak rabin who, without any doubt, was the architect of the oslo process, together with shimon peres. he used to say something that is still valid. we have to fight against terrorism, as if there were no negotiations, and we have to negotiate as if there were no terrorism. that is the approach we have to rally around today. it is necessary to continue the negotiations, to continue talking, to continue moving the political scene – the centre of gravity has to be politics. until they put politics at the centre of gravity, it will be very difficult to move the process forwards. we can be proud of what we as europeans are doing. we do not have the capacity to solve the problem, but we can move in the right direction as soon as possible and aim for peace. this is not a question only of values. it is part of our history, no doubt about that, but it is also part of our future, the future of this european union, of the countries in an enlarged european union and of the countries of the mediterranean and the middle east, which are part of our family. madam president, i have no doubt that the existing arrangements for cooperation in the area of vat fraud are inadequate in the context of the evolved single market. vat fraud costs the eu and its member states several hundred million euro each year. although measures have been taken over the last few years to come to terms with it, vat fraud is still a considerable problem today. i agree that the best way to tackle this ever-increasing fraud is to have close administrative cooperation between member states. by allowing direct contacts between local offices, the fight against fraud will become less bureaucratic and more effective. however, let me sound a note of caution in relation to the efforts inherent in this commission proposal to base this measure on article 95 of the treaty. article 95 specifically states that it may not be used for fiscal provisions. the commission's view is that this proposal is merely about administrative cooperation and that it does not relate to actual tax collection or tax measures. with respect, i do not agree – my country does not agree – that by stealth the present position should be eroded. i do not think that scac – the existing administrative committee in the tax area – should have more of these functions assigned to it. it is the thin end of the wedge. this proposal relates to fiscal instruments which member states use and it should certainly be adopted, but it should be adopted with the correct legal basis, which is article 93, providing for unanimity of voting at council level. the regulation that this proposal aims to replace is based upon article 93, and quite simply this proposal should be also. mrs kauppi has referred to the concerns regarding the legal basis in her attached explanatory memorandum. in the past where conflicts have arisen in relation to the legal basis, the council has always rejected the commission's view and has changed the legal basis to article 93 or 94. as pointed out by my colleague, it did this most recently on the proposal for a directive on the mutual assistance for the recovery of claims. the commission has decided to take the council to the court of justice in this matter and ireland will be joining the action on the side of the council. while i welcome the substance of what this proposal aims to do, for the reasons i have outlined in relation to the legal basis, i and my irish colleagues will be voting against the report.

mr president, on a point of order, at yesterday's vote on the watson report on the european arrest warrant, there was confusion on the numbering of amendments. you will see from today's report that what was amendment no 3 has been penned over as 4. even in the official report it is not quite clear on some of the pages. amendment no 3, which dealt with the legal concept of habeas corpus, had been circulated to us in the irish delegation of the ppe-de group. we knew that the amendment would be defeated but nonetheless i and a number of my colleagues decided to vote for it because of our firm belief in the principle of habeas corpus and that it is a good one. we wish to indicate our vote that this legal remedy should have a place in european law. looking at the record of yesterday's proceedings, amendment no 3, which we received yesterday morning, became amendment no 4 at the vote. our decision to vote for the principle of habeas corpus was negated by this change in the numbering of the amendment. i wish it to be recorded here that our vote was intended to support the principle of habeas corpus.
madam president, parliament must deplore in no uncertain terms president bush's military order permitting the secret trial of prisoners in guantanamo bay by a military commission, which may adopt its own rules of evidence, judge and pass sentence. this is outside american jurisdiction. as has been pointed out by other speakers, the only american al-qa'ida member so far captured is to be tried in a court in virginia with full legal representation! this military order breaches all provisions for a fair trial as guaranteed by the international covenant on civil and political rights, to which the us is a party, such as the presumption of innocence, choice of counsel, impartial and timely hearing, and the right of appeal to a higher court. the us government has introduced a category of unlawful combatants, an unknown term in international law, while refusing to grant the suspected al-qa'ida fighters and taliban troops captured in afghanistan the status of prisoners of war. these concerns have been highlighted by renowned lawyers throughout the world, who contest the legitimacy of forcibly taking those now detained in cuba out of afghanistan without any extradition order, as well as their status as combatants, and calls for them to be treated as ordinary criminal suspects with all associated rights. we must also take into account the fact that some of these people, who are merely suspected of being al-qa'ida supporters, have been deported from bosnia to guantanamo bay. the reports of ill-treatment of prisoners is absolutely shocking. nobody can deny what we have seen for ourselves on television, including reports that they have been shackled, hooded, sedated during transfer and their beards forcibly shaved. this sensory deprivation is something that was criticised in ireland in the past in relation to prisoners in northern ireland – even by our own government. yet everyone is turning a blind eye to what is happening in guantanamo bay. we have to speak out in the interests of international justice, respect for human rights and respect for the rule of law. america should abide by those international covenants as well. parliament would do very well to speak out and send a very clear message that we do not agree with the policy they have adopted.
