counsel. - mr president, the honourable member, i am sorry, but the speed of time and the fact that you are handling it so well have prevented me from replying. i'll do it with pleasure. first of all, i have to tell you that our information does not match the information that the honourable member has handled. i have information, which i do not need to declassify at this stage, which ensures that depleted uranium munitions have not been used in afghanistan and this has also been indicated by units with nbq detection equipment in afghanistan itself, within the isaf. secondly, as regards your question about the protective measures taken: apart from being equipped with nbq detection equipment, the units that the various countries have deployed, either in kabul or - as in the spanish case - also in bagran, the medical units observe very precise rules of conduct and carry out a constant monitoring, both of this type of possible injury to health, as well as of risks that could arise from the internal situation of the country itself or from some resistance. thirdly, i should remind you that the belgian presidency has started a study, which is being continued by the spanish presidency, on the most appropriate measures to ensure the health of the troops. and finally, mr president, i have to tell you that the scientific committee which studied the problem in spain - and they were independent scientists of a university and clinical nature - guaranteed that no direct link could be established between the use of depleted uranium and certain tumours which had been observed in some of the combatants.

- the next item is the statements by the high representative for the common foreign and security policy, mr solana, on the situation in the middle east. before inviting mr solana to open the debate, i would like to formally thank, on behalf of this house, mr solana and commissioner patten, who have both made special arrangements to be able to be present for today's debate, and the spanish presidency.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i think that today's debate is one of the most difficult i have ever been involved in and we must approach it with the usual political sense and responsibility. the problem we are dealing with this evening, which is close to home, is important, it has to do with our values, it has to do also with our security and our interests. i therefore believe that it is the duty of all of us, of all the institutions that are gathered here this evening, to try to find ways of solving the problem. we have to be part of the solution, not part of the problem. ladies and gentlemen, the present situation in the middle east is undoubtedly dramatic, tragic and dangerous, because of the consequences it has not only for the people who live there, but for the whole region. and we must face the harsh reality with the sense of responsibility that we europeans have always had. i honestly think we've reached the limit of acceptable. the facts that are developing on the ground are not leading anywhere, are not leading to the solution of the problem and are only leading to hopelessness and misery. i therefore believe that we must act on all possible fronts, not only to solve the immediate crisis we are experiencing at this hour, but also to try to solve its causes. mr president, i shall briefly reflect on these three points: i believe that there is no doubt that all of us in this parliament and all the citizens of europe have condemned, condemn and will condemn terrorism. i think we can therefore say, with the frankness we have always had with our friends in israel, that we will condemn terrorism a thousand times, as many times as necessary, and that we have nothing to do with it. with equal frankness, we can tell our friends that we disagree with the activity they are developing. (applause) we believe that without reservation, because of friendship, because of the openness that allows us to see how we have spoken in other moments, today we have the obligation to say what we think. say it with the same simplicity, but with the same sense of responsibility. mr president, i sincerely believe that the military response being given by the state of israel and which we are witnessing in the occupied territories is intolerable and we must stop it immediately. it must be stopped immediately, ladies and gentlemen, because it leads to nothing and it does not lead to the solution of the problem which, as has been said, is to end terrorism. (applause) ladies and gentlemen, we already know the enormous suffering of the civilian population, who do not want to participate in a war, who want to live in peace, together, one country with another. denying water and electricity to entire populations is either an issue or an unjustifiable action for security reasons. there are certainly violations of humanitarian law, and even of military law, which cannot go unmentioned. the government of israel, mr president, has the right and the obligation to protect its citizens. what we are witnessing, however, in our judgment, is not going to contribute to that end. this is not just an anti-terrorist operation, but it is dangerously headed for war, and i say this with great sadness. ladies and gentlemen, we have at least two resolutions from the united nations security council which are clear, very clear, which do not allow for different interpretations, and the unambiguous interpretation of those resolutions is that the situation we are experiencing at the moment with regard to the territories must end. and these resolutions, clearly, must be implemented immediately. the military operation must be stopped, not in stages, not city by city, but once and for all, and immediately. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, international law must be respected by all, and this statement allows me to say that it must also be respected by the citizens who live on the other side of the northern border. israel must fulfil its obligations to the united nations security council. we also denounce the attacks on israeli citizens from the northern border of israel. i repeat: we will always be in favour of respect for international law. mr. president, these military actions are not the right ones, if you want to end terrorism. we can ask ourselves all sorts of questions about these operations and whether, when they are over, the citizens of israel will be better protected or not, whether they will be strengthened in their security or not, whether this operation will combat terrorism and whether it will decrease. unfortunately, ladies and gentlemen, we believe that this is not going to be the case, that these operations are not going to lead to that end, and therefore, honestly, as the united nations security council has done, we ask that they be terminated. ladies and gentlemen, this afternoon i would like to stress that one of the consequences of this military operation is the destruction of the palestinian authority. we are extremely concerned about this, because if a ceasefire is to be reached, ladies and gentlemen, with whom will it be reached if we do not have people and institutions on the other side, the palestinian authority, with whom to talk. i have been able to do so on many occasions, in the numerous trips i have made in recent months - as the honourable members know - with the palestinian authority security officials. we worked with these people, israel and also the us authorities. today some of them have lost their credibility and all means of action. therefore, ladies and gentlemen, we must make an effort to recover the palestinian authority. progress towards peace, after this military operation, is inconceivable with a shattered palestinian authority. we must therefore, ladies and gentlemen, from this parliament, from the european union, make a more serious and forceful call for the palestinian authority to be respected. ladies and gentlemen, we believe that the tenet plan, the security plan, should be supported, but which person or persons on the palestinian side are going to make this negotiation of the tenet plan effective? unfortunately we do not know, and therefore we must continue to insist that the palestinian authority regain the value, responsibility and meaning of the oslo agreements. that said, ladies and gentlemen, we must continue to act on all fronts. i sincerely believe, and i will say this a thousand times, that president arafat must be free to move about and to meet with his collaborators. mr president, there is no military solution to the conflict between israel and the palestinian people. unless the root causes of conflict are addressed, no peaceful solution can be secured between the opposing sides. prime minister sharon has offered an uncompromising war on terror, but he has not offered any diplomatic solution to avoid the escalating spiral of violence and brutality. the tenet and mitchell proposals are still on the table and, together with the recent proposals from the saudi arabian government, they too provide a basis for the resumption of peace talks if there is a full compliance with the recent un resolutions by the israeli government. i firmly believe that yasser arafat is the political leader that the israeli government must be negotiating with at this time, and that seeking to topple the palestinian authority is a recipe for long-term instability and will only intensify the hatreds between the palestinian and israeli people as well as between israelis and other arab countries in the middle east. the two sides will not be brought together unless there is an immediate and serious third-party mediation, and the us government must be seen to be vigorously involved in this process in a firm and meaningful way, as must the european union. consideration must be given to suspending the eu-israel euro-mediterranean association agreements which exist between the union and israel if israel's military attacks on the palestinian people continue. i would like to conclude by saying that i condemn the recent and ongoing violence in the middle east and any acts of anti-semitism which have been and are being committed in europe or elsewhere in the world.

(applause) and i think it is essential that, for the first time, there should be a public and joint statement of this nature by the secretary-general of the united nations, by the european union, by the russian federation and by the united states. and i think we have to be the europeans behind that proposal and behind that kind of statement. secondly, i believe that everything must be done to ensure that the major players who will be meeting tomorrow do not allow the palestinian authority to deteriorate further. we must do everything possible to restore the palestinian authority to its capacity. it is a great contradiction - as has already been pointed out - to ask the palestinian authority to sign a ceasefire agreement, to arrest terrorists who are free in some part of palestine, when it does not have the means to do so. this morning you saw on the news that israeli forces have withdrawn from a city. as they left that city, they bombed and destroyed the headquarters of the palestinian authority. at the same time, it is highly contradictory to ask tomorrow that the palestinian authority be the leader in finding the solution to a ceasefire. i think it is essential that this message should be conveyed, and that it should be rigorous and clear. it is a message that must be understood and clearly expressed so that everyone understands it and so that our friends in israel also understand it. we all have many friends in israel who share this reflection. the corollary of this reflection is that the international community must be prepared to deploy on the ground. it's something i'm saying, for the first time, with force. i think we have to start thinking about it seriously. but that's not gonna happen in 24 hours, it's not gonna happen without some warrant. when it was said that europeans should deploy military or police forces - or i do not know how - over the territories, it is clear that this will require some mandate to do so. and that is what we have to work on: to ensure that the next security council resolution allows, once the necessary conditions have been created, the possibility of an international presence on the ground. i think that is a reasonable measure which the european union can support but which it must support jointly with others, especially the united states and the russian federation. that's what we should do. thirdly, we must send a clear signal tomorrow - not just the europeans, but collectively all the major players - that there must be a political perspective. and this perspective does not have to be invented, it has already been invented: it consists of two states, with secure borders (one of which is the palestinian state, which must have the borders delimited in accordance with the security council resolutions, that is, the borders fixed in 1967) and which have the capacity to live together. that's the end goal. how can we reach that goal? there is the difficult question we have been working on for many months. it is possible that the only way forward is the tenet plan and then the mitchell plan, which i know very well because i drafted it with senator mitchell. i am beginning to have some doubts - and that is where my deep pessimism comes from - that the tenet plan, followed by the mitchell plan and followed by a negotiation - which i do not know when it will take place - will be the ideal formula. if we do not have a partner on the palestinian side, it will be very difficult - as i said before - to achieve a successful outcome through this gradual process. that is my concern and my pessimism. i'm not going to pull out of my pocket some miracle solution and it would be naive, stupid and unworthy of you to expect it. however, if we are to find a solution, i said on one occasion that we need a mitchell express plan, a fast mitchell plan, not for the times for which it was conceived, but a much faster mitchell programme, which will bring us as quickly as possible to the final agreement. finally, i think it would be essential for us to ask that the beirut resolution - which has not been read properly and which must be read, because some of its points are very important - should also become a un security council resolution; that this commitment, that this hand extended by the arab world to the security of israel should also become a security council resolution. i think it would be an additional element in restoring the trust between the parties, a trust which, unfortunately, they do not have now. (applause) finally, a personal reflection: i know that many of you have suffered a lot. i have seen some people who have suffered especially, some of them even being expelled from the region. i can tell you that i understand your feelings as i also understand the feelings of the palestinians and the israelis. i have seen many palestinians die and i have seen many palestinians suffer and i have also seen families of my old friends from the israeli peace camp who do not take their children on the same bus to school and who separate their children in two for fear of dying from a terrorist act. we have to understand all this. if we don't understand both things, we can never solve the problem. so we understand the problem to the core so we can solve it. the last question: as far as i am concerned, javier solana, you can be sure that i will risk my life working for peace in the middle east as i have done so far. i have been working towards this since the madrid conference many years ago, and i hope to continue working until i have energy and strength. mr president, before i give my explanation of vote i would like to congratulate you on your handling of the vote on the middle east resolution. it was quite clear from the result that the majority in this house wanted that resolution passed today and it would have been an absolute tragedy if it had been deliberately scuppered. i am very pleased with that. our group voted against the arms industry resolution because using more funds and resources to promote the arms industry in europe goes against what the european union should be about. we do not need more arms in this world – we need less. it is quite clear this is all driven by profit. we are particularly concerned about depleted uranium because depleted uranium is a small-scale nuclear weapon. it is very alarming that this parliament, and indeed the eu institutions as a whole, have very little concern about the use of depleted uranium. if we look at what has happened in iraq, and even in afghanistan, we can see that people still suffer as a result of the use of this weapon long after wars are over. but it is easy to see that the arms industry as a whole is pushing the policy. apparently the western european union assembly wants to be able to contribute to the convention on europe to ensure that the arms industry is boosted so that it can compete with places such as the united states. when we look at the conflicts around the world we must realise that the production and sale of arms is one of the major factors contributing to global insecurity. we should be helping communities and civilisation by putting resources into education, health and other important areas where money is needed, instead of using resources to boost the arms industry. it is an absolute tragedy that the european union is moving in this direction.

mr president, we have to address this question of the ageing of our population from the point of view of having a society for all ages, as our motion indicates. there are real risks if we simply address this question from an economic point of view, regarding and valuing citizens simply for the contribution they can make to the economy or the workforce. society, as this house knows, is a much reasons: the situation in the middle east posed enormous uncertainties, posed serious risks and, at times, many people could doubt that such a meeting could even take place. i therefore believe that know, the delegations from syria and lebanon ultimately decided not to attend because they did not agree with the israeli delegation, but the other countries of the mediterranean basin did attend and the twenty-five, by consensus, approved an action plan, a programme on such sensitive matters as justice and home affairs and also a programme to set up a dialogue between cultures and civilizations. i think that - which has been the subject of a lot of work beforehand and also of intense work throughout the conference - is in itself remarkable. i would also like to point out that virtually all the member states of the barcelona process have come at ministerial level and therefore with a very high level of assistance and decision-making capacity, which i would like to thank both the countries of the southern and eastern mediterranean and all my colleagues in the european union for. as i said, there's been solid back-up work. if that had not been the case, with the enormous difficulties and the enormous tension in the middle east, this conference would not have been able to take place and would not have produced good results. i am referring to documents such as the presidency's priorities, the commission's communication, the guidelines for action, the guidelines of the recent general affairs council, all the documents and all the contributions from the countries of the southern and eastern mediterranean. but i also want to refer in a very special way to the report by the european parliament, which was also drawn up by a spanish member of parliament, mr esteve. it is a magnificent report, which i particularly value. we have taken up a good number of their proposals and we will continue to make efforts to incorporate some more of them, because we think they are all worthy of consideration. i would therefore like to say that everything we have achieved and approved in valencia - and i repeat, by consensus - is not only the result of this will to agree, but also the result of the contributions of everyone. it is the first time - i will refer to this later - that, since the barcelona declaration of 1995, documents of this kind have been adopted with the agreement of all and not simply as mere statements by the presidency as conclusions after a series of debates. i would also like to emphasize in this context - and i will come back to this later - that we have approved the creation of the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly. i think it is a great step forward: it is an idea of the european parliament which we have adopted and which we consider to be of enormous importance. in any case, in an international context marked by 11 september and for a european union on the verge of the largest enlargement in its history, which will mean practically doubling its current membership, i believe there is no doubt that the mediterranean is shaping up as our strategic frontier, as a scenario in which to build a zone of peace, stability, development and shared prosperity, a zone in which dialogue and cooperation between cultures and civilizations are possible, as the barcelona declaration aspires to. and like any process, the one in barcelona is built step by step. looking back, we have come a long way since barcelona, and the proof of this is that we have already concluded eleven of the twelve association agreements that were planned to be concluded with the countries of the south. in valencia we have signed an agreement with algeria, and the agreement with lebanon has already been concluded and is only pending signature. the rest are all signed and many of them are in force. but despite all this, these advances, which are important, are not enough. the barcelona process, whose conception and existence are in themselves of irreplaceable value, needs a new political impetus, a kind of navigation chart capable of bringing the objectives of barcelona from paper to reality. and to this challenge, to this ambition to give a new political impetus to the barcelona process, which we all thought was languishing, the valencia action plan, the joint programme on justice and home affairs and also the programme on dialogue between cultures and civilizations respond. we have all agreed to this, i repeat, by consensus at the fifth euro-mediterranean ministerial conference. and that means not only preserving the whole transformative potential of the process, but also bringing new things both in form and in substance. i have already spoken of the form: this is the first political document adopted jointly by the partners in the process at a ministerial conference. that gives the action plan and the other documents i have mentioned the character of a euro-mediterranean social contract, of a shared project and commitment. i would like to reiterate this message: the barcelona process, the euro-mediterranean dialogue, is not something the fifteen have to do with the twelve, but something the twenty-seven have to do with, and we want it to be increasingly understood and accepted as something the twenty-seven have to do with. and the background of the documents adopted has also had transformative potential, because they respond to a series of principles which we believe should inspire the transformation of the process and because they envisage a series of important initiatives which, taken together, have the virtuality of giving rise to a qualitative leap in the construction of the euro-mediterranean partnership. what are these principles? i was referring to one of them: the principle of co-ownership. the principle of visibility is also important: the process must be perceived as such not only by governments but also by the civil societies concerned. the principle of capillarity: that it be transmitted to the whole of all the actors present. and other principles, such as structuring, credibility, efficiency and the concreteness of the process. the process needs to be made concrete. the full report obviously requires reading the action plan, which is a very comprehensive action plan, but, apart from the importance of each and every one of these initiatives, i would like to summarise by highlighting those which now seem to me to be of greater political relevance in the three chapters of the process: in the political and institutional chapter, in the economic and financial chapter and in the social, cultural and human chapter. in the political and institutional sphere, i would like to stress the need for greater democratization of the process, through the proposal to create the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly, which we must see to it that it is set up as soon as possible. the european union must also develop new mechanisms for cooperation and political dialogue between the twenty-seven, including issues such as security and defence policy, which i consider very important, or terrorism - to which i shall refer later - or the promotion of human rights. and trust and partnership building measures are also being taken. as i said, terrorism is included for the first time in the barcelona agenda, which i think is absolutely essential at this time for obvious reasons. and it is also planned that the plan, for the first time, will be the subject - as a specific action plan approved by all - of a follow-up and an evaluation of its implementation at the next sixth ministerial conference in barcelona, which i believe contributes to its credibility. turning to the economic and financial chapter, the valencia action plan reaffirms the objective of creating a euro-mediterranean free trade area by 2010. to do that, we must conclude each and every one of the association agreements to which i have already referred, and also complete south-south integration. it is extremely important that progress towards free trade areas in the south should be made, and that is why we have welcomed and given our full support - not only politically but also technically, thanks to the commission - to the so-called agadir process, initiated by morocco, tunisia, egypt and jordan. we all know that the success of the euro-mediterranean process requires the economic and, therefore, social and political development of the countries of the south. and that is, among other things, but very importantly, through the proper channelling of investment flows, so that the plan reflects one of the main priorities of the presidency, namely to promote the creation of a new financial instrument, which will start to operate as a strengthened facility in the european investment bank to support infrastructure works and to support the private sector fundamentally. we have then foreseen that, within a year, a decision will be taken, if necessary, to transform this strengthened facility into a bank, a subsidiary of the european investment bank, with capital open to other possible countries or institutions and which, in any case, will make it possible to allocate more financial resources to the region. the plan also includes the conclusions and decisions adopted at the euro-mediterranean ministerial meetings on trade and industry held in toledo and malaga respectively. in the area of trade, it includes a series of measures to facilitate investment and to develop the liberalization of services. in the industrial field, it contains provisions to promote legislative harmonization to facilitate the integration of our partners, to encourage innovation and access to new technologies and to strengthen the role of the private sector in building the euro-mediterranean partnership. i would also like to make a special reference in this chapter to the measures to promote investment in infrastructure and the interconnection of the transport, telecommunications and energy networks of our mediterranean partners with the transeuropean networks, and i would like to thank the commission again for the enormous and very positive work it has done. in this context, i would also like to stress the european union's willingness to facilitate the integration of the mediterranean partners into the galileo satellite navigation network. finally, as regards the social, cultural and human dimension, the presidency has tried to respond to the challenges posed by such important issues as immigration, dialogue between cultures and civilizations or the participation of the various actors of civil society in the construction of the euro-mediterranean area, by incorporating into the action plan a series of measures, among which i would like to highlight the following: firstly, the adoption of a framework document, to which i have already referred, on justice and home affairs, which covers, for example, such important issues as the fight against drugs, the fight against organised crime, the fight against terrorism, the treatment of migratory flows and the movement of people, etc. and that is why we also voted in valencia to convene a euro-mediterranean ministerial conference on migration. it was also decided to create a foundation for dialogue between cultures and civilizations and to promote cultural, intellectual and social exchanges. it is a project shared by all and therefore must be a response to the challenges posed in this field, a concrete response, the adoption also of an action programme, which can be channelled through the foundation or as you wish, so that the dialogue of cultures and civilizations focuses on three areas which we consider fundamental: youth, education and the media. we have also decided to extend the tempus programme to the mediterranean partners, which will make it possible to develop university cooperation between the two shores of the mediterranean and, very importantly, to incorporate the two shores of the mediterranean into the university world as actors in the construction of the euro-mediterranean partnership. there is also a call for the development of decentralised cooperation between mediterranean cities and regions and the adoption of conclusions stemming from the civil forum held in valencia prior to the ministerial summit. in short, we are facing a new stage, if you will, a new phase of the barcelona process. we are now facing a relaunch of the barcelona process, despite the difficulties arising from the middle east conflict, which in my view demonstrates something essential: the enormous capacity of resilience of the barcelona process. the barcelona process has shown that it is able to withstand the middle east conflict, and this leads me to a new conclusion: barcelona was a great idea in 1995, the euro-mediterranean dialogue was and is a great idea today, and if we had not adopted it then, we should adopt it now. naturally, mr president, in these two days, with the presence of arab countries, including all those directly involved in the middle east conflict and israel and the european union, it was absolutely essential that we should devote a good part of the sessions to the debate on the situation in the middle east. valencia has served us to assess and discuss this situation, and to do so - despite the enormous tensions and emotions that exist - in the framework of a debate which has at times had a frankly constructive tone, which has shown a will for peace on the part of the parties and which i believe can be useful throughout the process. we all know what the situation is on the ground. we are witnessing an unprecedented level of violence, with a staggering number of victims. despite the quiet of these last hours and these last days, the events of the last few weeks are truly impressive. there have been terrible terrorist attacks, which i condemn once again, without any reservations or palliatives. there has been - and still is - israeli occupation of towns under the palestinian authority, in respect of which i want to reiterate the demand for the immediate withdrawal of israeli troops. we all know that there is no military solution to the conflict, that the only way forward is negotiation within the framework of a political perspective and that therefore an immediate ceasefire is also urgently needed. in the wake of the events of the last few days, i think we are all very aware that there is a serious risk of the destruction and dismantling of the palestinian national authority, of its ability in the short and medium term to constitute the germ of a future palestinian state, and that is why i again call for the immediate end to the isolation of president arafat. i also welcome, on behalf of the international community, the statement by the palestinian leadership and president arafat himself condemning the terrorist acts. i would also like to express my very serious concern about the humanitarian crisis. it is absolutely essential that medical and health organizations can do their job. a very important meeting is taking place in oslo today which must define what we can do to meet the most urgent and immediate humanitarian needs, and also what we can do for the reconstruction not only of the physical, but of the institutional, of the territories and of the palestinian authority. these days, when it seems that the withdrawal is beginning - with all the nuances that this requires - we are going to see clearly the consequences of military attacks. yenin is without a doubt a dramatic example. it is essential that we know what has happened and its real dimensions, that the united nations has the necessary support - and i certainly believe that it should have the full and total support of the european union - to carry out an impartial international investigation. i would also like to mention that, as a result of the events, there is a very serious risk of regional destabilisation. there is grave concern about the violence on lebanon's southern border. we have made direct appeals - to the lebanese authorities and also to those of other countries - to the presidency of the council, to the troika, to make every effort to prevent attacks on israel from its territory. i must say that they have shared that concern and i understand that they are taking action. i would also like to mention another very important point: it is very regrettable that the consular representations of our countries are unable to carry out their duties because of the continuing obstacles posed by the israeli army in the occupied territories. the commission has already started to develop new possibilities, some controls are being relaxed, but the situation is still unsustainable and absolutely unacceptable. our consular representatives must have full freedom of access to the should now like to refer very briefly, mr president, to the efforts we have made in recent weeks. the european union has always shown a firm commitment to helping to solve the problem in the region. at the barcelona european council we insisted on addressing the security, political and economic aspects as inseparable and interdependent elements of the same process. you can't put one in front of the other. they're elements that have to run in parallel. and the basis for a solution to the conflict was reiterated in barcelona: the security council resolutions, principally 242, 338 and 1397; the principles of the madrid conference, and particularly the principle of peace by territories; the principles of the oslo accords and all subsequent agreements, which would allow two states, israel and palestine, to live in peace and security. we have therefore strongly supported peace initiatives such as the saudi plan, which was supported by the arab league summit in beirut and which put on the of the relevant un resolutions. i believe that a sign of this support was the presence of the president of the spanish government himself, in his capacity as president-in-office of the council, and of the high representative at the opening of the beirut summit. we also held an extraordinary general affairs council because of the gravity of the crisis. we wanted to send a clear message of concern, but also of the european union's involvement in the events. we decided to send the presidency and the high representative to the area to meet with the parties at the highest level and to demand an immediate ceasefire, the implementation of un resolutions 1397 and 1402 and a return to negotiations on a political agreement. i think we should have done so and we did so, underlining with facts the urgent need for the international community to be involved on the ground. as is well known, that mission was extremely difficult, and we were unable to visit president arafat because of the opposition of the israeli prime minister, mr sharon. i must say that attitude has changed. at the moment - and that is why mr solana is not here today - both mr solana and mr moratinos are visiting the region - and i have not gone there precisely to be able to be here - and they are planning to visit president arafat and, if possible, the other leaders of the region. i would like to refer to another event, which i consider very important, as regards this willingness of the international community to get involved: the meeting in madrid of the so-called quartet, that is to say, the united states, the russian federation, the united nations and the european union, at the highest diplomatic level: secretary of state mr powell, foreign minister mr ivanov, secretary-general of the united nations mr annan, mr solana and myself, on behalf of the european union. i think that reflects something that we in the european union have always advocated: the international community must be involved with the greatest possible unity of action and position, because we are all aware that there is no solution without the united states, but there is no solution with the united states alone either. and i think it is extremely important to maintain the concertation of the entire international community on the basis of common positions. as you know, we have issued a joint statement setting out a common position on the conflict and endorsing secretary of state powell's mission to the region. it also expressed its willingness to continue the quartet's examination of the situation in the middle east through regular consultations at the highest level and to continue the efforts of the special envoys on the ground. they're doing it and they're doing it very well. i would like to mention in this context the representative of the russian federation, mr vdovin, the representative of the european union, mr moratinos, the representative of the united states at the moment, mr zinni, and - i want to say this very clearly here today - the special representative of the united nations, mr larsen, who are doing a magnificent job. as for the continuation of the quartet meetings at the highest level, i think we can conclude one in the coming days to review the situation again and to make further progress on political initiatives. in that madrid declaration we specifically called for the immediate implementation of resolution 1402, as required by resolution 1403, and therefore for an immediate ceasefire, the immediate withdrawal of the palestinian cities, including bethlehem and ramallah, and in particular of president arafat's headquarters. the declaration calls on israel to cease military operations, to comply with international humanitarian principles, to allow full and unhindered access for humanitarian organisations and services, to refrain from excessive use of force and to make every effort to ensure the protection of civilians. but that declaration also calls on president arafat, as the recognized and elected leader of the palestinian people, to make every effort immediately to stop terrorist attacks against innocent israelis, to use all his political authority to convince the palestinian people that any and all attacks against israelis must stop immediately, to authorize his representatives to resume immediately, as soon as possible, security coordination with israel, and it also calls on him to act decisively and take all measures within his power to dismantle the terrorist infrastructure, including its financing, and to stop inciting violence or justifying certain types of attacks. that is not what the declaration says, but i want to say it: suicide bombers are terrorists, they are not martyrs, and it is worth repeating this constantly. terrorism, and i return to the declaration, is illegal and immoral, has seriously damaged the legitimate aspirations of the palestinian people and must be condemned, as security council resolution 1373 clearly states. finally, we express our joint willingness to help the parties implement their agreements, for example the tenet security plan, the mitchell recommendations, including mediation through an impartial mechanism, as agreed by the parties. various scenarios have been discussed within the union in view of the current situation. we have put all our political weight into diplomatic efforts, ranging from statements by the presidency to contacts with all parties, from support for general zinni's mission a few weeks ago, and of course support for the mission in the area by the us secretary of state, mr powell, and also with our visits on the ground, such as the one that is taking place today. the possibility of applying pressure measures against israel, such as suspending the association agreement, has also been raised, and i know perfectly well what the position of this parliament is. last week, at the last general affairs council, it was considered appropriate to await the results of secretary of state powell's mission, to which i will now refer, and for the moment what i can say is that all options remain open. as regards secretary powell's tour, it has had more positive and useful results than it seems at first sight, and i think we will be able to observe it over the next few days. a new perspective has been opened up by establishing a timetable for withdrawal, but it is clear that there are exceptions which are not admissible. one is the nativity basilica in bethlehem and the other is the headquarters of president arafat. the first point is still being worked out. there is close contact with all the interested parties and in particular with the vatican, which i hope can bear fruit. and on the second, we are continuing all our efforts, and the visit of mr solana and mr moratinos today is largely aimed at finding a solution that will lead to the end of the siege, which would allow a ceasefire to be established. we are all also looking forward to the forthcoming visit of the director of the cia, mr tenet, accompanied by general zinni, who can also be of great help on the ground. if we can solve these problems - and we are devoting all our attention to them - and achieve the withdrawal of troops, an effective ceasefire and, therefore, also the cessation of terrorist activities, we can create the conditions for moving towards a peace conference. a peace conference that cannot start from scratch. it must be a closing peace conference, taking into account all that has already happened, not reopening what was agreed in madrid, what was agreed in oslo or what has been agreed over the years. it is not to reopen the international legal order clearly defined by the security council resolutions. it must be something which really serves the purpose of a lasting peace and which must therefore be done as effectively as possible. in my view, such an effective approach is only possible if it has the full support and participation of all the relevant actors in the international community and, of course, the european union. i hope that at the next quartet meeting - very soon - we will be able to analyse all these elements and continue to bring new ideas and new efforts so that, in the end, palestinians, israelis and the arab world in general can offer themselves and future generations a prospect of peace, coexistence, stability and prosperity that has been denied them for many, many years. mr president, in many ways we have become so desensitised to the violence that takes place around the world that what happened in jenin, what has happened with the suicide bombers in israel, has seemed to pass us by completely. the reality is, of course, that we must try and find solutions and work towards them. but let us remember, first and foremost, that we are dealing with human beings. let us put into context the sanctity and the blessedness of each single, individual human life. when you look at the situation from that reality, finding a solution or a compromise is not difficult, because despite what some speakers have said, it is not love of one's country or nationalism that causes war violence; it is lack of respect, lack of tolerance of differing viewpoints and of diversity within our society. this is what causes violence and conflict. the only real solution to the problems in israel, palestine and the whole middle east region, is to bring the combatants together. you must make peace with your enemy, not with your friend. there is no point in us saying that we support israel or palestine. there is no point in the americans saying "we support the israelis in what they are doing" or "we are calling on them to be more moderate in their response." unless the israelis and the palestinians sit down together and work out their problems, nothing we do or say can be more effective than what they can achieve themselves. the difficulty, however lies in bringing them together. each side must give up something. each side must reduce its own bargaining position or its own ultimate goal, by some degree, because, in a peace process, there can be no outright winners, nor outright losers either. as rightly as we condemn all forms of violence, as rightly as we condemn the episodes that have taken place in jenin, in the church of the nativity around bethlehem, and the suicide bombers in the cafes and restaurants in israel, we must also be willing and aware in order to assist in bringing the people together. the only way that can be done is by taking them out of the area of conflict and bringing them into dialogue, giving them the support and the strength and the backbone that they need, not only to convince themselves that peace is achievable and that harmony can be achieved between the peoples of israel and palestine, but also that they will be given full support from the european union and each of its member states to achieve that. let us put our hands on our hearts and commit ourselves to peace, to justice, but, most importantly of all, to humanity. mr president, i want to welcome commissioner patten´s statement today. it was a model statement which was at once calm and rational and strong and balanced, outlining the situation as it exists and the steps that are necessary on all sides to create a sustainable peace in the region. i am puzzled by the council's excessive caution. i say 'excessive' caution. i am not arguing against caution, but the council expressed views today which were not balanced. i have also been to jenin and seen the destruction there, the destruction of homes and of people's lives, the burying of people in the rubble of their own homes. i would like to suggest one practical thing here today. what we were asked for was heavy equipment to enable the people in jenin to dig out the bodies that are still there. there was no heavy equipment when we were there yesterday. i appeal for urgent aid in that regard. we have a responsibility as parliamentarians to avoid extreme language and extreme solutions. we need to demonstrate that the sharon extremism will not bring security to the israeli state, nor will palestinian suicide bombers bring a palestinian state into existence. only through slow and painful negotiations with compromises can that occur, only then can the israelis and palestinians be secure in their own states. i met with ambassadors in tel aviv, moved on to jerusalem to meet israeli peace groups and then on to jenin to talk to the residents there. the objective of the sharon government at this point in time is the destruction of any possibility of a palestinian state. i have no doubt about that at all. europe, therefore, must bring pressure to bear on sharon and his government to see that this is not a viable option for israel. in conclusion, the most important and effective weapon we have is the association agreement. what we are calling for is the suspension of that agreement, not a suspension of all contact with israel, but a suspension of the preferential arrangements that europe has with israel so that at least it will begin to recognise that we are prepared to take action. it is a moderate approach which can be stepped up or cancelled when progress is made by israel in withdrawing her troops from the palestinian area, giving free access to humanitarian aid and free access to the united nations mission in jenin and elsewhere. there are many other conditions we could perhaps apply. there is no problem about an exit strategy. we simply state what our conditions are and what is necessary in order to begin talks under the quartet based on oslo.
mr president, i welcome both commissioner patten's contribution to this debate and kofi annan’s decision to send a fact-finding team to ascertain exactly what happened during the israeli bombardment of jenin refugee camp. i am, however, somewhat concerned at the motivation underlying attempts by israel to delay the investigation. israel claims that its invasion of jenin and other areas was an attempt to destroy the palestinian terrorist infrastructure. however, serious allegations have been made that the israeli defence forces were involved in extra-judicial executions and the use of human shields. if these prove to be true, then israel itself and its army are as guilty of acts of terrorism as those who plan, support and carry out suicide bombings. when he was defence minister, ariel sharon masterminded the “operation peace for galilee” invasion in 1982. his objective then he claimed was: “to eradicate the palestinian terrorist threat in lebanon”. this resulted in the massacre of 800 palestinians in the sabra and shatila refugee camps. a subsequent israeli commission of enquiry concluded that he bore responsibility, as they put it “ having disregarded the danger of acts of vengeance” are we seeing history repeat itself? mr sharon must take personal responsibility for what has happened in jenin and elsewhere on the west bank. it is a consequence of his policies, his prejudices and his hatred of yasser arafat. if the un team concludes that war crimes have indeed occurred, then the international community must take action including referring the matter to the international war crimes tribunal. mr sharon does a grave disservice to the people of israel. single-handedly he has caused his country’s political isolation. furthermore, he has fed the hatreds that have resulted in the escalation of anti-semitic activity which i deplore. he humiliated the us government during colin powell’s recent visit to the middle east. perhaps, however, this will have a positive effect and lead to a reassessment of us policy in this area and encourage them to abandon their one sided approach of unequivocal support for israel and instead to work with the eu and others for a balanced, peaceful resolution to this terrible conflict which has already cost too many lives. mr president, many of you this week will have noticed the exhibition about the work of herman hesse in the spinelli building. anyone who has taken the time to look at the exhibition must have been impressed by one of his statements and i quote, "for me the world is not made up of nations, but of people." would not the world be a different place if, in our shaping of policy and legislation, in in all aspects of our dealings with third countries. if we could move away from thinking in terms of facts and figures, sums and statistics, markets and merchandise; if we could remember at all times perfectly legitimate to link financial incentives to human rights and democracy questions through our funding of key projects. practical steps are being taken to make an ethical foreign policy a reality. i firmly believe that continued action in this direction would ensure that the support of projects would have a real and positive impact on the lives of poor people living in developing countries.

- report (a5-0125/2002) by mrs hanja maij-weggen, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the incorporation into the rules of procedure of the european parliament of a list of parliament documents directly accessible through the register (2002/2055 reg).
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission, like parliament itself, generally attaches great importance to the transparency of its activities and therefore to compliance with the rules on access to documents laid down in regulation (ec) no 1049/2001. the commitments made by the commission in this area support this statement, and among them i would like to mention here to the honourable members the commitment to forward the so-called comitology documents to this forum. this commitment goes beyond the obligations imposed on us by regulation (ec) no 1049/2001, and confirms our desire to move forward and to achieve further progress, both in terms of transparency and interinstitutional cooperation. i am sure you will agree with me that this cooperation is particularly important in the area of access to documents, given the complexity of our working methods and the interplay of our activities; and it is precisely within the framework of this interinstitutional cooperation, channelled through the already established interinstitutional committee, that the indispensable mechanisms for consultation of the institution originally responsible for the documents whose disclosure is proposed must be agreed. the commission therefore welcomes and supports parliament's initiative on direct access to documents. however, in so far as the report presented by mrs maij-weggen provides for the disclosure of a list of documents from other institutions without including any mechanism for prior consultation of the other institution, the commission prefers that a generic reference be made to documents transmitted by the other institutions with reference to the rules in force and the procedures agreed to frame the transmission, rather than establishing a list of documents which can be transmitted. in our view, this sufficiently guarantees both the objectives of parliament and the commission in terms of transparency and compliance with regulation (ec) no 1049/2001, on which - as i have said before - we are already taking steps even further than required. in any case, i would like to thank and congratulate mrs maij-weggen for the work she has done and the other speakers.

mr president, the funding of destructive embryo research is against the constitutional position of ireland, as it is against the constitutional, legal or political position of four other member states. the european union does have competence in research and technological development – title xvii of the ec treaty. this has to be exercised complementing the activities carried out in the member states – article 164 of the ec treaty – and always in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity – article 5 of the ec treaty – and respecting the national identities of its member states – article 6 of the eu treaty. therefore, contrary to the opinion of the commissioner for research, the eu does not have the right to overrule national legislation, regulations and ethical guidelines or to insist that member states have a duty to draw up regulations in the field of embryo research. i regret the irish government's silence regarding the unacceptable situation whereby irish taxpayers are obliged to fund destructive embryo research under its participation in eu funding and i reject eu funding of destructive embryo research as contained in the caudron report, in line with the majority view in the ppe-de group.

high representative for the cfsp. - mr president, i will try to answer those who have asked questions and who are in the chamber and also those who have asked questions and for reasons of greater interest have had to leave the chamber. i fully agree with what mr galeote has said and i think it is absolutely essential to use a window of opportunity which is not large but small. i think that all the speeches by the honourable members of this house have made this clear in one way or another. there are some grounds for hope, but there are still enormous grounds for frustration and despair. what we have to do is take advantage of these moments, this window of opportunity -- and i think that's what the international community is trying to do -- to move forward. there will be no circumstances like those we have these days and which have been pointed out by mr patten, myself and many of your honourable members. so let's get down to business. that's what we're trying to do. i think we must try to avoid and do everything possible to prevent the peace process from being hijacked. we have lived too long, as a consequence of a great political error, of the famous seven days of total peace. that famous decision of seven days of total peace led, without any doubt, to the process being prolonged and there being no decision-making. i think we should now do everything possible to ensure that there is no previous behaviour which prevents us from starting quickly and in parallel to work in all three directions: security, the new composition of the palestinian authority and the new legitimisation of the palestinian authority and the political process. the three vectors - in my view - should move in parallel and one should not hijack the other or vice versa. the third point i would like to mention - as i have said many times and i repeat today, because i am convinced of this, although i may be wrong, although i know that even in this parliament there are people who are wrong - is that i think we have had a long experience since the madrid conference, through the oslo conference to today, of peace processes; however, what we have not had, unfortunately, is peace itself. i think the time has come for a short process and a long peace. we've had long peace processes but no peace. it is time to make a short and quick process that will get us as quickly as possible to peace and, from there, to build the middle east, a process in which the offer made by the countries of the region is an offer that we can measure in real terms. what we are offering today is an outstretched hand with commitments which, for the first time, are contractual in nature. i would like to say something that has not been said and i want to reiterate. yesterday, president arafat said on television something i had never said before, or at least had never heard: he spoke of the state of israel as a jewish state. i don't think president arafat has ever expressed himself in those terms before. that short, three-word sentence sums up a very important part of the solution to one of the most difficult problems: the refugee problem. we must therefore take a good look at each word, spoken by all of us, not just one person, because sometimes we find in certain sentences that we do not analyse in depth, thoughts that can have important consequences for the solution of the problem and, without a doubt, the refugee problem will remain a fundamental problem for its solution. if you ask me what the most realistic agenda or agenda for the conference should be, i would answer you honestly that i do not know it at the moment. i believe that the agenda must be based on the basic principles, namely peace by territories, the resolutions of the security council and, as i said earlier, it should include a fundamental element, which is new: the beirut initiative which, as i said before, not only also offers a framework in the classic madrid negotiating lanes, but also introduces a regional framework which can be of fundamental use in solving the problem. it has been said that recognition of the palestinian state must be done as soon as possible. i agree, but it does not have to be before the palestinians want it. if you were to come with me and ask arafat at this very moment if he would like the palestinian state to be proclaimed this afternoon, he would surely say: 'do not go so fast and wait a little longer.' now is not the time, therefore, to do things in accordance with the pace that the palestinians themselves also want. the palestinians know that if the palestinian state were to be established today, they would not be in a position to do so with the efficiency with which we would like them to do so, and therefore they must also be given the opportunity to prepare themselves properly and to have the guarantees that the palestinian state will be a functioning state, that it will be viable and that it will defend the values which we all, and above all all all they, or most of them, want to be respected. as regards the issue of terrorism, i think we must keep saying, over and over again, that peace is not possible as long as there in the development and intensification of relations between my country and the european union. that is why i want to take this opportunity to thank you for the support you have always given to the process that has allowed millions of mexicans to achieve democratic change in our nation. thanks to this determined effort of the mexican people, mexico today enjoys unprecedented freedom and a firm and robust democracy. in mexico, as in europe, the exercise of democracy involves the convergence of very diverse efforts; the joint work of different political forces, individuals and non-governmental organizations, businessmen and public servants, directed towards a common goal: the sustained and sustainable development of our nation, within a framework of unrestricted adherence to the law. today mexico and its democracy is a big, strong tree whose shade protects all of us, especially those who have traditionally been marginalized and excluded: children, women, indigenous people. since july 2, 2000, i have made a commitment to lead the country in the new direction chosen by the mexican people. this path starts with democracy and the rule of law and leads to a future of shared prosperity, justice and equity. that is why one of my priorities as a government official has been to ensure that each and every official in my government acts with absolute honesty and total transparency. today, every alleged act of corruption is investigated and punished with rigor by the way of legality. we have strengthened the monitoring and oversight of public expenditure and are determined to eradicate corruption, which hinders the development and strength of democratic institutions. of course, honesty and accountability are not enough; i have also demanded that public servants respond efficiently and effectively to the economic and social demands of mexican society. the first results are in sight: today mexico has a stable economy with an inflation rate of 4.4% in 2001 and which continues to decline, with interest rates - the lowest in history - at 6% and which allow entrepreneurship, growth and the creation of more jobs; with an unemployment rate, last year - a difficult year - in economic terms of 2.5% and with a legal framework that gives broad legal guarantees to investment. we are also allocating significant resources to modernising infrastructure and power generation. in the social field, my government has developed extensive programmes to improve the health and educational level of large sections of the population, particularly in the poorest areas of the country. i want to mention, for example, that last year, apart from having free public education, we awarded over 4 million scholarships to children and youth across the country. this year we will have to add 1 million more: 5 million scholarships of which 300 000 will be allocated directly to indigenous youth, to young people from poor families so that they can go to university. over 500,000 new homes will be built this year, 50% more than last year. today in mexico, in political terms, there is a real balance of power. the legislative and judicial branches enjoy not only formal autonomy as in the past, but real autonomy. this is evidenced by the absolute independence which the congress has shown in respect of the various initiatives sent to it by the executive. equally demonstrative has been the judiciary, which has resolved constitutional controversies between the legislative and executive branches of government that had never been done before. another important challenge is to promote scientific and technological development to underpin economic and social growth. together with representatives of the scientific community and private enterprise, much needed changes have been put in place, including decentralisation, increased investment with a commitment to reach 1% of gross domestic product and, above all, strong incentives for companies and researchers to invest in this strategic area. another very important challenge concerns indigenous peoples. in mexico we have 10 million indigenous citizens. for this purpose, the law on the rights and culture of indigenous peoples was adopted, which is the most advanced and cutting-edge law in this field. since the outbreak of the conflict in chiapas, this parliament has expressed its concern very clearly and on several occasions about the situation in that mexican state and has thus expressed its concern for respect for the rights of the indigenous peoples, especially their human rights. my government has given clear signs of its political will to continue the dialogue with the zapatistas, as demonstrated by the protection we gave to their march to mexico city. throughout my administration, we have sought to ease the situation and have undertaken programs of investment, development and attention to the needs of indigenous communities across the country. i am grateful for the support that the european union has been offering to this process and, in a very special way, for the statement it made last year in recognition of the efforts of the mexican government. in order to advance the protection of the rights of these communities, i promoted a constitutional reform on indigenous rights and culture; this is proof of our firm will to achieve unrestricted respect for the human rights of all mexicans, which was complemented by a promotion in favor of respect for these fundamental rights anywhere in the world. on this subject, i would point out that from the outset we have declared ourselves to be a humanist government and have had a clear and firm policy in favour of human rights. this policy has two aspects. the first is to promote the support and cooperation of international organizations and the international community for all those actions which will bring about the changes required to overcome any backlog in this area. the second pillar is the recognition and promotion, at international level, of human rights as fundamental values of a universal character. mexico has therefore decided to play an active role in various international forums, in particular in multilateral bodies such as the un commission on human rights, where mexico's voice and vote are strengthening international scrutiny on the matter and reinforcing the validity of these fundamental rights in the world. our concern for respect for human rights inside and outside our country has led us to wage a relentless struggle for the defense of mexicans working in the united states, regardless of their immigration status. we also fight for the rights of mexicans sentenced to death in that country. we join the european parliament in its commendable work for the abolition of the death penalty, and we deeply appreciate the support shown in the case of gerardo valdés in the state of oklahoma, whose life has finally been saved thanks to your intervention and that of our country. we mexicans believe, like millions of europeans, that the deprivation of life of a human being - regardless of the wrong he has committed - is a violation of the most fundamental of his rights, that it is an attack on the dignity of our species, and that it places the public authorities in the same attitude of violence as criminals. (applause) the promotion of democracy as the best form of government, respect for human rights and the promotion of sustained and sustainable development of the peoples are an essential part of the foreign policy of mexico that my government is pursuing. a foreign policy aimed at participating in the construction of the international architecture required by our societies in the new millennium. in september last year, by signing the inter-american democratic charter, mexico joined the nations of our hemisphere determined to defend democracy in our region. through our participation as a non-permanent member of the un security council we are contributing to the construction of a new architecture that will better safeguard international peace and security. the recent united nations conference on financing for development in monterrey, mexico, is further proof of our firm determination to take a leading role in shaping a more equitable international system, one that offers new opportunities to the least developed nations. in a world of interdependence, only by joining forces will we succeed in these and other fields, such as protecting the environment, combating drug trafficking and the illicit trade in arms, cultural goods or people, fighting extreme poverty and fully implementing the rules of international law. we must join forces with those of other nations, parliamentary groups, civil society organisations, research centres, families and individuals. we are all co-responsible for our future, a future which must be shared. that is why, as josé martí said, i am convinced that today we must bet on the 'diplomacy of peoples', because what ultimately endures is the furrow that knowledge, human closeness and permanent interest in the other have left in the conscience of each citizen. ladies and gentlemen of the house, mexico has proposed a new regional development scheme, the puebla-panama plan, which includes seven central american nations and eight states in south-southeastern mexico. a region of very low development, of great poverty and of urgent need of development. the plan expresses my government's commitment and explicit recognition that in the new economic and political conditions of the 21st century, it is not enough to modernise development policy without transcending national borders. i would like to ask the european parliament to support this effort of regional integration, which will enable the states of the central american area between puebla and panama, which is the belt of the american continent, to move towards a steady development, to combat poverty and to promote education and knowledge. as regards the european union-latin america and the caribbean summit, which we will be holding in madrid in the near future, i am sure that it will be an excellent opportunity to examine, from a bi-regional perspective, the various problems affecting our regions and how best to deal with them jointly. i thank the european parliament for approving a proposal to establish a comprehensive partnership and a common strategy of the european union with latin america and the caribbean. the heads of state meeting in madrid will examine its contents with great interest. i would like to reiterate to you all my country's determination to strengthen its exchanges with europe, both with its institutions and with each of its countries, regions and communities. it is very gratifying to report that the first and second years of the mexico-european union free trade agreement have been successful with levels of growth in the trade balance of 18% or more, when, for example, last year the global recession left exports to other regions without growth. this fills us with hope and optimism and we see great potential in this relationship. mexico is a nation that has been enriched by the different civilizations that have arisen on our land or have met there. like europe, mexico has been, and continues to be, a meeting and convergence point between different cultures. like europe, mexico affirms its identity in diversity and in the multiculturalism that gives it strength and richness. i invite you to expand our exchanges, to continue to drive forward our relationship, to be part of the strengthening of a mexico committed to its time and a europe at the forefront of the world. let us make our democratic present the basis of a future of shared well-being. with boldness, with effort, with the conviction that the well-being of our neighbour is also our own well-being, let us together shape the world we deserve. thank you very much for your attention. mr president, in the parliamentary tradition from which i come, we were not confined to minutes, we were very often asked at a short notice to run down to the chamber and talk for an hour or so, on every sort of insignificant subject. here we have a different situation. i am happy that i am able to contribute on this subject because, while i am not a member of the relevant committee, nevertheless, it is a subject that i have thought about. this morning when we were discussing the lamassoure report on the competences of the european union and defining the competences, i thought that we should from time to time re-examine the various competences of the union. perhaps we have given ourselves excessive competences over the years and taken on excessive responsibilities in areas where it was not all that fruitful and, indeed, could be an irritant to the citizens of the union. however, i have often thought that development cooperation is one area in which we could improve our cooperation. i should have said that i want to congratulate mr miranda on his report. his explanatory memorandum sets out what exactly we are doing and, in his motion for resolution, he has drawn up a strategy for more effective policy cooperation between ourselves and the united nations. there is point at which we have to arrive before that cooperation can really become effective. in the european union we devote something like 0.3% of our resources to development cooperation as a whole. as the previous speaker pointed out the ideal is approximately 0.7%. i think only sweden and denmark have exceeded that, and the average european state produces something like 0.3%, so we have arrived at half the ideal objective. within the european budget itself, we produced something like eur 4.6 billion in this year's draft budget. this seems like a very small amount of money, but we have the experience of being unable to dispense the money which we provided for many reasons. nevertheless if there is one objective we should set ourselves in this area, it is to use our economic trading strength and our economic resources for the betterment of the third world. if we look at what we are discussing here, the problems we have in the union today, the rise of the right or whatever it may be, the slowness of economic growth, the unemployment which we have in parts of the european union, we find that these are not serious problems at all. and we should not hesitate to tell our people who live in western europe today, that they have better lives than any previous generation anywhere. what is our responsibility as a result? the greatest responsibility we have as a european union – and this was mentioned by the leader of my party, mr bruton, when he addressed this parliament as president-in-office – is to extend our good fortune to less fortunate peoples throughout the world. if we could develop a single policy, if we could pool our resources and if we could achieve that target of 0.7%, we would have something like eur 70 billion to dispense throughout the world. in dispensing that money, we could offer to the children of many third world countries something like the hope that we can give to our own children, something like the life expectancy and opportunities for education. we could revolutionise the world. we should not forget that. i was looking at some figures a few days ago. one hundred and twenty years ago there were 1.6 billion people in the world. europe was one quarter of the entire world. today there are 6.5 billion people in the world and europe makes up only 9% of it. we are becoming a smaller component of the entire world. there is the risk that we could become irrelevant. if there is any thing we should do while we still have power and influence in the world, while we still have riches beyond the dreams of the vast majority of people who live on this earth; if there is any objective we could set ourselves which would be a historic achievement for a united europe, it is to help along the less fortunate peoples of the world. while every individual state in this union insists on going its own way and designing its own policies for foreign aid, we will not have the political influence, or the material effect on the wellbeing of the people to whom we extend aid. pooling our resources is an ideal proposal on the part of this house. we do not necessarily have to administer it all from brussels. we can tap into the expertise of the various nations in the various regions of the world. we can distribute responsibility around the various member states, but we must have a coordinated policy. we must not be competing with each other and we must not be dependent on the united states – or any other country which makes a far lesser effort than we do – to design the policies to which we will contribute. mr president, this is a subject we could fruitfully discuss for a long time yet. i should like to thank you for giving me the opportunity at least to stretch my thoughts a little bit further than i have ever been allowed to do in this house before.
