- the next item is the commission statement on the common fisheries policy.
mr president, i had hoped that the extra time taken by the commission to fine-tune the proposals would have resulted in documents which would fully reflect the concerns raised by this house when we adopted our opinion earlier this year. i had hoped that they would pay particular attention to the social and economic implications for those regions on the periphery of the union. these areas are heavily dependent on fishing, as by and large there is no alternative source of employment. i regret to say that i have been disappointed with what the commission has produced after its long deliberations at many levels. instead of carefully crafted measures which would address the real problems affecting the fishing industry, the commission has delivered what can only be described as a blunt instrument which, if adopted, would fail to protect fish stocks or to address the issue of fishing effort. ireland fully meets the legal commitments under the multi-annual guidance programmes. our fishing fleets keep within the legally imposed tacs and quotas on fleet sizes. in this context, it is totally unacceptable for the commission to put forward proposals that would penalise all countries for the sins of a few. i do not have time to refer to the sins of those greedy countries, the member states from other parts of the union that try to exploit the fishing resources in areas far from home. these proposals underline an 8.5% reduction in fishing fleet. this is being somewhat economical with the facts. it may be a reduction of 8.5% in the fishing fleet but it is a reduction of at least 18% in capacity. the commission's proposals to forbid all state aid for the upgrading of the fleet is nothing short of irresponsible. the essence of fleet renewal policy is to improve the safety and living conditions on board ships, not to improve the capacity or the effectiveness. failure to do this would be a dereliction of duty and we must insist on the right of member states to continue the policy. therefore, i am extremely disappointed that the commission have not reinstated the policy prior to december 2001 – that was the safety capacity clause. how can the commission claim to advocate a safer working environment for fishermen and crew members while at the same time penalising the owners of the vessels who want to carry out measures to improve safety on board? in simple terms, if you want to put a whaleback on a vessel to protect the crew and create a safer environment, you are now penalised. the commission must take this into consideration and be much more reasonable. in conclusion, i believe that these commission proposals are just that. it is fortunate that the watchdogs of the council of ministers and the european parliament will be there to protect fish stocks and also, but equally as importantly, to protect the interests of fishermen from areas, where, as i said at the outset, there is no alternative source of employment.
mr president, while the greens fully support the efforts of the commission to create a sustainable fisheries policy within the eu, we reject any attempt to simply transfer our problems to the developing world. for far too long the eu has sent its distant water fishing vessels to scour the oceans off africa and other areas where they can cause immense harm to fish stocks and to local artisanal fishing communities. we have to clean up our own house without transferring our problems to those who are economically worse off than ourselves and who are desperate for any money they can get. commissioner fischler has stated that the eu must work for sustainable fishing wherever eu fleets operate and we shall hold him to that goal. in relation to the over-capacity of eu fleets, i would like to ask the commission how it feels about the announcement by the irish government yesterday for a eur 56 million investment package for eu vessels? this conflicts quite strongly with what the commission is trying to do. if the irish government is allowed to go ahead with this, how would it square with other member states who could follow suit and do exactly the same? this is at complete odds with what the commission is trying to achieve. finally, in relation to the whole saga regarding spain's involvement in recent weeks in the reform of the fisheries policy – and a spanish minister actually admitting on television that he was ordering his commissioners what do to – this goes completely against the eu's rules. this entire saga needs to be properly and thoroughly investigated because, forgive the pun, as far as i can see, the whole thing is very fishy.
mr president, like many other things in this world, if we were designing from the beginning a common agricultural policy today, i doubt very much it would take the shape or form we presently have. when i first became a member of this parliament, the union was a lot smaller than it is today. there were 9 countries with 20 million farmers. today the union is much enlarged and there are only 6 million farmers. so we have not succeeded in our original aim of maintaining the population in rural areas. nevertheless, the people of the european union have not seen the common agricultural policy as a great failure. they recognise that it has given us security of food supply. they recognise that the quality of that food has improved over the years and, in spite of the fact that, from time to time we have scares and always will, the consumers of the european union are relatively happy that we have given them a safe product. i would like to point out that while we spend, relatively modestly, something like 0.4% of the gdp of the union on this policy, the farmers, for example in denmark and the united kingdom get an average of about eur 19 000 per capita, but if you go down to the bottom of the list, the half a million small farmers of portugal get eur 1 500. so it is not a socially just policy. ireland is somewhere in between at eur 11 000 per capita. we have not succeeded in establishing a socially just situation. nevertheless, and in addition to having done what i said, we have also saved many rural areas; many habitations in towns, villages and communities have been saved by the policy. we must re-design it in a way that will make it more socially just. we must not forget that the business of agriculture is about producing food in the first place and we must ensure that food is safe. two things worry the farmers of europe at the moment: the excessive paperwork they are required to do and the restrictions that are being imposed on them. food is being imported from other areas like, for example tinned food, chicken and other things, for which they cannot guarantee the safety and they are not happy about this. the third thing is that we cannot see the future because we cannot get an agreement with the americans. we have to establish a system by which traceability of food, wherever it comes from, will be assured and we have to reach an understanding with our competitors in the world markets.
president, i want to congratulate the rapporteur on her persistence. this report contains provisions for the listing and phasing out of environmentally harmful subsidies and for environmental taxes at appropriate national or community level. as well as this, all legislation arising from the strategies will be adopted under co-decision. the improved management and use of natural resources as well as waste management is an essential step if we are to establish a more sustainable production method and pattern of consumption. the programme supports a reform of subsidies which have had an adverse climate effect. it clarifies the target for holding climate change by stricter reduction targets in the second period of the kyoto protocol. it also seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from industrial production by providing incentives with the development of environmentally friendly, benign alternatives. the report is, of course, not perfect, but it will prove itself in the concrete implementation. i hope, therefore, that we can all support it.
madam president, this is important for all our citizens, but we have also experienced difficulties in our own work in parliament as a result of spam mail. we had a recent example in the food supplements directive. the green/ efa group has fought right from the beginning for an opt-in and i am glad that parliament has adopted that, because no other system could defend privacy and data protection efficiently. however, we were critical that the proposal opens the door for member states to force providers of electronic services to retain personal and other data for a certain period of time. i have voted against this paragraph. it is unacceptable, on the one hand, to allow eavesdropping and, on the other hand, not to establish any safeguards against these practices. therefore i have voted against.
madam president, access to environmental information is a fundamental right and i am glad that the rapporteur has sought to restrict the use of confidentiality. this can be misused so that information which should be available is restricted under the guise of confidentiality. the report explicitly mentions the internet and that account should be taken of future development of information and communication technologies. it requests member states to create publicly accessible databases where environmental documents would be held. this makes it easy for the public to access and locate information and is very welcome. in seeking to reinstate parliament's original amendments, the rapporteur has moved to strengthen the position of the citizen. i very much welcome this and voted in favour of her report.
madam president, the common agricultural policy cannot stand still, it must adapt to changing circumstances. however, all proposals referring to agricultural policy must respect articles 32 to 38 of the treaty and, particularly, the objectives of article 33, namely ensuring the rational development of production and 'a fair standard of living for the agricultural community'. they must not involve any re-nationalisation of the common agricultural policy, hence my voting strategy. i would be concerned at any budgetary solution which would entail transferring part of the aid for cereals to provide an incentive to produce protein crops as per paragraph 31. using land set-aside to produce these crops could jeopardise the blue box status of the area payments in wto and result in switching production to set-aside land with existing protein land being used to produce more cereals. i am also opposed to the restoration of a differential, higher rate of aid for oil crops as per paragraph 32 as this would mean a return to the limit of some 4.9 million hectares placed on oilseed production in the eu by the blair house agreement as part of the uruguay round. it is not clear, madam president, what paragraph 35 means. arable area payments are based on a fixed rate per tonne, which applies throughout the eu and only differentiated according to historical yields in each member state or region in order to decouple these payments from production. application of a uniform rate of aid would disadvantage northern regions, including ireland, which traditionally has had higher yields. it is difficult to know what is in mind in the text of paragraph 43. i do not support the increased use of intervention for any product, let alone certain fruit and vegetable products, neither does the commission. support should be channelled through strengthened producer organisations.
madam president, would you allow me the luxury of a point of order before i address fiori. listening to my esteemed colleague on my left here, i think there might be a case for revising the rules on explanations of vote, whereby any of us are allowed one oral and as many written as we like in any one plenary session and i say that, really, to make business as efficient as possible. perhaps, madam president, you could bring my views to wherever they should go for consideration on that point. it would speed proceedings up for yourselves and the interpreters.
madam president, i very much welcome mr lannoye's report because of the increasing evidence that pesticides cause problems for human health. after ten years of this directive, we can see that implementation is very haphazard and that citizens do not receive the protection from pesticides that they are entitled to expect on the basis of the scientific evidence available. it is particularly important to note this legislation relates to maximum residue limits. this is the concept that there is an acceptable dose. however, we know that the concept has been disproved and that there is no safety threshold for certain substances. what is more, no account is taken during the evaluation procedure of some important aspects such as endocrine disruption and the existence of vulnerable groups. in addition, the arrival of seeds genetically modified to resist herbicides should have entailed re-evaluation of these herbicides as a priority. this clearly has not happened. there are other issues, such as the delay in dealing with dangerous substances, such as lindane, which are regrettable but i believe the rapporteur has addressed all these issues very thoroughly and i was very happy to endorse the report.
madam president, it is important that we have, or that we at least discuss, the johannesburg proposals for legally binding international frameworks on corporate accountability and liability, particularly on the basis of core labour standards. i voted for this report, even though it was much weaker than originally proposed. it has indeed disappointed some of the citizens' organisations active in this field, because amendments were not sustained by parliament on social and environmental reports on all levels of company and supply chain, on ethical pension funds and their investment policies, on the creation of multi-stakeholder platforms which include business, trade unions, ngos, public authorities and those from development countries. it is, nevertheless, welcome as there are some important issues which at least have had an airing and which we can hopefully pursue further in johannesburg. so i support the report although i regret that it has been weakened in transit through parliament.

- as you know, ladies and gentlemen, the principle of transparency is enshrined in article 1 of the treaty on european union. its entry into force heralded a new era in which decisions must be taken in an open atmosphere, as visible and as close to the citizen as possible. the aim is to ensure greater legitimacy, accountability and efficiency of public authorities in a democratic system. on 30 may 2001, parliament adopted by codecision regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 on public access to european parliament, council and commission documents. the regulation required institutions to open a register with electronic access for citizens by 3 june 2002. i am pleased to announce today on behalf of parliament that this register has been opened to the public on 3 june 2002 on our website. this register is accessible via the usual internet address 'europarl.eu.int/register'. 24 000 documents are already available on this site, and the upload of parliamentary documents to this register continues at a rapid pace. this is a key instrument for strengthening our democratic principles, which is well within the framework of the fundamental rights set out in article 6 of the treaty on european union and in the charter of fundamental rights. it is good that our parliament is at the forefront - in european terms - in promoting such a level of transparency.

mr president, i support the rapporteur's position. it is completely unacceptable to torture animals in order to, supposedly, improve ourselves. contrary to what the cosmetics industry states, it is possible to produce and sell safe products whose ingredients have not been tested on animals. many companies moved away from these archaic practices years ago and the overwhelming majority of consumers want an immediate ban. it is unfortunate, therefore, that both the commission and the council are still taking the side of the cosmetics industry and those responsible for profit-driven torture of animals. the proposed ban would apply only to products tested in the eu and would allow companies to export testing to other parts of the world. this is unacceptable. we want the practice to stop, not to be relocated. the commission's failure to implement a marketing and test ban – which was meant to come into effect in 1998 – is completely unacceptable, and to argue that a marketing ban would face problems in the wto is nonsense. there is a legal precedent. the adoption of the dog and cat fur act in the us showed that animal welfare can be a legitimate reason for restrictions. as far as labelling goes, i am very disappointed that the council did not adopt parliament's recommendation in the first reading that "tested on animals" should be clearly stated on the product label. the consumer has a right to know this. in relation to cmr substances, which are allowed in cosmetics, the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy reaffirmed its first reading position of the scientific committee. in the light of the fact that the commission recently banned cmrs in its review of chemical directives but has included it as an exemption, it is ridiculous that a substance can be banned from paint and polish but not from something that is put on your body. it is completely hypocritical to argue for the continued torture of animals in the interests of safety, mr president, in many eu countries – including my own – a lot of work still needs to be done to restore full confidence in the blood transfusion and blood products services generally after a period of tragic lapses in safety. this directive will go a long way and is extremely important because of that. i will come straight to the point i have difficulty with, and i support completely what colleagues – in particular mr bowis – have said. i cannot understand why blood from a remunerated source must necessarily be banned in europe. quite frankly, the biggest threat to our hundreds of thousands of patients in the eu who need blood and blood products is the lack of an adequate supply. the supply must be safe but, by definition, a voluntary patient who might have hiv is no safer than a person with no health problems and who is paid. it comes down to the proper screening and treatment of the product regardless of the source. we must not become emotional about this issue. i wish that all blood and blood products came from voluntary, unpaid sources. it is the ethos in my own country, and i would like to encourage it. we must encourage the public to donate blood. there is a scarcity of donations in my own country and many others. we are 50% dependent on imports into the eu. self-sufficiency has to be a goal. however, to even consider, by definition or otherwise, banning all products that come from remunerated donors is a retrograde step. i am not alone in saying that. the voluntary organisations that look after the interests of patients who need these products are pleading with us in this parliament and the eu not to ban all sources of paid donations. we must encourage the ethos of voluntary donation, but we cannot ban paid donations. if the patients – not the pharmaceutical or blood companies – are asking us, we should listen to them and respond to them. with the greatest of respect, it would be arrogant on our part not to do so.

mr president, each year in europe alone 38,000 animals are routinely killed after being used to test the development of new cosmetic products. for nearly ten years the eu has had a ban on the sale of products tested on animals but we have yet to implement this. there is no reason why we should not do so, especially in cases where scientifically validated alternatives to animal testing are available. the commission proposal to now replace this sales ban with a mere test ban is totally unacceptable and of great concern in view of massive public demand to end the use of animal testing for cosmetics. the test ban alone only serves to export the problem as cosmetics tested on animals in countries outside the eu will continue to be sold in the eu. only a sales and test ban will remove such products from our shelves. this will not compromise the safety of cosmetics, as products sold in the eu must fulfil legal safety requirements. we need to speed up the development of alternative testing.

i tabled this question not out of concerns about health or trading issues but out of concern for the credibility of the european commission. i was in this parliament when the ban was introduced originally and i voted for a minority report that was proposed by professor tom raftery, an expert on all these matters. he firmly believed that the motivation behind the proposal to ban these products was political. as a german member of parliament told me: "professor raftery is right, but there is a wave of hysteria in germany so i must vote against him". i do not think that a wave of hysteria is sufficient grounds for legislation by the european commission. my understanding is that the commission's position is not supported by the best scientific evidence from the united nations, the united states, canada, new zealand or australia. these people are not noted for putting the health of their own citizens at risk, and they too base their policies on what they regard as sound scientific advice. i want to ask the commission if it agrees with me that in the present climate, when the european commission is being put into a position of banning so many products and processes – even research itself in some instances – it is extremely important that what we do is seen to be soundly based and reliable. to do anything else will undermine the long-term credibility of the european commission. i believe that we are doing that in this case.

mr president, i should like to thank all the rapporteurs for their hard work. i will confine myself to the nuclear question. the euratom atomic energy community was founded in 1957 and is now well past its sell-by date. it is a closed institution and is regulated solely by the council. codecision with parliament is excluded. we really need to change this. its separation from other eu norms is also highlighted by euratom having its own framework for its research programme. this nuclear technology is the only area to have its own ringfenced budget. moreover safety requirements, as mr schwaiger has pointed out, are not at all coordinated. this is more than regrettable. the nuclear fusion budget remains the largest single area – eur 750 million – of energy research and proposes funds allocated to the development of the next generation of fusion research. most experts anticipate that if fusion is ever to achieve commercialisation it will not be for at least another 50 years. therefore the fusion budget is a financial black hole in pursuit of an ever-receding holy grail of fusion energy. despite around half a century of commercial operation of nuclear reactors, the solution to the long-term management of nuclear waste remains unsolved. the framework programme for additional funds to research geological disposal of radioactive waste means that eu-funded research for what is effectively a commercial waste problem represents yet another subsidy to the nuclear industry. this is unacceptable.

- the agenda calls for the statements by the council and the commission on the preparation of the seville european council of 21 and 22 june 2002, including the situation between india and pakistan.
the council. - mr president, i shall speak very briefly on the subject raised by mr van orden. parliament is well aware that the council has been concerned about zimbabwe on several occasions and that it was indeed discussed at the barcelona european council. i take very good note of this and would point out that there is a general affairs council next monday. we hope that we can deal with it at the level of foreign ministers and then if necessary or appropriate it could be raised at the european council in seville. with regard to the seville european council, mr president, the second and last european council of the spanish presidency of the european union will take place in seville from 21 to 22 june. the council will deal mainly with five subjects: the process of economic reforms, following on from the barcelona european council; the state of play of the enlargement negotiations, in which we have made substantial progress; justice and home affairs, in particular immigration policy; the debate on the future of europe, with a report by the president of the convention, mr giscard d'estaing; and the subjects of greatest concern in the context of the cfsp (foreign and security policy and defence). i shall briefly refer to the issues i have mentioned. i shall start with economic issues - follow-up to the spring european council. one of the essential elements of this next european council will be this follow-up, since the spring european council set out a programme and follow-up on certain issues and set out a number of tasks to be reviewed in seville. barcelona marked the launch of the process launched at the lisbon european council, focusing on an economic reform programme with the aim of making the european union the most dynamic and competitive economic area in the context of the new information society economy. the following issues will therefore be discussed in seville, following on from barcelona: first, the ecofin council - which is due to meet on the 20th before the european council - will present a final report on the adoption of the broad economic policy guidelines. the presidency intends to present a report on the state of play of the work on the fiscal package, which covers a number of initiatives on taxation of savings, energy taxation and cooperation with tax administrations. the issue of corporate governance will also be addressed. in this respect, the high level group on company law should reflect in its report on three issues: the role of non-executive directors and boards of directors, the remuneration of company directors and the responsibility of management in the preparation of financial information. other issues pending at the barcelona european council and to be addressed by the seville council are: simplification and improvement of regulation - known as 'better regulation'; economic services of general interest - the commission will also present the report it has been asked to do; energy supply - on which it will present another report -; telecommunications, education, research; the outermost regions and sustainable development. the second major issue i had announced was that of enlargement negotiations. unless you ask me otherwise, mr president, i would prefer not to dwell on the subject of enlargement, since there is going to be a substantive debate on it today. so, as enlargement is the subject of a specifically scheduled statement this afternoon, i think we could cut the debate short and leave that for later. justice and home affairs have been one of the main priorities of the spanish presidency of the union. in seville, we are going to make progress in four main areas with regard to these issues: firstly, there will be a review of the community's asylum and immigration policy - essentially a review of the commitments of tampere - as well as a state of play and a clear programme to fulfil the commitments we adopted in 1999 during the finnish presidency, as a result of the com munitization of justice and home affairs, which took place in the treaty of amsterdam. secondly, the heads of state and government will discuss a global plan to combat illegal immigration. a programme and policy for the protection of the union's external borders will then be discussed. the european council also welcomed the commission's proposal to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment. on the first point i have mentioned, the european council, in line with the conclusions of the tampere council and subsequent ones, will urge the council to adopt, within the time limits laid down in the treaty of amsterdam, the legislative instruments necessary to adopt a common policy on asylum and immigration. this policy must respect the balance between a number of principles, such as the protection of refugees, the reception capacity of the union and the member states and the integration of legal immigrants. secondly, the ongoing negotiations on a common policy on asylum and legal immigration will be given a boost if the union is also equipped with a common policy to combat illegal immigration, which will produce effective results in the short and medium term. in this context, the council adopted the plan to combat illegal immigration on 28 february. this will also be dealt with by the european council. in addition to the reinforced surveillance and control of borders and border crossings, it aims, inter alia, to prevent the illegal crossing of the external borders of the member states of the union, while ensuring that asylum seekers can exercise their right to international protection. in this context, the commission's recent communication entitled 'towards an integrated management of the external borders of the member states of the european union' is of particular importance. finally, on the basis of the agreement reached at the laeken meeting, the european council in seville will express its desire to further integrate migration policy into the union's external action. the guiding principle of external action on immigration and asylum with countries of origin and transit should be a comprehensive, integrated and balanced approach, using in a coordinated manner all community and member state instruments to establish a cooperative relationship with a view to jointly managing migration flows and addressing the root causes of those flows and poverty, with a view to mainstreaming this dimension in development aid policy. the development of an external strategy for immediate frontier areas will also be considered in order to cooperate in the management and control of migratory flows. the other major package of subjects, to which i referred at the beginning, is all that concerns institutional matters, the debate on the future of europe and the reform of the council. the institutional issues on which the council will focus are essentially two: the debate on the future of europe and the reform of the council of ministers. as for the first, the convention on the future of europe held its inaugural session on 28 february, as you will recall, because it was held at the european parliament, and before seville, the convention will have held five plenary sessions. it seems possible to draw some preliminary conclusions from the discussions which have taken place so far. on the one hand, most members of the convention have expressed their support for deepening the process of european integration in a realistic way, particularly as regards the division of powers. the bureau also agreed to set up six working groups to present their conclusions during the months of september and november. in seville, as provided for in the laeken declaration, the president of the convention, mr giscard d'estaing, will make an oral report on the progress of the convention's work. as regards the reform of the council, in accordance with the conclusions of the barcelona european council, the presidency is to present a report in seville on the improvement of its functioning and on reforms to increase its effectiveness, on the basis of the report presented by the secretary-general of the council, with the aim of ensuring greater transparency in the legislative process and proposing concrete measures for its adoption. i would naturally like to clarify something that seems obvious to me, but i think it is worth repeating, that these council reforms concern only reforms of internal order, internal organization, that in no case does the council intend to deal with issues requiring a reform of primary law, because, of course, that is the subject of the intergovernmental conference and the subject of the european convention which the intergovernmental conference is preparing. it is therefore a question of tackling a series of practical reforms which will make the european council's work faster and more dynamic and which, moreover, naturally lead to the system of councils which support the european council. i hope that the european council can now begin to make an attempt to simplify administrative tasks in order to prepare the union for a scenario where we will have 25 members after accession. finally, the european council will, as is logical and customary, have to deal with the field of external relations, focusing essentially on the following issues: firstly, the situation in the middle east. the european union will continue its efforts to achieve a negotiated solution to the conflict, condemning the use of violence and advocating conciliation as an instrument of joint action aimed at progress in the economic, political and security fields. in particular, with regard to the crisis at the church of the nativity, the council welcomed the resolution of the crisis in accordance with the memorandum of understanding reached by the parties. the palestinians affected by the agreement have been sent to various countries of the union - spain, belgium, ireland, italy and portugal - for humanitarian reception, in accordance with the common position reached by the council on 21 may. the adoption of this common position underlines the european union's commitment to achieving lasting peace in the middle east region. i therefore believe that, in the context of these latest actions, the european council will examine the situation and try again to give a boost to the latest initiatives being put forward by the high representative, mr solana, to convene a peace conference as soon as possible. at the same time, the council will examine developments in security and defence policy issues, in particular in relation to the fight against terrorism and the follow-up to the laeken mandate. and it seems to me that the european council will not be able in any way to avoid dealing with the conflict between india and pakistan, to which i shall refer specifically at this time. this conflict, despite its strictly bilateral historical nature, now has a new dimension which transcends its subregional consequences by affecting the entire asian continent and the whole world as a potential destabilising factor. in the face of the possibility of a fourth india-pakistan conflagration, which may spiral out of control into a nuclear escalation, the international community must react unequivocally. at the end of last year, following the tragic terrorist attacks on the legislative assemblies in srinagar and new delhi, the presidency had already been in contact with both capitals to urge the parties to avoid military escalation, to resume political dialogue and to find political formulas for resolving the kashmir problem. after president musharraf's hopeful speech on 12 january, new delhi reacted with a sense of historic opportunity to this conciliatory gesture by pakistan and agreed to halt the military mobilization. however, new devastating attacks - in kaluchak and srinagar -, border skirmishes and the reappearance of the dialectic of confrontation with the latest ballistic tests of pakistan, which are added to those of india in the month of january, have placed both armies on the brink of war. suffice it to recall the tenor of the disappointing speech of the president of pakistan on 27 may and the cold indian rigidity in the face of calls for restraint from the highest political levels. we must remember the visits to new delhi and islamabad by secretary of state powell, commissioner patten, foreign office secretary straw, the calls by presidents chirac and putin and, finally, the current tour by the united states secretary of defence, mr rumsfeld. the union has so far sought to maintain as equidistant a position as possible in this conflict, insisting on the need for efforts by both sides to bring their positions closer together. this was the idea behind the presidency's statement on this matter on 21 may. despite pakistan's undoubted efforts against the strongholds of al qaeda cells, the international community must not tolerate the linking of the nuclear umbrella's operationality to cross-border political demands. in this sense, pakistan's commitment to fighting organised terrorism must be total and unconditional and not selective in its efforts or timelines. i would just like to recall that at the general affairs council last monday the ministers agreed to send a new message, this time not in the form of a council statement but in the form of a press release, which was given to the media by the minister president of the general affairs council, mr piqué, precisely to encourage the parties at a time when there are already signs of détente, such as the fact that indian airspace has already been opened to pakistani civil flights and the fact that there seems to be a more relaxed and less alert atmosphere at the moment on the militarised lines. i think we should also not forget the european victims of the attacks in islamabad in april and may. the bombing of the protestant church in a diplomatic quarter and the suicide attack in karachi on a bus carrying french military advisers and technicians are dramatic proof that innocent citizens of the union have not been excluded from the terrorist irrationality in the area. in these circumstances, the presidency considers that the strategy of diplomatic accompaniment of both sides should be maintained, although it is now calling, with greater firmness, if possible, for new conciliatory gestures by both sides to satisfy the legitimate demands - especially those of india - in the matter of counter-terrorism firmness. new delhi and islamabad must be aware that there is - and will be - no international understanding if either country resorts to military force. since 17 may, more than 60 people have died on the indo-pakistan border; a million soldiers are guarding both sides from the line of control, awaiting orders to start a conflict that will bring, if it occurs - and whatever its final outcome - desolation and death to the population of both countries. the european union will therefore, as i have already said, continue to help to convey to both sides the need to keep the lines of dialogue open, in order to avoid a military scenario, the consequences of which would dramatically affect the entire asian continent. i think that next week in seville the message from the heads of state and government will be in this direction, with the hope that the de-escalation measures which are already in progress will increase more and more and that by the end of next week we will have a more reassuring picture than we had a few days ago. mr president, let me conclude this statement by expressing my hope and conviction that the european council in seville will be a successful conclusion to the spanish presidency, during which none of us has spared a single effort to advance our common idea of europe and to make more realistic the slogan we set out to at the beginning of our presidency: making more europe. regulation have in common. in this same spirit, mr corbett has made similar proposals for the reform of parliament, proposals which you are considering these days. they involve all the institutions in different ways and all the institutions will therefore have to work in harmony with each other to ensure that the objective is achieved. let us start with better regulation. the idea behind the white paper on governance was precisely this: exploit all the possibilities offered by the current legal framework to improve the decision-making and legislative process. the very large participation in the debate launched by the white paper and your contributions - in particular mr kaufmann's report - confirm the correctness of the strategy adopted. the system must therefore become more streamlined, more transparent and more efficient. we must show that we are able to meet the demand for greater responsibility and greater proportionality in the exercise of the powers which the treaties confer on the council, parliament and the commission. and we must base our action on a new objective, which is to give greater substance to the idea of citizenship, to make the relationship of citizens with the union more transparent, more direct and more tangible. i presented our draft to the conference of group chairmen of the european parliament last week, but i think it is necessary to stress some fundamental points here. first, we propose to improve and simplify european legislation by reviewing the whole legislative cycle, starting with the exercise of the right of initiative. the policy is based on three pillars: first, to establish clear rules for consultation; secondly, to assess the impact of decisions; thirdly, improving the legislative technique. we must move forward with our legislative work through wider consultation with all stakeholders and through a more thorough analysis of the economic, social and environmental impact, in line with the decisions of the gothenburg european council, and we must do so without creating unnecessary procedural complications. good community legislation also requires that it be fully in line with the original spirit of the treaties and, in particular, that it make use of framework directives, which are one of the most effective instruments for ensuring greater respect for the principles of proportionality and subsidiarity. it is also time to reconsider the implementation of our policies, as the implementation of policies is the stage that has the most direct impact on citizens. transparency and democratic accountability require each of the institutions to refocus its activities on its essential tasks. in this way we can already contribute to the practical renewal of the community method. i would like to stress once again that this is not just the commission. this approach is binding on all the institutions if it is to achieve a useful result: the institutions are bound to work together. finally, the institutions themselves must be refocused on their core missions. each institution must therefore take on a clear responsibility to reach an interinstitutional agreement by the end of the year. the council, too, with the solana report, has launched a new reflection and concrete proposals on possible internal organizational reforms, in accordance with the treaty. the commission strongly supports the council's efforts to renew the system. i can only welcome, for example, the fact that the council is preparing to distinguish, in its internal organisation, the procedures applicable when it exercises a legislative function from those applicable when it exercises purely administrative functions. i also support the reflections contained therein on the continuity of its work, the need to strengthen internal coordination of its activities and the possible reduction of its staff. all of these are indications that make their work and ours easier. these actions help us to deal with the problems that the forthcoming enlargement will cause to the functioning of our institutions. i am assuming that a target of this magnitude cannot be achieved without a coordinated approach by the commission, parliament and the council. it is a question of moving beyond 'better regulation' together, to face with serenity but with conviction the 'better organisation' of all the institutions. the commission is ready to participate in this joint work. better organisation means more speed, more coordination and less formality, and it means giving up acquired - but obsolete - positions in order to work better and faster than before in a system which has become more complex. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, among the other issues which the european council will have to deal with - as i mentioned at the beginning - immigration is of the utmost importance. it is worth reiterating that we are not proposing solutions that are contrary to the fundamental values of our union, but are promoting an integration model that combines freedom with the legitimate security needs of our citizens. i have already expressed my support for the presidency's decision to put the issue of immigration at the centre of the agenda in seville. the issue of immigration, in the eyes of the majority of citizens, is increasingly linked to aspects of their protection in the area of freedom, security and justice that we have jointly committed ourselves to building. the reasons are many, and they have been somewhat accentuated in the wake of the events of september 11. we need to address these issues, but not demonize them. our ongoing discussions on legal immigration and asylum rights risk failing if we do not take seriously the concerns of our citizens about illegal immigration. we agreed a number of objectives in tampere which are still valid today. we also have before us proposals to achieve these objectives, such as those contained in the commission's communication on illegal immigration, on which the council based its action plan. other proposals concern the management of our external borders and readmission policies. the political signals we have received recently are very clear. we cannot put the question of security on the back burner, nor can we allow the idea that a return to nationalist positions can offer a valid solution to transnational phenomena, which are beyond the capabilities and sphere of action of individual states and which can therefore only be addressed and managed at european level. it is not just about fighting illegal trafficking. it is also about laying the foundations for the full integration of legal immigrants into our societies, and it is about regulating the access of the immigrants we need. the enlargement process itself is presented by some as a threat, precisely because of the immigration problem. but why - i ask myself, ladies and gentlemen - should the citizens of the candidate countries leave their country, radically change their lives, at the very moment when, thanks to accession, they are being offered a new prospect of prosperity? did the same not happen when spain and portugal joined? it is not the same for my country when the european community was created? we must therefore act swiftly in different directions. first of all, we must strengthen control of the external borders of the union, on the basis of the recent proposals of the commission and the italian government. i expect the european council to decide to convene the heads of the border police to determine what actions and what instruments are needed, immediately, to start these initiatives. the control of external borders must also be linked to our neighbourhood policy, which aims to establish special relations of mutual trust with all the countries neighbouring the union, especially after enlargement, also with a view to taking joint action in the fight against illegal immigration. in the euro-mediterranean context, we have already launched initiatives with morocco for a comprehensive approach to immigration. we must also speed up the adoption and implementation of asylum measures, also to give more substance to european citizenship and to certain principles proclaimed in the charter of fundamental rights of the union. all this, ladies and gentlemen, is not enough unless it is accompanied by an appropriate policy of cooperation and development and by the systematic use of all the instruments at our disposal: the european union has a policy on the causes of migration, bilateral agreements, readmission agreements. we shall soon be submitting operational proposals on these points. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall ask the council in seville to take the appropriate decisions on these points quickly, with the same reasonableness and responsibility that we have already shown in brussels and ghent in the autumn of last year. the two themes i have mentioned in this speech are of crucial importance to us today. the more democratic, transparent and accountable functioning of the institutions responds to the demands of our citizens for a more efficient europe that is closer to their daily reality. the immigration issue is about the very reason we're together: the european union is committed to building a prosperous, just and secure europe. mr president, firstly i would like to express my sincere thanks and appreciation to the spanish presidency for its very professional and successful approach to its many responsibilities and obligations. i note with satisfaction that we did not have any embarrassing incidents during the presidency, as we have had in other recent presidencies. under the spanish presidency, negotiations for future european enlargement are continuing at a strong pace. the european union is currently dealing with difficult areas such as agricultural affairs, regional policy and budgetary matters. we all know the moral arguments for enlargement of the union. developing democratic and civil societies, respecting the rule of law and promoting human rights are central goals of the union. the european union is a political model that has helped to bring peace to our continent. this process will be furthered, not diminished, by the enlargement of the union. but we must all reflect on the key practical procedure being used to streamline the enlargement of the union. in december 2000 european union leaders agreed a set of treaty reforms in nice which they considered would be the best procedure for bringing about enlargement. already 13 out of the 15 countries in the european union have ratified the provisions of the treaty of nice. if the treaty of nice is not ratified by all 15 member states, enlargement will undoubtedly be delayed. if the treaty of nice is rejected by one member state it is not valid law, because the proposed treaty changes do not command the unanimous support of all the member states. delaying enlargement would have a very negative effect on the development of the union. prior to the birth of the eec in 1957, europe was bedevilled by hatred and division. the european union has now ensured that the tools of war have been put aside in favour of the development of new policies. the european union is not simply about mutual economic progress. thanks to the european union, europe's past has been put aside in the interests of peace and prosperity for all the peoples of europe. that is not to say that the irish people do not have clear concerns which they want addressed before any further referendum on the treaty of nice. the majority want assurances that ireland's traditional military neutrality will be fully protected and respected by all member states of the european union. it is very important that a declaration is agreed by all european union leaders, spelling out in unequivocal terms that ireland's military neutrality will be respected now and in the future. irish troops have always served in peace-keeping and humanitarian operations under the auspices of the united nations. the provisions of the treaty of nice do not change that. the situation is not altered by ireland's participation in the european rapid reaction force, but it is still very important and politically necessary for a declaration to be made in seville expressing the support of eu governments for this special foreign policy issue, which means so much to so many people in ireland. finally, the european union is the natural home of the irish, both geographically and politically. we recognise that standing alone is of little benefit when international cooperation is increasing. the european union must ensure that the interests of each individual citizen are protected at all times.

enlargement process. i want to speak directly to the spanish president-in-office at this point. the seville european council is important for the many reasons outlined in our resolutions here today. anti-european union sentiment in the candidate countries, to the detriment of all europeans. i am also concerned at the grandstanding by some member states, which are resisting the budgetary mr president, as mr de rossa has pointed out it is expected that the seville summit will discuss the holding of a second irish referendum on the treaty of nice. such a step, regrettable as it is, and no further' – moves it closer to the british position on europe, which places more emphasis on a free trade area rather than pursuing political union. i take this opportunity to warn the irish government that it is following a very dangerous path. opportunistic eurosceptic stances by some of its leading members played into the hands of those who opposed the treaty of nice, thereby contributing to its rejection. it does not help that a leading eurosceptic has been promoted to full cabinet rank. pandering to the same prejudices again could well result in a second failure and consequently leave ireland in a semi-detached relationship with our eu partners, and that would be disastrous.

the council. - mr president, i do not think it is idle to repeat once again the historic importance, the political priority and the irreversible nature of the process of enlargement of the union. that said, i think that when we assess the prospects for the enlargement process of the european union with a view to the next european council, we should take as a starting point the objectives we set ourselves at the beginning of our presidency and, in view of what has been achieved so far, consider what we can expect in seville. you will recall, mr president, that in the debate we had this morning on the preparations for the seville council i avoided discussing the issues of enlargement, precisely to reserve them for this debate, in which we shall deal with these matters in a monograph. it is clear that the enlargement issue is one of the key issues of the seville european council and i therefore believe that the information i am about to give will provide the key to what the presidency and the council are going to propose to the seville european council. at the beginning of our presidency we presented the work programme entitled 'more europe'. in that document, enlargement of the european union was listed - as it could not be otherwise - as one of our fundamental priorities, i would say more than a priority, it is a fundamental objective of the union. it stated that the presidency's aim was to make a decisive contribution to the conclusion of the negotiations with all the candidate countries which were ready by the end of the second half of 2002, thus continuing the conclusions of the previous european councils in gothenburg and laeken. more specifically, our main task was to reach common positions among the 15 on the most complex chapters of the acquis, that is to say, precisely those to which we have been assigned in the road map, those with the greatest financial and budgetary impact. the european council has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. at the same time, we thought we were going to proceed with the provisional closure of all those chapters pending at the beginning of the semester because, as you know, mr president, as does the house, spain not only found its road map, but also a very large number of what are euphemistically called left overs, but which are really unfinished negotiations, very important negotiations, which had been pending since the swedish and belgian presidencies. two fundamental principles must continue to inspire and frame the whole negotiating process, namely that the negotiations should be conducted on the basis of the current acquis and that the financial perspective adopted in berlin in 1999 should set the ceilings for the accession of the new member states by 2006. the negotiations also sought to avoid any overlap or interference between the enlargement process and any reforms of the common policies, because anyone who wants to make the reform of the common policies conditional on enlargement runs the risk of causing a delay in the planned deadlines. in other words, the union has an objective which parliament fully supports: that accession should become effective in the course of 2004. in addition to this general objective, the specific work programme of the presidency for enlargement, which was presented to the council last january, contained a whole series of related tasks. first, the verification of the third condition of accession, which refers to the administrative and judicial capacity for the effective application of the acquis. this is not a topic that is talked about much, but it is a very important topic. this is the famous so-called 'madrid criterion', which is absolutely essential if enlargement is to be effective. during this six-month period the commission has drawn up and developed an action plan with each of the candidate countries and will present a report to us in seville. the drafting group for the accession treaty was also to be set up during the presidency and started work in march. we have already conceived, together with the commission and the general secretariat of the council, the idea of starting to think about a working group on the drafting of the accession treaty, so that its drafting and the corresponding annexes will run parallel to the negotiations so that, when the negotiations are over, we will not have to waste time drafting the treaty, because we all know, and parliament in particular, the difficulties that exist in the national ratification processes. we therefore have not much time if we are to meet our objective in 2004, especially to have everything ratified so that the candidate countries can stand as full members in the european parliament elections. we therefore had this purpose - which, by the way, we have fulfilled - and, as has been the case in previous presidencies, the spanish presidency has also devoted particular attention to four specific cases, because it seems that the 10 countries designated in the first wave were the sole objective of our efforts, but this is not true. we have to look at bulgaria and romania, two countries which are lagging behind and which need specific support in order to open as many negotiating chapters as possible, and we also wanted to contribute in some way to the efforts to find a final political solution to the cyprus problem. finally, we must not forget that we must also promote the pre-accession strategy with turkey in some way. the commission's proposals are not only a means of improving the situation, but also a means of ensuring that the community's policies are not disrupted by the economic crisis. i am pleased to say, mr president, that with the invaluable help of the commission - and i want to publicly commend commissioner verheugan, who is responsible for enlargement, and who has indeed been instrumental in all the progress we have been able to make - the progress made during the spanish presidency can be summed up as follows: the council, in its various formations, has begun to examine the notes presented by the commission on 30 january on the general financial framework and agriculture, in which the absence of consensus was evident. the fundamental difference - and we are still negotiating - concerns the granting by the union of direct agricultural aid to the applicant countries and the fact that these may, according to some countries, prejudge the future reform of the cap. as a result of these disagreements, we have not yet been able to reach a common position on the agricultural chapter; i would say that there is a common position, at 95%, but there is 5% left, which concerns direct aids, where a consensus has not yet been reached. we are trying to promote a compromise formula because we understand the reasons for the four countries blocking the common position, but we also understand that these countries must understand that in agriculture there are fundamental principles of respect for the acquis, respect for equality between the member states and the candidate countries and above all the fact that the itinerary, the road map, cannot be delayed. in other words, all those countries which, for whatever reason, are preventing the adoption of the common position on direct aid will have to take political responsibility before this parliament - which i hope will know how to demand it - and before public opinion for not having made possible the common position which would completely close the entire road map for the enlargement negotiations. we are making efforts; we had a general affairs council on monday, we are in coreper today dealing with this issue; there will be another extraordinary coreper on friday; we will deal with the issue again at the general affairs council on the 17th and, if necessary, we should go to the european council with it. we do not want the european council to be a place of confrontation on these issues, but everyone must be aware that we have to make a collective effort to close the agriculture chapter completely; it is not possible to say that 95% is closed and that we will then close 5% for direct aids, because it cannot be postponed because it is a matter of principle: the principle must be accepted even if the modalities can be discussed later. after the first two negotiating conferences in march and april, and the ministerial meeting we just had with commissioner verheugen and myself on monday, and also with mr piqué on monday and tuesday this week, a total of 83 chapters have already been negotiated, of which 49 have been provisionally closed and another 8 opened. in april, for the first time, three of the four chapters of the roadmap allocated to the spanish presidency, namely regional policy, financial and budgetary provisions and institutional arrangements, were discussed and closed with some candidates. the fourth and last chapter - and certainly the most complex, agriculture - is still being discussed in the council, and we have not yet reached a common position and have therefore not been able to close it. our aim has been to reach a consensus, as i said earlier in the general affairs group on 10 june; it has not been possible and we will continue our efforts. with regard to the two countries lagging behind, all the outstanding chapters have been opened with bulgaria, while with romania 7 chapters have been opened, leaving only 6 outstanding; i would like to inform this house that together with the commission we expect to be able to make further progress this month and, certainly, before the end of the presidency, on 27 or 28 june, we will hold a new negotiating conference at the level of alternates and it is possible that we will be able to open more chapters with romania and, of course, close a few more chapters, in addition to those which have been closed at ministerial level. it is very likely that the spanish presidency will end up opening all the chapters on romania and closing between 90 and 100 chapters with the other member states. so, if we look at the overall picture, as i said this morning, most countries have closed between 25 and 28 chapters. the drafting committee, to which i referred, has been working since 13 march on the technical adaptations and the legal implementation of the commitments agreed so far during the negotiations. we have left a good legacy for the danish presidency and we have given it the opportunity to finalise the drafting of the accession treaty by the end of the year. the committee and the association council met in january and april respectively. the most important event was the adoption of a programme of meetings of the eight subcommittees responsible for carrying out the detailed prescreening of their legislation, as mandated by laeken. the european union has been insisting on the need to step up internal political reforms with a view to fully complying with the copenhagen criteria. ankara reiterates its wish that a date for the start of accession negotiations be fixed in december, but it is clear that, however much goodwill it may have, the european council cannot set dates for the start of negotiations until the copenhagen criteria are fully met. on that, our position is going to be firm. we can't do otherwise. this is not an exercise in wishful thinking, to use the british word, but an exercise in actually applying the principles to which all the institutions are bound: the commission, the council and the european parliament. with regard to cyprus, the ordinary negotiations have continued to develop normally; i must say that cyprus is an excellent candidate, the southern part of cyprus, the republic of cyprus, is certainly the candidate with the most negotiating chapters closed and with the highest level of progress in the negotiations. we are naturally following closely the development of direct contacts between the leaders of the two communities, the talks which started in january between mr denktash and mr clerides, which have so far produced no tangible results. i myself was in cyprus last thursday, on behalf of the presidency, and i had a long interview with mr clerides and mr denktash and we conveyed to them the union's position and the importance we attach to the programme set out by the secretary-general of the united nations, the importance of agreement on the core issues, that is to say, on the question of forms of government, property, territory and security. some progress has been made, but there have also been some dramatic setbacks in recent days, and so i have been there on behalf of the president of the council, not only to send you a message - a message which will be articulated in some way in the conclusions of seville - but also to listen, so that the northern part of cyprus can never reproach us with not having been sensitive to their arguments or with not having had time to listen to all their arguments, because of course, each side may or may not be wrong, but it has its arguments, which are worth knowing. i therefore believe that we have accompanied the process as far as we can, supporting as much as we can alvaro de soto, the representative of the secretary-general of the united nations. we believe that things have gone well, but we have sent them a very clear message: we know that the objective they had set for june and which the secretary-general has reaffirmed has not been met, but we have told them that we cannot wait forever, that we need a clear political signal and that before 24 october, when the european council of brussels under the danish presidency will be held, the union needs to know about that agreement between the parties, in order to be able to include the whole problem of northern cyprus in the course or in the mainstream of the negotiations. in accordance with the laeken mandate, the seville european council must also give its opinion on the commission's report on development and its action plan for institutional strengthening in the applicant countries, and the general affairs council on 17 june will give its first consideration to the report presented by the commission on 5 june. the spanish presidency also introduced, as an institutional innovation, the first time in history that the candidate countries for accession would actively participate in the spring european council - everyone remembers that they took part in the session, not in a lunch at the end, but madam president, i shall deal with two main points in this question of enlargement. firstly, i should like put on the record of this house that the treaty of nice needs to be adopted by all existing member states of the european union to facilitate the enlargement of the european union by ten countries, which we hope to see in the not too distant future. i would hate anyone to misunderstand or misinterpret the decision of the irish electorate not to approve the treaty of nice, because the irish population in general, even those who oppose the adoption of the treaty of nice, is in favour of enlargement. this house, as an institution, and the irish people, need to guarantee that we can deliver on ratification of the treaty of nice in the short term. the irish government will therefore be proposing a declaration in seville on traditional irish military neutrality, which i hope will be approved by other member states. my last point is that, in our negotiations with the accession countries, we should not stand in the way of their progress towards the adoption of the acquis communautaire. we should not set up unfair barriers to their accession. when these countries join the european union they will bring a new impetus, a new ideology, and a new belief in the vision the founding fathers of the european union had of a europe of peace, prosperity, progress and respect for europe's diversity.
mr president, i compliment mr olsson on his work and may i commence by again putting on the record my support, and that of my irish colleagues, for eu enlargement. for the candidate countries of central and eastern europe, the academic debate should be well and truly over. we must now proceed in a planned way with their integration. i compliment the candidate countries on their efforts to conform to the stringent requirements for entry. for some of them it has been, and continues to be, difficult. from an agricultural perspective, mr olsson has addressed the challenge of enlargement in a reasoned and practical way. for me, integration depends on our success in fusing the agricultural economies of candidate countries with existing member states in a manner that causes least disruption to both and in time provides for their full participation in the common agricultural policy. anything short of that would undermine the principles of cap that, by and large, have served european farmers and consumers well. as we face a mid-term review of the berlin agreement and the inevitable long term cap reform, we must not allow the review to deviate from what was agreed in berlin or to contemplate a move towards re-nationalisation of cap in future reform. farming in europe as evidenced by yesterday's 15,000 farmer demonstration continues to be difficult. with the benefit of hindsight we have not in the context of world trade provided the degree of protection necessary for our farmers from the obvious unfair competition and market manipulation by our competitors. with the completion of enlargement, europe has the potential to be a dominant player in world trade. we will only succeed, however, if we are committed in the short term to supporting the european model based on family farming. i alert the house, not for the first time, to the serious threat to the survival of that model because of long-term uncertainty and the availability of alternative, attractive and more financially rewarding employment for young people who would in normal circumstances take up farming as a career.
mr president, this is a very important report because the european community is discussing recovery plans for fish stocks for the first time. since this is the first time, it is very important that we get it right. we must make sure that the actions we take will reverse the declines in several cod stocks and northern hake and allow them to recover. the commission proposals were tough and will definitely have an impact upon the fishing communities involved, but they had to be tough because the state of the stocks is so poor. as the rapporteur has said, if we do not do something about fish stocks, there will be no fishing industry in the future as there will be no fish. ices says that cod in the north sea is at its lowest level since 1963. while hake may not yet be in such dire straits, it is still far below the level which is appropriate, and the warning bells have been ringing now for quite some time. the commission, the committee on fisheries and the council all claim to agree with the precautionary approach, which states that the absence of definite proof should not be used to refuse action to prevent a decline in fish stocks. in other words, as soon as there are reasonable grounds to believe that cod and hake stocks need a degree of protection, we should act. that is exactly what the commission has done. however, what did the committee on fisheries do? it argued that there is no crisis involving hake and completely removed it from the proposal. we must vote against this amendment. i agree with the rapporteur on this point. it is completely unacceptable. this is not a precautionary approach to fisheries management. the committee is simply paying lip service to the idea and continuing with business as usual. we are not going to solve the problems if this is the way we go on. we cannot keep refusing to face up to reality. we must realise that these stocks are endangered and we must protect the fishing industry. it is doing the fishing industry no favours in the long term if this is the kind of simplistic, nationalistic short-term approach that has been taken. if the report goes through plenary as it is, the verts/ale group will have to vote against it.

mr president, the non-binding motion for a resolution accepts for now the voluntary agreement by the european car industry. but we are calling for eu legislation to take its place. we welcome manufacturers' development of pedestrian-friendly car fronts, automatic braking systems and the use of daylight running lights, although obviously there is controversy on that particular topic. we welcome this because we are assured that these measures can be implemented relatively quickly. however, the motion for a resolution recognises that this agreement is not the best way to protect pedestrians in the long run. what if one of the partners fails to act? it is not as binding or as transparent as legislation, and there is a real lack of confidence expressed by the pedestrian protection bodies. the car industry itself admits – and none of us can be happy about this – that it has not been proactive in the past 22 years. phase i will take five years to implement, with phase ii in 2010 and a review in 2004. we are taking only a first step. the car industry states that the framework allows it to move forward more quickly, that a directive will slow down implementation. but we ask the commission to come forward with a framework directive that will lay down a clear timeframe and detailed monitoring methods because at the end of the day we must protect the most vulnerable and pedestrian safety in our communities is of the utmost importance.

mr president, it is important that the european parliament makes its views known on the deteriorating human rights situation in equatorial guinea. since march this year, opponents of president obiang's regime have been arbitrarily detained and tried under deplorable and unacceptable conditions. detainees have been subjected to brutal and inhumane torture and often prevented from contacting their families and lawyers. in some cases, detainees' family members have been arrested merely because of their connection to the accused. independent journalists reporting on political trials have come under extreme pressure, while several human rights organisations report that deaths have occurred from injuries sustained from torture while in detention. the nature and timing of the arrests lead me to detect a cynical attempt by the authorities to spread fear in advance of the elections due to be held next year. i believe the red cross should be given immediate access to detainees, international monitors should be introduced and arbitrary detention must be brought to an end. equatorial guinea is in clear breach of every human rights convention it has signed. it is undermining its own commitment to the union on democratisation and the full implementation of human rights. this union must take a firm stand with the authorities in equatorial guinea and demand that prior commitments be honoured. to speak of justice in that country is to speak the language of torture and of systematic brutality. this betrayal of core human values serves to remind us of the often-tragic gap between words and action and human rights in many parts of the world. this house must meet the challenge of bridging that gap with vigour and authority. we demand that the eu as a whole makes its concerns known to the authorities in equatorial guinea and call for an end to the current abuse of human rights.
mr president, since the attacks of 11 september, the malaysian government has stepped up its internal security measures, allegedly against suspected islamic militants. it increasingly resorts to the use of the internal security act, which allows it to detain people indefinitely without trial if, in the government's view, they are suspected of threatening national security. human rights groups have consistently criticised the abuse of this draconian legislation. the high court of malaysia has also called for the parliament to review its use. this resolution quite correctly calls for the abolition of the internal security act and any other laws that permit detention without trial. it is also clear that the government is using the pretext of the crackdown on terrorism as a means of suppressing government opponents and critics. the repeated use of the internal security act has often been politically motivated and politically selective. it has been used to arrest and detain without trial various members of malaysian civil society, including opposition leaders, academics, trade unionists and students, frequently without charging them and often denying them access to a lawyer. the resolution highlights the fact that some 40 political activists have been arrested since 2001 under the act. the resolution rightly calls for either the release or charging of all political prisoners of conscience, including the six political prisoners specifically named in the resolution, who have been imprisoned for exercising the right to legitimate political organisation and dissent. we want to see them either released or for them to be formally charged and receive an immediate and fair trial. in conclusion, i would urge that all future political cooperation with malaysia be conditional upon the malaysian government's abolition of the internal security act and also the release of all political prisoners, so that all malaysians may be assured that their basic human rights as enshrined in their constitution are respected.
