- the commission's statement on the stability and growth pact is on the agenda. this statement is important because it is closely linked to the economic and monetary policy of the union, because it encourages structural change in the budgetary management of many of our economies, because we are witnessing an economic slowdown and because it has sparked a debate on how to respond to it. if we are to have a debate on this subject, it is important that we act with a great deal of calm, reason and strategy. in recent days, this subject has been the subject of considerable controversy, triggered in particular by the remarks published in the newspaper le monde. i know that many members wanted us to be able to debate the matter briefly today, at the beginning of the week. i am glad that the president of the european commission is here today to make a statement on this subject on behalf of himself and the commission and then to have a short exchange of views.
president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is in an atmosphere of joy and confidence in the future of europe that i address you today. by approving the treaty of nice by a large majority, the irish people have clearly expressed their support for the ideals and designs of the european union. i would like to thank the prime minister, bertie ahern, and the president, pat cox, for their efforts. this will give us even more determination to go on the last stretch of the road between copenhagen and the final approval of enlargement. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is with pleasure, with great pleasure, that i have accepted your invitation to come here today to parliament, together with mr solbes, who will explain the commission's work and the current state of the economy. i am pleased to be here to discuss with you the question of economic policy coordination and, more specifically, the stability and growth pact. the theme i intend to play out before you is simple. economic and monetary union needs clear rules, effective rules and, above all, rules that are respected. this requires an authority which, in accordance with the rules laid down and within the framework of cooperation between the european institutions, is able to act in the interests of the common good by adapting economic policy responses to changing circumstances. the stability and growth pact is and has been valuable for economic and monetary union. the commission, as the faithful and loyal guardian of the treaties, has strictly monitored its application and will continue to do so in the future. as president of the italian government council, which promoted and approved the stability and growth pact and led the country into the single currency, and as president of the commission, i am deeply and intimately convinced of the virtue of the rules underpinning economic and monetary union and the stability and growth pact. i am a firm defender of these rules, of this union, of this pact. economic and monetary union has brought immense benefits to the states which share it and to the other members of the union. the time of the large deficits of the past few decades is over. the time has come for individual national currencies to be exposed to the winds of speculation. however, alongside these benefits, economic and monetary union also entails specific responsibilities, responsibilities for all: member states, european institutions and ordinary citizens. with a single currency, the euro, growth and employment in each member state depend not only on the common monetary policy but also on the fiscal policy of each member state. in economic and monetary union, stability is a necessary condition for growth and employment. the stability and growth pact has been the basis for defending and governing the culture of stability introduced by the maastricht criteria. on the other hand, however, to be aware of all the extraordinary things the covenant has enabled in the past and will still enable in the future does not mean refusing to see the limits of the framework within which we are called upon to apply it; it is even less a matter of applying the covenant rigidly and inflexibly, blindly and deafly in the face of changing circumstances. that's what i've defined and i define as "stupid". i do not think it is the role of the commission, my role as president of the commission, to apply the rules in this way. the commission was not appointed, i was not appointed to apply the rules blindly, turning a blind eye to the limits of such application. the european citizens have a right to know from us, and we have a duty to tell them what we believe is right and is working properly and what, on the other hand, we believe can and should be improved. politicians like you, economists, bankers, businessmen with whom i have spoken on this subject many times, have repeated for months and repeat in private, in everyday conversations, the same things that i have said openly, frankly and honestly in defence of the credibility of our institutions. it is time, therefore, that we learn to say in public the same things we say to each other in private. (applause) i would like to thank citizens are suspicious of us and our institutions, not least because they think that public debate is limited to marginal issues while the real decisions are taken behind closed doors. i am therefore pleased and proud that parliament is at the centre of this important debate today. the pact is and should have been simple, but the reality underlying the pact is complex. it is therefore part of the responsibility of the european institutions to grasp the complexity and diversity of the economies of the member states - large and small alike, with the same criteria - just as it is part of this responsibility to keep our eyes wide open to the turn of events, in our continent as in the rest of the world. we have seen the deterioration of the european and world economic cycle: the deterioration was so marked that a significant part of the world economy was exposed to a deflationary danger that was thought to have disappeared. at the same time, we had to acknowledge that the pact had failed to prevent some member states from adopting fiscal policies which were not consistent with the objective of stability. what should we have done under the circumstances? should we have taken a hard line, trying to force the countries with the highest deficits to maintain their budgetary targets, without any regard to changes in the economic situation? should we have added a new mistake to those made in the past when countries still far from balance had not been able to seize the opportunity offered by strong growth to put their internal accounts in order? this, ladies and gentlemen, would have been a misapplication of the pact: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the single currency is not used as a barrier to trade. if they had tried to impose objectives which were now unrealistic, the european institutions would today be accused of acting against growth and employment. i, on the other hand, want europe to win the battle of stability as well as the battle of growth. it would be a tragedy if, in order to win the battle for stability, we lost the confidence and support of our citizens, the confidence and support which are the basis of the democratic europe you represent. (applause) i would like to thank for this reason, we put forward ideas last month to make adjustments and to adopt more refined criteria in the implementation of the pact, so as to make it an increasingly intelligent instrument for stability and growth. we suggested setting objectives that would lead to balance and identifying the instruments for controlling this path. we have also suggested that, in this difficult time, we should give more breathing space to those countries which still need to adjust, and that we should draw up more realistic paths for consolidating deficits. these are criteria which ensure both stability and growth; indeed, they allow stability and growth to reinforce each other. these criteria apply to all member states, large or small, to the benefit of all countries of the union. these are ideas which are, ladies and gentlemen, fully consistent with what we have been saying for a long time. last year, in our communication on strengthening economic policy coordination, we proposed some important improvements within the current institutional framework. as you may recall, we proposed: develop economic information and analysis for the euro area; to strengthen the statistical system underpinning it; to clarify the common principles of fiscal and structural policies; and finally, to improve the effectiveness of our decision-making system. looking specifically at the recent experience of portugal, which was forced to revise its statistical series substantially, i would particularly like to stress how clear it has become that an adequate system of monitoring of statistics on budgetary positions is essential. we will also be following this line when, as stated in the conclusions of the barcelona european council, we will shortly be putting forward our proposals to improve both the transparency and the rigour of the pact. we will do so by seeking to clarify both the core concepts of the pact and the basic principles which should guide national budgetary policies, so as to take full account of the reality of european economic integration. we will show, for example, how the need for clear rules can be made compatible with the recognition that the rules of the pact apply to countries with different situations in terms of debt levels, financial commitments arising from an ageing population and urgent public investment needs. the stability and growth pact, when applied in this way, will be able to fully express its nature as an instrument for the coordination of economic policies, beyond its predominantly disciplinary aspects: the european council has adopted a resolution on the future of the european union, which is fully and finally consistent with the strategy for growth and jobs adopted by the european council in lisbon two years ago and which parliament has always strongly supported. new and better rules are not, however, enough. the protection of the common european interest requires that, once those rules have been adopted, there is the capacity to put them into effect. if we really want to solve the problems of growth and employment in europe, we must achieve coordination of economic policies, including the necessary structural reforms, coordination that is not only smarter but also more effective, more applicable. (applause) i would like to thank responsibilities for the coordination of economic policies must be clearly defined. the european citizens must be sure that the system has a reliable guide, a guide capable of ensuring the coherence and direction of the system, both in times of calm and, even more so, in times of difficulty or crisis. you will remember, ladies and gentlemen, that i raised this question with you two years ago and that i have returned to it several times since. we need an authority that has the power to steer the system in a way that, given the complexity of our economies, is both rigorous and intelligent; a body of law which is able to act in the interests of the common good, so that each member state adopts economic policy measures which prevent its economy from having a negative impact on the economies of other member states. only a strong authority can at the same time apply the rules rigidly to avoid deviating behaviour and adapt the rules to changing circumstances where necessary. i want to be even clearer on this point. budgetary policies are the responsibility of the authorities of the member states. that is the way it is today and that is the way it will be in the future. the commission, for its part, is an institution whose sole mandate is to act in the service of europe's common interest and in full equality between all the member states. this very nature makes the commission the natural candidate to exercise, on the basis of the mandate and the rules laid down by the council and under the control of parliament, the role of driving the system which must ensure the coordination of economic policies at european level. there are many examples of the desirability of entrusting this responsibility to an independent and impartial arbiter such as the commission. i would like to mention just one today, and i want to mention it precisely because it relates to a very controversial case: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council. well, as you all remember, that proposal was not accepted. nevertheless, both the council and the member state directly concerned agreed with the substance of the measure proposed by the commission and in fact adopted it. the failure of the decisionmaking mechanisms, however, remained evident. in its first formal contribution to the convention's work, the commission therefore put forward proposals to prevent such situations from recurring in the future, suggesting that the treaty should certify the authority to issue such early warnings. it also proposed amendments to the treaty to integrate economic policy coordination more fully into the framework of interinstitutional cooperation guaranteed by the community method. finally, it put forward proposals to respond fully to the need for a unified representation of the euro within international bodies. these are the proposals we have put forward, ladies and gentlemen, at the convention. but there is nothing to prevent some of these proposals from being adopted today. these are changes which are already of great importance but which will become even more so with the forthcoming enlargement of the union. we therefore the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the taxation of savings income. i share president prodi's conviction that the stability and growth pact is an essential regulatory framework within the union's institutional system, providing member states with rigorous, yet flexible rules for the union to meet the challenges that arise in the short, medium and long term. over the last four years, the commission has repeatedly stressed that compliance with the medium-term budgetary equilibrium rule is the best way for fiscal policy to play its stabilising role in the economic cycle. of course we need to put more emphasis on cyclically adjusted balances when we analyse fiscal positions, and we have been working along those lines. this will make it easier to avoid expansionary fiscal policies when economic growth is strong and thus enable us to meet the possibility of implementing non-restrictive fiscal policies in periods of low growth. the pact has also provided us with a suitable framework to meet the challenges of fiscal policy in the medium term. we all agree that tax and expenditure reforms are essential to increase the union's growth potential, and the commission has stressed that a correct interpretation of the rules of the pact provides a proper benchmark for assessing whether these reforms actually improve the quality of public finances. finally, the pact has also shown that it is able to incorporate the challenges we face in the long term, especially those related to the ageing of the population. a majority of member states are now well placed to allow fiscal policy to play its countercyclical role in the current economic climate, when growth is forecast to be slower than expected at the beginning of the year. the average growth in the euro area in 2002 will be below 2%, and we expect to reach average potential growth over the next year. in this context, the lower than expected growth is only partly explained by the divergence from the budgetary objectives formulated at the beginning of the year. in some countries, overly optimistic projections of income and expenditure trends have been influenced, but also some slippages from the policy forecasts. as a result, the area's budget deficits will amount to more than 2% of gross domestic product this year, instead of the 0.9% forecast. in this context, and in line with the vision of the pact i have just outlined, president prodi and i presented a strategy at the end of september on how to deal with the current budgetary challenges. to strengthen the implementation of the pact, while taking account of the complexity of economic reality, we proposed a strategy based on four points: first, the 3% of gdp deficit threshold is, and will remain, binding and any breach of this threshold will require corrective action by the member states concerned; second, the pact objective of a budgetary position close to balance in the medium term, and the adjustment path towards it, should be interpreted in terms of adjustment to the cycle; third, countries that have not yet achieved the target of a budget close to balance should achieve a reduction in their structural deficits of at least one half-point of gdp per year; and, finally, in strong growth years, any procyclical budgetary easing that may lead to a breach of the budgetary balance norm should be considered a breach of the pact provisions. these four principles reinforce the implementation of the pact and explicitly incorporate the effects of cyclical developments in budgetary surveillance. i am pleased that two weeks ago in luxembourg the eurogroup ministers took a similar position and supported this proposal. all countries, including those in deficit, except france, have accepted this approach and are making efforts to implement it from 2003 onwards. the budgetary situation is particularly difficult in four countries which were unable to consolidate their public finances during the period of strong growth: portugal, germany, france and italy. the deficits in some of these countries are dangerously close to, if not above, 3%. i am aware that in these countries adjustment is necessary in order to achieve substantial budgetary balance, but i also believe that it is crucial to make this adjustment so that each country can create enough room for manoeuvre for the automatic stabilisers to operate fully. in the case of portugal, last week the commission took a number of important decisions in connection with the excessive deficit procedure and in our opinion to the council we concluded that there is such a deficit in portugal. there are indications that germany will exceed 3% of the deficit in terms of gdp. in france, the deficits are dangerously close to 3%, and no significant adjustment is foreseen next year. in italy, apart from the significant deviation from previous targets, the apparent interruption in the reduction of the still very high debt levels is a matter of concern. if official notifications or the data in the commission's possession confirm such prospects, as we agreed in the amsterdam declaration, the commission will apply the provisions of the treaty. these are the thoughts i have on behalf of the commission on the economic situation and the budgetary outlook. i am happy to share them with you as representatives of the european citizens, as we have done on previous occasions, and of course to answer any of your doubts or questions.

pharmaceutical interests, health stores and numerous individual constituents. each group has its own particular concerns, but one common theme emerges: the proposed legislation does not take sufficient account of the different situations in the member states. this is surely a lesson for the commission. in an ideal situation, the legislation proposed would take account of such diversity. we in ireland breed horses primarily for sporting purposes and meat does not end up at the end of the food chain. consequently, the same safeguards are not required for medicines given to horses. i could cite many more instances and i have tabled a number of amendments for my group to deal with some of the difficulties. i would say to the commission that if we are to guarantee the democratic legitimacy of decision-making, we must reassure our citizens that their specific concerns have been taken into consideration. if we proceed with 'one size fits all' legislation which ignores the particularities of individual countries or regions, we risk alienating our citizens. in conclusion, we have just concluded a long referendum campaign in ireland, with a successful outcome for the nice treaty, and one of the major issues throughout the campaign was the sense of powerlessness and distance. we, as legislators, have a responsibility to ensure that we bring the people with us and keep mr president, i welcome mr duff's report. it important that we incorporate the charter of fundamental rights into the existing european union treaties, but i also hope that the european convention on human rights will be incorporated into the eu as an institution and not simply into the legal systems of the individual member states. it is unthinkable to have a modern european union constitution – which is what the convention on the future of europe is looking at – without a binding bill of rights. if the convention drafts such a constitution without the charter it will, in my view, be a disgrace. far from giving more rights to the european union institutions, the charter limits the exercise of power by the eu institutions because they must explicitly respect human rights. the charter should be legally binding and enforceable under eu law. it is not, as the rapporteur says, a substitute for the fundamental rights systems of the member states but a complement to them.

mr president, yet again we are discussing the issue of terrorism in the context of the appalling atrocity in bali in which hundreds of people lost their lives. like others, i want to express my deepest sympathies to the relatives and friends of those who have died. i agree with most, though not all, of what has been said here. it is clear what needs to be done: respect for the rule of law, protection of rights, scrutiny of the action our states take to deal with terrorism, democratic dialogue to try and deal with underlying issues and so forth. all are very necessary. what more can one add? it seems to me that one thing we can add is the notion that we are not going to destroy terrorism by simply killing or imprisoning those who carry out these acts. of course, it is not the poor in general who carry out the acts but those responsible for the acts are often poor. we have to try and deal with the hopelessness that motivates them. we have to try and overcome the idea that there is one true faith, one true version of history and one version of truth expounded by the chosen ones. i am not speaking here just of religion but also of politics. we must try to engage with people, so that we can open their minds and our own to what underlies their hopelessness. it is not enough to contain terrorism, although i have no doubt of the power of our states to do so. not all the european union member states have experienced terrorism since the end of the second world war, but a significant number have. that is quite extraordinary, considering that we are one of the most stable and peaceful regions in the world. we need to engage in education in the real sense, to open minds to the fact that the world is extremely diverse and could be a very tolerant and good place to live if we could only live with each other.
mr president, nothing justifies the use of terrorism. equally importantly, there should be no ambivalence about this evil. but, regrettably, this is not always the case. when the united states justifiably initiates a global campaign against organisations responsible for terrorism and the regimes that sponsor it, it is important for us to remind them that they allied themselves to osama bin laden and saddam hussein when it suited their foreign policy objectives. in addition, condemnation of terrorism rings hollow when they fail to take a strong line against the incidences of state terrorism committed by israel, which have the potential to create future generations of terrorists in that region. just as i would criticise the united states, i am not blind to the inconsistency of the eu on these issues – the council in particular. for example, during the present global fight against terrorism we have, on occasions, turned a blind eye to the shortcomings of the undemocratic regimes we have enlisted to support us. whether for geopolitical reasons, in the case of pakistan, or giving precedence to trading interests over human rights, in the case of china, we have at times failed to take a strong and consistent line against countries whose very structures of government are based on instilling fear in their citizens. they flout democratic principles, abuse human rights and ignore the rule of law. inconsistency and hypocrisy such as this leaves the west in general open to the charge that it is selective in its definition of terrorism and is primarily influenced by the perceived threat to western interests. a global fight against terrorism will be successful only if it is free of inconsistency and hypocrisy in its approach and if it tackles the injustices that feed terrorism in the first place.
mr president, like other speakers, i think it is deplorable that nothing has happened since parliament's echelon report. people still do not feel adequately protected. the council should adopt a framework decision which provides protection against the activities of intelligence services of other member states or third countries. the very existence of systems for the indiscriminate interception of communications is a violation of article 6 of the eu treaty, as the commissioner himself has recognised. it is also essential that an agreement should be negotiated and signed between the european union and the united states, stipulating that each party should observe the provisions governing protection of the privacy of citizens and the confidentiality of business communications. my group is strongly opposed to the actions taken by the council with a view to bringing telecommunications interception capabilities into line with the new technologies. we particularly oppose the adoption of the directive under which member states may, inter alia, adopt legislative measures providing for the retention of data for a limited period. the presidency needs to produce some sort of strategy to bring an end to the existence within the european union of parallel data protection systems and the proliferation of monitoring authorities – for example schengen, europol or customs conventions. they work on the basis of differing protection standards and outside true democratic and legal scrutiny. finally, the promotion of encryption cannot be a substitute for efforts to find political solutions – more strict legal guarantees and effective parliamentary control, for example. to say that encryption will solve our problems is an admission of failure.

mr president, over the last month, serious momentum has been building up with regard to the process of eu enlargement and the fulfilment of our political vision in this respect. in fact, a trinity of events has taken place which has guaranteed that the pace of eu enlargement has accelerated and is now an unstoppable process. firstly, on 9 october 2002, the commission concluded that 10 candidate countries were in a position to accede to the european union. secondly, on 19 october 2002, the irish people approved the provisions of the treaty of nice, which ensure that eu enlargement can take place within an agreed timeframe. thirdly, the eu leaders in brussels on 24 october 2002 endorsed the findings of the european commission that 10 countries fulfil the necessary political and economic criteria to assume membership of the eu by 2004. i welcome the brussels summit decision to allow the european union to present negotiating positions to the candidate countries on all outstanding issues by early november. this will ensure that enlargement negotiations can be concluded by the copenhagen summit of eu leaders in december 2002. a target date of april 2003 has also been set for accession treaties to be signed in athens under the presidency of the greek government. there are now elements of both legal and political certainty with regard to the enlargement negotiations. we are shortly going to cross the final hurdles so as to bring about the accession of 10 new member states to the union. the momentum towards eu enlargement is bringing real challenges to the eu institutions in terms of implementing the internal changes as laid down in the treaty of nice. this includes a range of issues including the extension of qualified majority voting at council level, the re-weighting of votes in the council, the extension of codecision measures to the european parliament and the reform of the european commission. the future financing of eu enlargement was a centre-stage issue at the brussels summit. it is clear from the presidency conclusions that the financial perspective, as laid down in berlin in 1999, is going to be respected in its entirety. the cost of the eu enlargement will be borne from within the budgetary parameters of the berlin agreement. it is also clear that programmes such as the present cap arrangements for the period 2000-2006 are not going to be affected by the decision of the eu leaders in brussels. this is only right and proper because our farmers, their families and rural communities were all given legitimate expectations by the cap deal of spring 1999. they were told how the common agricultural policy was going to operate for a seven year period until 2006 and they were basing their commercial decisions on this framework as laid down in the berlin agreement. as the corollary decision to this decision taken by the eu leaders, the mid-term review of the common agricultural policy will be just that – a review of the cap rather than a reform. this may not be music to the ears of the proponents of sweeping cap reform but that is the reality of the conclusions of the brussels summit. in conclusion, when it comes to addressing the challenges of eu enlargement, certainty, determination and commitment are all words that can be used to sum up the opinions of the vast majority of the people living in europe as well as those of legislators working on these important issues within the different eu institutions.
mr president, the danish presidency is indeed to be congratulated on its skilful handling of the negotiations which resulted in a successful outcome to the two-day summit in brussels. agreement on the financial aspects of enlargement has removed the last major obstacle which stood in the way of concluding the accession negotiations with ten countries at the december copenhagen council. i welcome the fact that in relation to the sensitive area of the future financing of the common agricultural policy that eu leaders agreed that direct payments to farmers in current eu member states would remain stable until 2006. this will guarantee the continuing goodwill of current eu farmers towards enlargement. if this is to be maintained, it is important that degressivity is not introduced after 2006. on a related issue, it is important to note that some concerns had been expressed that the applicant countries would have been able to export food products which were not up to current eu food safety standards. i should add that these concerns were not necessarily motivated by opposition to enlargement. they were rather more influenced by a wish to prevent any repetition of the bse and foot and mouth disasters. i am therefore pleased that one of the important declarations at the summit confirmed that there would be a safeguard clause on food safety included in each of the accession treaties. under it, if a candidate country does not meet eu safety standards, it will not be allowed to sell food products in the internal market. as well as reassuring consumers, it will also remove another weapon from the armoury of those who have reservations about enlargement going ahead as quickly as possible. i would like to conclude by not only congratulating the danish presidency once again and welcoming the fact that its confidence proved to be right, but also by wishing it a similar success at the copenhagen council.

mrs malmström and mr schulz have raised the question of turkey and what decision can be imagined to be taken at the copenhagen summit on turkey. first of all, i would like to point out that the very crucial decision that turkey is now a candidate country was taken back at the helsinki eu summit in 1999. turkey is a candidate country, as the eu decided in 1999, and i am of the clear opinion that turkey as a candidate country should be treated like all other candidate countries. this means that turkey can be given a date for the start of accession negotiations if and when it meets the political criteria. but it is also important to stress that the political criteria must be fully met for the country to be able to obtain such a date. turkey should not be measured by a different standard than other candidate countries. turkey must be treated exactly like other candidate countries. we have expressed our appreciation at the brussels european council for the progress made. the commission has made it clear in its progress report that turkey does not yet meet the political criteria. we will of course be following very closely the political developments in turkey after the elections and we must then find a balanced solution at the copenhagen summit. i think it is too early to give a definitive answer today on what decision may be taken at the copenhagen summit, but let me stress that in order to get a date turkey must meet the conditions like all the other candidate countries. the second theme that has been raised from several angles is agriculture and the budget. mr poettering began by asking why the long-term financial perspectives are even being discussed at the eu summit here in brussels. the answer is very simple: it was a prerequisite for the presidency and the commission to be given a mandate to complete the negotiations with the applicant countries, because certain countries demanded that a decision be taken on the long-term financial perspectives. i have always been of the opinion that no new preconditions should be set for a decision on enlargement of the european union, but we reached this compromise, which i think is a reasonable compromise. then mr barón crespo and mrs malmström asked: does the decision taken at the eu summit in brussels mean that we can still discuss reforms and agricultural policy? i would like to make it clear that the eu summit in brussels did not expressly take a position on the question of future reforms of the agricultural policy; therefore, the conclusion is that the commission's mid-term review is still on the table. the council will continue to examine the commission's mid-term review of the agricultural policy. i know that there is a debate this evening, in which the danish minister for food will take part as president of the council, and that is an indication that the mid-term review is still on the table. i can refer to some important words in the conclusions of the brussels summit, namely paragraph 12, which states that without prejudice to future decisions on the common agricultural policy and on the financing of the union after 2006, or to any results resulting from the implementation of paragraph 22 of the conclusions of the berlin european council, and without prejudice to the international commitments the union has entered into, in particular in connection with the implementation of the doha development round, direct payments would be introduced, etc., etc. these are very important words, because it means that the eu can of course still live up to its international obligations in the framework of the doha negotiations, and it also means that the mid-term review is still on the table and can still be negotiated and will be decided in accordance with the procedures applicable to it in the council. so there have been questions about the security clauses. mrs malmström and others have also been involved in the question of the safeguard clauses. i would like to emphasize that there are two types of security clauses. there is one general safeguard clause and two special safeguard clauses. the two special safeguard clauses concern the internal market and justice and home affairs. as regards the general safeguard clause, it is symmetrical in the sense that it can be required to be implemented by both old and new member states. as regards the special safeguard clauses, they can only be applied to the new member states, but it is an important point that the existence of these safeguard clauses is actually to prevent them from being applied; they are applied only if the new countries do not comply with the acquis they have committed themselves to comply with, and since we expect them to comply with this acquis, it is hoped that it will not be necessary to apply safeguard clauses either. i would like to stress that the general security clause is also known from previous enlargements of the european union. in fact, we've always had safety clauses. i can mention that when my own country - denmark - joined the then ec, there was a safeguard clause for a period of five years! so the only thing that was more important was that five years were required. when spain and portugal joined the eu, there was a safeguard clause for up to seven years. when sweden, finland and austria joined, there were safeguard clauses lasting up to one year. we already know the security clauses, and therefore there is no discrimination against the new members. then there is kaliningrad, which mr poettering was in on, which mr titley was in on, as was mr brock. i would just like to say to mr poettering that the eu-russia summit was not moved to brussels at the request of russia - it was a decision taken by the danish government without anyone having asked us to do so. we are not going to put ourselves under pressure, but i am not going to waste time discussing with anyone where a summit should be held. if mr putin does not want to come to copenhagen, we can go somewhere else. i don't want to waste time on this. we give priority to the enlargement of the european union; therefore i do not concern myself with diplomatic and protocol questions about where meetings should be held. the most important thing is that the meetings are held and we discuss the issues that need to be discussed and reach the decisions that need to be made. i hope that we can then reach a decision on kaliningrad at the eu-russia summit. a decision which must be in line with the principles emphasised by several members of the european parliament, namely that whatever solution is found must be based on full respect for lithuania's sovereignty. i would like to stress here that, in principle, enlargement of the european union can take place without a solution to the kaliningrad question. if there is no solution, then the visa will be introduced. it's that simple. but we all have an interest in finding a solution in common with russia, because we have an overriding interest in developing a strong strategic partnership between the eu and russia. but russia does not have a veto over the enlargement of the european union. we must try to find a sensible solution for transit from russia to kaliningrad, but this must be done in full respect of lithuania's sovereignty. the danish presidency is watching over this. let me thank you again for a very fruitful debate. with a debate on the future of europe, with a proposal for the framework for a new constitutional treaty and with the possibility of concluding accession negotiations with 10 new member states in about a month, we are in the midst of crucial decisions, we are at the beginning of a new era in the history of europe. and the enlargement of the european union is the driving force behind all this, it is the key to europe's future. the european parliament, the commission and the presidency have worked together to achieve enlargement. the goal is now in sight and we have today confirmed our common determination to pursue this great cause and to conclude the first round of enlargement negotiations in copenhagen by december. mr president, this new directive outlaws tobacco advertising in the printed media in the whole of europe and will also prohibit the advertising of tobacco products on radio and on the internet. equally, sponsorship by tobacco companies of events or activities involving several member states will be outlawed. as eu legislators we must bring forward proposals which will help to protect the health of our citizens and i believe that the dangers for our health from cigarette smoking must be vigorously highlighted at every opportunity. in fact we have a moral obligation to do more than to warn young people, in particular teenagers, of the acute dangers of cigarette smoking for our health. a recent survey has suggested that child smoking in germany alone has increased by up to 50%. the cigarette industry claimed that their cigarette products are for adults, yet every piece of practical evidence suggests that clever marketing and advertising only results in recruiting the next generation of smokers, who are teenagers. the budget for the european commission to highlight the dangers of cigarette smoking is only eur 6 million and this pales into insignificance when one looks at the staggering levels of money available to the tobacco lobby to put in place innovative pro-tobacco marketing and advertising campaigns. we need to do more to spell out clearly to young people the brutal consequences for one's health from cigarette smoking – that three thousand people in europe die every day from cigarette smoking. this means that a half a million citizens die needlessly in europe each year because of an addiction to tobacco products. cigarette smoking is the single biggest cause of premature death and illness in the whole of the european union. a recent study shows that american male smokers lose 13 years of life to the habit of cigarette smoking and that woman smokers lose 14 and a half years of life from smoking. if we are going to put in place comprehensive marketing campaigns to warn young people of the dangers of smoking, we need the necessary financial resources to oversee such a programme. the commission, parliament and the eu governments must substantially increase the financial budget for public health campaigns which highlight to teenagers the real dangers of smoking. preventing tobacco-related illnesses would do more to help the citizens of the union than any other life-saving measure, and tobacco companies are wrong to claim that advertising does not promote smoking but only promotes brand loyalty for a legal product. advertising does have an influence in promoting smoking; that is why all member states in europe have rules which restrict or ban tobacco advertising in some shape or form. advertising for other legally sold products including pharmaceuticals and alcohol is similarly restricted. this directive does not mean that member states cannot bring in more stringent measures to curb cigarette smoking if they so wish. matters falling outside the remit of directives, such as indirect advertising or billboards and cinema advertising, remain within the competence of the individual member states.
madam president, i fundamentally disagree with many of the aspects of the european commission's proposals on the reform of the common fisheries policy. however, it is true that a more balanced approach is needed. the current com on fisheries policy has not been a success. it has not done any favours – and in some cases has been discriminatory – to irish fishermen. the opportunity must not be missed to redress the current imbalance during this reform process. that is what irish fishermen are asking for at the moment, and that is what i am asking for. one of the issues which is currently being discussed relates to the issue of access to the irish box. the spanish government, for example, is claiming that it is entitled from next january to even greater access to the irish fishing waters. this simply cannot be allowed to happen. it would have absolutely disastrous consequences for irish fishermen, their families and irish fishing communities. fish stocks in the irish sea at the present time are at a precariously low level. opening up our waters to more spanish vessels than is presently allowed will only result in a decimation of our stocks. the irish sea is a biologically very sensitive area. it is the spawning ground for many of our fish species. only last week parliament's committee on fisheries passed an amendment stating clearly that fish balances shall not be disturbed in western waters and therefore it is in this context that relative stability must be understood. we must protect fishing regions where our fish stocks are under threat and the irish box and the irish sea is one such region. the last thing we want is to have our waters opened up to more effort by spanish fishermen, or indeed any other fishermen. we need to protect our fish stocks and not decimate them. any new conservation measures which are introduced at european union level must be brought about in consultation with all interested parties involved in all member states in order to protect what is a very valuable natural resource for all of us.
madam president, we make this subject sound very complicated but for me it boils down to two questions: how much fish can we take, and who can take them? if we could agree on those two questions, we would have an amicable solution to all the other questions that arise. i do not agree with those who say that the common fisheries policy is responsible for the present state of stocks. the reason the stocks are in their present state is because the scientists were not heeded. when the commission took the scientists' message to the council of ministers it was not heeded and its advice was not put into effect. i do not agree with the present policy, but within its framework stocks could have been conserved if the advice of the commission had been taken through the years. the other problem with the common fisheries policy is that on the one hand the commission has the responsibility but can merely give advice. the council of ministers and the individual states are the people with the ultimate responsibility. there is a lot of evidence that in the past they did not discharge their responsibility, without fear or favour, in a manner which ensured that every fisherman took what he was entitled to take and every ship got its quota and no more. the common fisheries policy goes too far. there was never any need to take fish into common ownership. it does not make sense. we have a common agricultural policy. it does not give me the right or an irish farmer the right to pick grapes or olives in the south of spain. it does not give us the right to harvest forests in finland or sweden. neither should the common fisheries policy include the common ownership of stocks. it makes no sense. as far as i know, nevertheless, there is only one country which loses out and gets less than its natural share. you will not find a more convinced european integrationist than i am, so i can say that there is one region in the union, the west of ireland, that does not get its natural share. i have no special quarrel with the spanish, french or british fishermen who come into what are natural waters. however, in other areas – oil and minerals – and in every form of jurisdiction member states have over their oceans, natural resources fall within the remit of the national governments. that should also apply to fish. it would make a lot more sense.

- the next item is the report (a5-0371/2002) by mr brok, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on enlargement: progress report (com (2002) 700 - c5-0474/2002 - 2002/2160 (ini)).
mr president, much work has been achieved in recent weeks to accelerate the enlargement process, but a number of difficulties have to be overcome before eu enlargement becomes a practical reality. we must not underestimate the challenges we face in the run-up to the accession of the ten countries to the european union. the eu convention must remember that many candidate countries are due to hold referenda on eu accession. we should make this as uncomplicated as possible for the people of the candidate countries. that is where the eu convention could be running into trouble: it is going too far ahead of the peoples of europe. are we seriously asking the candidate countries to ratify the accession treaty by referenda next year only to ask them a year later to ratify another eu treaty on more changes to the day-to-day operation of the union? what would the people of the candidate countries be basing their decision in next year's referenda on? on the existing eu treaties – including the recently ratified treaty of nice – or on an array of new proposals from the eu convention? have we not learnt anything from the recent referendum on the treaty of nice in ireland? the treaty was fairly modest by any standards, but it was very difficult to explain the issues to the people. we succeeded in part the second time round in explaining the treaty, but the lack of understanding of eu issues is still prevalent. however, some people at the eu convention are rushing ahead with extensive reform in all matters connected with the day-to-day operation of the union. we are presenting conflicting messages and proposals to the people of the candidate countries. in fact i would go further and say that the eu convention runs the risk of blurring the enlargement process. i must remind the house and members of the convention that the convention is a consultative process – the real decisions should and must be made by the council of ministers. let us not underestimate the amount of work which must be completed before enlargement becomes a working success. the candidate countries must implement the full range of eu directives and regulations. the enlargement negotiations are broken up into 38 different chapters. it is going to take the candidate countries time to implement this full body of legislation. we all know that the accession of ten new countries is not an easy task. the pace of reform is the main issue. diplomats and politicians cannot be allowed to run too far ahead of the people of europe on the issue of future developments. we need to bring the people of europe with us at each stage and we cannot take their support for granted. from an irish perspective, any future eu treaty that appears to supersede the irish constitution will be extremely difficult – if not impossible – to sell to the irish people. any proposals that diminish the representation of small member states within the eu institutions will fly in the face of the principles of equality that are the stated aims of the european union.
mr president, i welcome the opportunity to participate in this historic debate and i look forward to the day, which is now just around the corner, when the representatives of each of the candidate countries will exercise their full rights as members of this house and in each of the institutions of the european union. i welcome in particular the confirmation by the council of foreign affairs ministers yesterday in brussels of the full participation of the new member states in shaping the treaty that will follow the convention. one of the key negotiating chapters remaining open relates to agriculture. the conclusions of the recent brussels european council clearly rule out any negotiation on the berlin agreement and agenda 2000. this is the framework in which we must move forward to conclude the agricultural negotiations with the candidate countries. it is in the interests of all those countries which support a strong agricultural policy, be they existing or future member states, to see the fastest possible integration into the common agricultural policy.

president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am here with my colleagues from the commission to present our programme with a new initiative, which is not yet perfect and which we must perfect together, because i consider that this meeting is today, and will be even more so in the future, a sort of starting point for all our annual activity. i am particularly pleased that today's sitting crowns two days of particular importance here in strasbourg: yesterday there was the big meeting on enlargement, which gave me, i must say, a certain personal thrill, and today i am solemnly presenting, together with the college of commissioners, the legislative and work programme for the coming year. as i said, the method is new. following the criteria of our agreement last january, the main union institutions have in fact set up a structured political dialogue. i thank parliament once again for the valuable contribution it has made to this process, which, i repeat, is still experimental but which i think we have started well. as with any new system, the process will have to be improved, starting next year, building on experience for the future. however, the results we have already achieved are positive. i would like to mention here the most important new features of this method of work which the commission has followed this year. firstly, this programme, which is the result of a structured dialogue with parliament and the council, is intended to make a major step towards more integrated and coherent planning throughout the european union. that is why, following the indications of the european council in seville, it also intends to contribute to the first annual operational programme of the council. to this end, for the first time the programme contains not only our new proposals but also the main proposals which the commission has already adopted and which still need to be examined by the council. this will enable parliament to participate in the planning of this essential aspect of legislative activity. the commission hopes, however, that by the end of the year the three main institutions will be able to reach an agreement on the interinstitutional dimension of the programming process. secondly, our new working method is based not only on interinstitutional dialogue but also on a constant exchange of information in the operational phase and on the utmost transparency towards the citizens. in 2003, therefore, the commission will send to parliament and the council monthly reports on operational planning, reports containing a quarterly open programme and information on the proposals adopted. these documents shall be public and accessible on the web pages. mr president, better coordination between the institutions, planning of legislative work and information to the public are proof of our desire to give the institutions greater effectiveness and a solid democratic foundation. in doing so, we are putting into practice the guidelines adopted in last year's white paper on governance. these are not only technical innovations but also of great political significance. the commission's priorities for work - i shall speak only of the major priorities, and then, in the debate with the other members of the commission, we shall deal with all the specific aspects - are: an enlarged europe, stability and security, a stable and solidarity-based economy. these priorities have already been agreed by the council and parliament. in what follows i shall explain how the commission intends to put them into practice. we have already spoken about enlargement yesterday. today i only stress the commission's commitment to ensuring that all parties involved in the process are able to meet their responsibilities from the day of accession. the applicant countries will have to make the acquis communautaire their national law, but above all, their de facto law. for our part, however, i must stress the extreme urgency of redefining the architecture of the union to meet the challenges of 2004. enlargement has a qualitative dimension which cannot be underestimated. i trust the convention and the intergovernmental conference to translate the necessary indications into a real constitutional text for our union. the commission's other two priorities for 2003 are also closely linked to enlargement. the objective of ensuring stability and security remains at the top of the commission's concerns, as the harmonious coexistence and prosperity of citizens depend on it. they can only be achieved by balancing the fight against terrorism and crime with full respect for the freedoms and rights that characterize our political and social model. this will help to build an area of freedom, security and justice for the union. we must also integrate the surveillance of our external borders. this implies a special preparatory work for us and above all for the future member states, which will be managing most of the union's land borders, even though we know that the problem is not just about land borders; it is true, however, that most of these borders will have to be managed by the new countries. we also need to strengthen our policies on migration flows, the right to asylum and the integration of citizens who arrive legally on our territory. we need to put the need to integrate legal immigrants back into our societies at the heart of our immigration policy. now that we are enlarging the union and deciding on its new structure, it is essential to give new impetus to our policy towards the union's nearest neighbours. i am more and more convinced that we must build a global strategy for a ring of countries surrounding the enlarged union: from russia to the mediterranean. the debate on the final frontiers of europe, which i mentioned at my first meeting with you, has finally begun. i understand that it is very difficult, but one day or another this debate must be taken to the level of parliament and the people, because we are the ones who have to decide what the borders, the soul and the spirit of europe are, and i therefore believe that, without the participation of the citizens in this profound debate, it is difficult to give the matter a true, unifying aspect. i would say that we must break with the logic that puts sharply at odds those who are inside and those who are outside the union. i realize that this will not be an easy task, but we must devise and propose new forms of partnership, using all the instruments at our disposal. we cannot imagine borders as a wall, but we cannot even think of them as a kind of elastic band, constantly stretching or contracting. we must therefore base these proposals for cooperation on the principle which i have summarized in a way which is a little too succinct, if you will, but which gives you an idea of what i have in mind to share with these countries, from russia to morocco, everything but the institutions. it would be a bond stronger than a commercial relationship, stronger than mere technical exchanges, bonds which can - indeed, which must - involve a great deal of financial commitment, because they will have the great result of seeing europe surrounded by a ring of friends. this has always been our dream, but this, of course - i repeat - forces us to debate our borders sooner or later. there is no urgency, but these are problems our people cannot put off. finally, the commission intends to play its full part as a leading player on the international scene. our first task is the balkans: the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force. i would remind the house that this is not a problem to be feared from an economic point of view: the entire area of the balkans does not exceed by much more than 1% of europe's gross national product. so this is always a manageable problem. the political aspect is still delicate. the third priority for the coming year is, as i have said, economic policy. in the current economic climate, citizens are rightly asking what the union will do to boost growth and jobs. let us not forget that we must achieve the goals of economic prosperity that we have set ourselves: we have given them to ourselves and we must absolutely reach them. a few weeks ago we discussed in this house the coordination of economic policy and the stability and growth pact. in the coming days we will put forward our proposals to improve the way the pact is implemented - which must be respected - and to manage the policies of economic and monetary union in a more coordinated and stronger way. the underlying objective is to make public finances more sound and more sustainable. it is about applying these rules with intelligence and authority to foster employment growth. i am speaking of authorities, as i have done on several occasions, because these proposals are part of a wider strategy to strengthen coordination of economic policy and governance. to this end, we will improve the commission's evaluation and monitoring work and its proposing function in 2003. this will usher in a more agile approach, able to bring all our procedures within a single large coordination cycle. in this way we will better integrate the spring report on the state of play of the lisbon strategy with the broad economic policy guidelines and the employment guidelines. in 2003, the union's internal market will be ten years old, and it will be our task to present a report on the benefits it has brought to european citizens and consumers. however, we must not forget that, although we have made great strides, we have not yet completed the work in some areas: i am thinking of the services sector and particularly financial services. the year 2003 is also the deadline we have set for the integration of the capital market and the securities market. yesterday we took another step forward; now we must complete this work. i would like to express my concern to parliament at this point, outside the context of the speech. everything we're saying is based on a great effort of innovation. all the lisbon goals have been under the word 'innovation': the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. but i must say that, while we say that the main challenge that will determine all our actions must be the creation of a knowledge-based society, the resources that are allocated globally by the member states to innovation in europe are not increasing. and here is where a great appeal is needed: europe is not investing in research, development, innovation and human resources in general the minimum amount it needs to invest to be consistent with the lisbon objectives. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. i was concerned about an empirical analysis of the budgetary strategies of many european countries, where the first cut, in the face of difficulties, is precisely in this area of human resources. now, let us remember that, in the face of the challenges with the united states and, above all, in the face of the capacity for technology absorption that asia is showing, if we do not act in this direction, all our objectives of liberalization, progress and democracy will be put at risk. this is a fundamental problem. finally, our integration project is widely recognised as the only example of democratic management of globalisation. we must continue in this direction, especially at some difficult moments in our agenda. next year, in september, we will have the ministerial meeting of the world trade organization in cancún: the commission will be monitoring the implementation of the commitments made in kyoto, monterrey and johannesburg. in other words, we must respond concretely to the great hopes that the world places in us for an intelligent and open management of environmental, trade and development problems. indeed, europe remains the only hope for many people. it is true that, as i saw in johannesburg, we are increasingly being classed by the third world - which is suffering from increasingly serious tensions - as the bad guys, but there is still hope for europe, there is still this idea that we can bring a new idea of development. and i think next year will be decisive. it is clear from what i have said that economic, social and environmental aspects are now woven into a single fabric in the formulation and implementation of our policies. this development of our philosophy and our way of working was confirmed and given impetus by the conclusions of the european council in seville last june. the legislative and work programme i am presenting today is therefore a step forward in this european governance in which we are all engaged. the commission will therefore start next year to carry out the subsidiarity and proportionality analyses, as we have undertaken to do, for some 40 selected proposals and will study the economic, social and environmental consequences. such analyses simplify and replace the commission's current impact assessment tools. it is a question of starting a new method of work in a pragmatic and gradual way, which is why there are only 40 of them at present. from 2004, this system will become operational and will be integrated throughout the regulatory process, starting with the annual policy strategy, which we will present next february. this programme of work, ladies and gentlemen, is intended to give continuity and coherence to our political action by means of ever closer cooperation between parliament, the council and the commission. the discussions which preceded it confirm the value of the community method, especially when it is interpreted in a spirit of cooperation. we can give the system the operational impact and political perspective that the union needs to achieve its objectives. the project of european integration is almost half a century old, but in terms of its history and its operational system it is still very young. together, we are working and thinking about the future of the union. it is very important to take account of and exploit all the potential of the system to understand which elements really need to be reformed. and next year will be the decisive year for this action of ours. mr president, first of all i would like to pay tribute to all who served on the recent eu election observation mission to pakistan, particularly the members of my core team and also the european parliament delegation led by miss grönfeldt bergman. secondly, i would like to thank the eu commission personnel involved in election observation. thirdly, i would like to express my appreciation for the moral support and political solidarity extended by commissioner patten. regrettably, i am unable to add the name of the council and the presidency to the list of those i would like to thank. the reason is that i am very angry at the statement issued by the presidency concerning the election and i regret that the same sentiments were expressed today. i would like to seek clarification on aspects of the statement. how can the presidency commend the pakistan authorities for their cooperation with the mission when it was fully aware that we never received a formal invitation from the authorities and that they also refused to sign a memorandum of understanding, including an agreement to provide security cover. this information was officially reaffirmed in a démarche to the danish presidency six weeks after we arrived in pakistan. the presidency should also have been aware of the public attacks on the eom by several government ministers, using such inflammatory language as 'these western whites have no interest in peace in pakistan; these people come from unfriendly nations and have hostile objectives; this mission is interfering in the internal affairs of pakistan'. how can you regard this as cooperation? security cover was indeed finally provided for the second half of our mission, but it came from the provincial governors and not from the federal authorities. furthermore, in its statement the presidency expresses 'concern' about reports of manipulation – very mild indeed – and you ask the election commission to follow up such complaints. did you actually read our report? surely you are aware that we expressed serious criticism of the election commission and its lack of independence? to ask the election commission to investigate election malpractice is like asking saddam hussein to head the un weapons inspection team in iraq. i would like to remind the council that the mission i led was not a parliament mission, it was an eu mission consisting of 88 dedicated people, who discharged their task professionally in line with internationally accepted criteria for election observation. as you and the commissioner have said, they worked in a particularly sensitive political and security environment at great personal risk to themselves. yet within four days of our preliminary report being published in islamabad you effectively distanced yourself from our conclusions that it was a seriously flawed process. you did so despite the fact that member states received full weekly reports of our observations. i and members of my core team also briefed heads of mission in islamabad on a weekly basis. yet never once did anyone challenge our ongoing assessment. and even at the final debriefing of heads of mission in islamabad, little or no opposition to our analysis was expressed. ironically, by comparison, the presidency strongly criticised the elections in togo on 27 october, where there was no eu observation mission, yet you chose to ignore the conclusion of the pakistan mission that had been operating for two and a half months. why was the initial draft of your reaction to the election toned down? who influenced you? who pressurised you? and because your statement is being used by pakistan's embassies worldwide to undermine our report, you betrayed the eu mission you sent into the field and i say on their behalf, shame on you. i would also like to take the opportunity to refute the untrue allegation made by the pakistan ambassador in washington that the eu/eom leaked an interim briefing report. in fact this was leaked by an islamabad-based diplomat for a member state government, who was in europe at the time, and was designed to undermine the work of the eu/eom. returning to your reaction, not only does your response betray the eu/eom, it is a betrayal of the interests of the people of pakistan, especially those who are courageously working for the restoration of democracy. your failure to endorse the conclusions of the eu/eom and other observer groups such as anfrel, ndi and the commonwealth, compounds your predecessor's mistake in failing to criticise the farcical presidential referendum and is directly responsible for encouraging the government of pakistan to behave as it does. but as well as betraying the eu/eom and ordinary pakistanis, you are also betraying the ideals of your own presidency. let me remind you that in your own presidency programme, you set yourself the twin tasks of 'increased effectiveness and greater openness in the field of human rights'. the statement on the pakistan election showed little commitment to this. but worst of all, tailoring your response for geopolitical reasons was a total betrayal of the principles underlying election observation, which is designed to enhance democratisation and human rights.

mr president, i too wish to congratulate the rapporteur on attempting to find a compromise between the different points of view on this issue. however, as was said on a number of occasions in the committee on employment and social affairs, we are starting with a flawed proposal. it is flawed because we have moved away from the social dialogue and social partnership model where there was agreement between both sides of industry before a proposal came before this parliament. this has put us all in a very difficult position, because we who are supporters of social dialogue, of protecting the rights of workers and of increasing the opportunities for employment of all the peoples in europe want to ensure the best possible conditions for those most in need. whilst i have no difficulty with the general tenor or the general intent of this directive, a number of facts have to be recognised before we give greater protection to those who are in temporary work contracts under the aegis of agencies. firstly, there are various pieces of national legislation which already protect workers and this is merely duplicating or replicating what is already in place. secondly, we have different types of employment systems in each member state and a 'one size fits all' approach will not necessarily work. thirdly, temporary workers work temporarily by choice and sometimes they can earn more money as temporary workers in an agency capacity. fourthly, there is no provision in the treaties and no place in this parliament, the council or the commission for laying down conditions relating to workers' pay – that is still exclusively a matter for the member states. my last point is on the question of the six-week period. there are amendments tabled for this to be extended to a one-year period. this is far more sensible and practical from the point of view of protecting all workers' rights.
mr president, i want to congratulate mrs van den burg for an enormously well done job and the commissioner for introducing this directive. the kind of detailed work that is involved in this kind of directive is never adequately appreciated outside of this house. anyone who has watched the way in which mrs van den burg has worked on this directive will appreciate the enormous amount of commitment and expertise that had to be brought to it. we are trying to balance flexibility with security for workers who, in many countries, still do not have any security at all. we have been told here that national legislation already exists in ireland to protect these workers. that is not so. we are told that it is best left to the member states to deal with these matters. the irish experience will demonstrate that is not so. there are close to 100 000 agency workers in ireland. the european foundation for living and working conditions, based in dublin, published a study in may showing that there is no guarantee of equal treatment for agency workers in ireland and that there is virtually no legal protection for agency workers at all in ireland. that is a study carried out by a foundation funded by the european union. it also points out that ireland has failed to implement the 1991 health and safety directive covering agency workers. incidentally, ireland has also failed to implement the part-time workers directive and is now seriously out of line with the rest of europe on these issues. so it is not a good idea to leave these matters in the hands of member states – and certainly not a good idea to leave it in the hands of the current irish government, the ruling party of which mr crowley is a member. i would challenge him to back up his statement in this house tonight that there is already adequate protection for irish workers in this area. there is not adequate protection. there is none.
mr president, i regret that the concept of social dialogue has been jettisoned by the commission with this directive. with talks having broken down, it has run with the views of one side, namely the eu trade union, etuc, and has largely ignored the eu employers' body, unice. if social dialogue is to work, then there needs to be a more balanced approach to social measures, particularly in line employment policy at eu level and there is no economic or social justification for it. it could even constitute gender discrimination. in relation to article 5, the reference to 'essential' employment the views of only one social partner. the same applies to article 6 and the matters governed by points 6.2 and 6.3. these should be left to the discretion of member states. point 6.4 in article 7 temporary employee's perspective and that of an employer. my congratulations to our rapporteur, to the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, and the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities for their amendments. we need them, without them this would be inoperable.
