- the agenda calls for statements by the council and the commission on the preparation of the copenhagen european council of 12 and 13 december 2002, including the institutional aspects of enlargement.
president of the council. - mr president, commissioner, members and former colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, the forthcoming european council in copenhagen will play a decisive role in concluding the danish presidency. the agenda will concentrate on two subjects: enlargement and the functioning of the council in the light of enlargement. at the meeting, the president of the convention will inform the european council of the progress of the convention's work and the european council will also meet with the president of the european parliament, mr pat cox. let me start with the last one. the meeting with the president of parliament is a well-established tradition at meetings of the european council. it is a tradition which the heads of state or government attach importance to and value. it is important that the institutions have the opportunity to exchange views and discuss key european issues at regular intervals, as we do here today - and as the danish prime minister and i did last week when we had visits from mr prodi, president of the commission, and mr cox, president of parliament. i'm sure they have the meeting in their memory. if enlargement succeeds in copenhagen, as it should, it will be another result of the hard work and good cooperation of the institutions over the past few years. enlargement will be the main item on the agenda of the copenhagen european council. we have been going through some months of very high speed in the accession negotiations. we are now approaching the decision that will seal the reunification of the european continent. completion of accession negotiations with the first group of candidate countries with a view to admission on 1 may 2004. it's been incredibly difficult and complicated, and it's not solved yet. the good result achieved at the brussels european council has contributed greatly to the fact that it now seems possible to conclude the negotiations. as you know, the brussels european council concluded that 10 countries would be ready for membership from the beginning of 2004. these days are the final and decisive negotiations. the presidency presented a negotiating package for each of the candidate countries last week. these packages are the presidency's bid for the final negotiated solutions. the packages take account, as far as possible, of the views of the candidate countries, which have been presented at separate meetings with each country, and the packages are within the financial framework for enlargement - that is, within the berlin agreement and within the decisions of the european council meeting in brussels in october. the presidency hopes that we can go as far as possible in the negotiations leading up to the copenhagen european council. it is no secret that the final negotiations are difficult. with the right willingness to compromise on the part of both present and future member states, i am convinced that we will achieve a successful outcome. but the expansion does not stop in copenhagen. the european council will also give new impetus to the accession process of bulgaria and romania. the commission will be presenting a report on the implementation of the new financial perspective for the period 2007-13 and will be presenting a report on the implementation of the new financial perspective for the period 2007-13. the commission's communication of 13 november on a road map for the two countries makes a good contribution to this. at the last european council in october, the eu welcomed the renewed reform efforts in turkey. the eu countries agreed to underline that the many important reforms in turkey had facilitated the opening of accession negotiations with turkey. turkey's accession will be based on the same principles and criteria as those applied to the other candidate countries. the eu is preparing the decision on the next step in turkey's candidacy. this decision will be taken at the copenhagen european council. the presidency hopes that a solution to the cyprus problem will be found before copenhagen. the eu fully supports the efforts of the un secretary-general to find a solution. if the copenhagen summit fails to find a solution to the political conflict in cyprus, the eu will take its decision on the accession of cyprus in the light of the conclusions of the helsinki european council in 1999. the setting of the date of accession of the new member states has a number of institutional implications and it is of course important that parliament is fully involved in the consideration of these implications. i myself have had the pleasure of informing parliament at all stages of these considerations. i have already had the opportunity to discuss this at the last part-session in strasbourg, where the question was raised by mr barón crespo, among others, and also last week in the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, where we had a longer discussion on it. the presidency is very much aware of the great interest of parliament in these institutional consequences of enlargement. and we are willing to discuss these issues openly. at the same time, i must also point out the complex negotiating process on enlargement which is taking place at the moment. we must not simply reach agreement within the council (and the other institutions). we must also - and this is not the least of our tasks - reach agreement with the future member states. so we are talking about an ongoing, intensive process in which not all the answers are yet clear! the institutional questions are pressing. it is a necessary part of the whole enlargement. issues such as the weight of each country's votes in the council and its representation in the european parliament are a necessary part of the accession treaty. clear provisions for the transitional period need to be laid down now. this is a fundamental right, in line with the treaty. i would remind you that the european parliament will have to give its assent and that the treaty of accession must necessarily be ratified by both the existing and the new member states. the agreement on the date of accession on 1 may 2004 is based on a thorough consideration of what is desirable and what is possible in the light of the ratification process in both the present and future member states. we owe it to the future members not to delay admission any longer than absolutely necessary. i think that applies to all of us: parliament, the council and the commission. this means that certain transitional arrangements will be needed. this has been the case in previous enlargements. there have been proposals in parliament to hold elections to the parliament in 2004 at an earlier date, such as 9 may. i personally sympathize with these thoughts. the issue was discussed in depth for several years in the context of the revision of the recently amended common act on direct elections (published in the official journal of the european communities on 21 october 2002). every date has been reversed. no results from that. i regret to say that i do not think that any further attempts to change the date will be successful. but it is not the presidency that is standing in the way of a different and earlier date. i hope that parliament will understand the situation in which the commission will find itself in the period between the accession of the new member states and the inauguration of the new commission. it is not a good solution to redistribute the commission's portfolios for a period of only six months. the presidency would like parliament to give its consent to the fact that the interim commissioners of the new countries will not have to be consulted and approved by parliament. in this way we can avoid prejudicing the position of the new parliament towards the new commission. it is not acceptable for the new member states that 'their' commissioners should be approved by a parliament in which the new countries are not yet represented by members with voting rights. the proposed solution avoids prejudicing the choice of candidates by the president-designate of the commission in the composition of the new commission. it goes without saying that when the commissioners of the new countries do not receive a portfolio in the period leading up to the inauguration of the new commission, it does not make much sense for the parliament's technical committee to hear the new commissioners and examine them in areas of expertise which they do not have. i therefore hope that parliament will support our appointing the new commissioners by a simplified procedure during the transitional period until a new commission can be appointed with the full participation of the new parliament. finally, there is the question of the full participation of the new member states in the forthcoming intergovernmental conference. the new member states must be on an equal footing with the old member states in the negotiations which will shape our and their common future. and of course they must have the same veto as the old member states. that's all we know. i have tried to explain the complex institutional implications of enlargement. i look forward to our debate. i will listen very carefully and welcome any good suggestions for alternative, realistic solutions. the council will again discuss the institutional implications of enlargement at the general affairs council meeting on monday and tuesday. it has already been agreed that i shall attend the meeting of the committee on constitutional affairs on 10 december. the committee on budgets will be informed of the latest developments and discuss their significance. i think it is natural that the debate should take place in this committee, but should parliament wish to have another forum for the debate at the appropriate time on 10 december, i am of course available. the european council in seville instructed the danish presidency to continue its work on the question of the future presidency of an enlarged union. the presidency was to present a first report at the copenhagen meeting. there we shall have a first briefing on the subject. the presidency report operates on three models for the future presidency, and it touches on the question of strengthening the high representative and the question of the possible president-elect of the european council. the european council is not intended to decide on the models. the presidency will ensure that further work on the design of future presidencies is continued both in the council and in the convention, where it is included in the general discussion of the institutions. at the copenhagen meeting, a report will be made by the president of the convention on the progress of the convention. this dialogue is very important. the work of the convention is at a crucial stage with the presentation last month of a draft constitutional treaty. the discussions on the filling in of the framework presented by the president are progressing rapidly. it is now that the basis for the final product of the convention is being created. it is a good thing that the draft constitutional treaty has given rise to a european debate on the shape of the future europe. it is a good sign for our common ambition to create a more democratic and popular european cooperation. throughout the presidency, the presidency has worked to ensure that the work of the convention developed in accordance with the intention of producing a sound and well-worked input to the intergovernmental conference. as will be seen from the report, the european council is to tackle a wide-ranging and ambitious agenda at its meeting. i hope and believe that all the countries present will show the necessary willingness to compromise and contribute to the important decisions i have outlined here. we hope to be able to take a historic decision in copenhagen on the greatest enlargement in the history of the community to date, and i dare say the enlargement with the greatest consequences and the greatest historical prospects. the great enlargement debate which took place in parliament last month is just one more example of the strong will which this parliament has shown and the efforts it has made to make this project a success. and as i said at the beginning, this major project can only succeed if the three institutions work closely together. i think they have, and i would like to thank parliament again for the clear messages we have been given all along about the enlargement we are facing. commission. - mr president, at the end of this debate i am pleased to be able to say once again that there is broad agreement between parliament, the council and the commission on the question of enlargement, and that is an important political signal. i shall now turn briefly to the main issues of the debate. first, let us look at the money. i think that it will not surprise anyone that in the final phase of a negotiation process, which involves a lot of money, the stakes are raised in public and those who are supposed to pay say that this is too much for us and those who want to get something say that this is too little for us. that's perfectly normal, and i wouldn't get too upset about it! but the structural question is raised, and some members of parliament have rightly raised it, namely: are our rules really such as to allow new members who are poorer than the current average of the european union to benefit from the fact of membership in the first years of membership? that's the problem. well, what i see today, so that no one worries for nothing, is this: the presidency's proposal is that the new member states will receive over eur 9 billion net in actual payments in 2004, 2005 and 2006. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. this means that no one will be a net contributor, and everyone is much better off than in 2003. in terms of commitment appropriations, ladies and gentlemen, the figure is very impressive indeed, i must say, and the term 'greed' is not appropriate. the net commitment appropriations available for these three years are eur 25.7 billion. that's a word, given the size of the economies of these countries. we must not forget that the countries of eastern and central europe account for only 5% of the gross national product of the present european union. i would like to say that these figures are fairly balanced. but it is also true that both sides must keep reminding us that the european union is not a cash machine! you don't put a card in the top, a membership card or a credit card, and you take out money at the bottom. we're something completely different. we are a legal community whose aim is also to ensure that people enjoy equal living conditions, and we contribute to this, but only within the limits of the possibilities we actually have. mrs schroedter has pointed out a particular aspect, and i regret to say that i agree with her, namely that this proposal to make rural development funds available for direct payments is actually to be deplored from the union's point of view. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i must point out, however, that it was a very strong demand from the candidate countries themselves to be able to make a relocation, at least for the first three years. the argument is as simple as it is convincing: without this measure there is no chance of winning the referendum in poland, for example. that is the background to this decision, which i am happy to admit is certainly regrettable from the point of view of a sensible development of agricultural policy. on the subject of turkey, let me say this briefly: mr nassauer spoke to me personally, and i will say nothing in private but what i have said in public. what was quoted in the newspaper, i have said many times, also here in the european parliament, namely: if we had had the opportunity in 1999 to develop a strategy for turkey without the whole 40-year history we already had, i would not have come up with the idea of offering turkey full membership of the european union as the right solution. but the problem is, we didn't have that option. this option had already been tried, it had already failed and there was no other. the whole discussion of the last few weeks, which was also initiated by mr giscard d'estaing, has certainly not achieved the result that the former french president wanted. it has led to the fact that even those who now preferred not to speak - and there were a lot of people who preferred not to speak - were now forced to reaffirm the outcome of helsinki, namely that turkey has the clear candidate status, that it is treated like all other candidates, that its membership prospect is unlimited and clear and that it is encouraged to continue on this path. this is the result of the discussion in 15 member states as far as governments are concerned. i am well aware that there are different views in the public, sometimes even in the majority. but we know that the 15 governments of the member states are unanimous in their view that the helsinki strategy must be adhered to. in this respect, mr giscard d'estaing's contribution probably did situation in the first year of membership. the financial package for each country is completely different depending on which date you are working from. in this respect, the decision was necessary. i believe that the council has decided to do so, taking account, first of all, of the time required for ratification by the member states. that is something to consider, as i have said many times. as for the commission, i would remind you once again that it had proposed to avoid the transitional commission with 30 commissioners and therefore offered to shorten the term of office, but this proved to be non-negotiable. the candidate and member countries have taken the view that the new commissioners must be present from the first day of accession. i therefore think it is reasonable to act now of time needed to appoint a new president of the commission, to have him confirmed and to give him time to put together a new commission. that's the whole background. i think we can discuss this reasonably and, as i said, the commission is ready to do so at any time! mr president, first of all i want to be associated very much with the words of sympathy expressed with the people of galicia and i fully concur with the speakers and my colleagues who called for solidarity with them at this time. i broadly welcome the jové peres report in its present form. the commission proposal is based on the principle of sustainable development and the poor state of fishery resources. the starting point is indisputable but many views, including my own, differ as to the quantification of the state of stocks. the basis of the proposal is that account is taken exclusively of scientific reports as regards management measures. however, no credible measures are proposed to improve scientific knowledge even though the shortcomings in this area are well recognised. they envisage a common fisheries policy which is geared more to the short-term interests of some member states than to fishermen. i say to the commission that the cfp must be geared towards keeping alive regions which depend on fishing rather than making it a battlefield between member states. fishermen share common interests. they all need fishery resources to carry out their activities. decisions and objectives of the recovery plans cannot discard the social and economic consequences which they may have. recovery plans must seek a balance between the recovery and conservation of stocks and measures to limit the impact on the fishing industry. the exclusive coastal zone is something that irish fishermen are adamant about maintaining and so are fishermen from scotland, wales, england, france, portugal and holland, from denmark, germany and others – it is something that i am adamant must be retained. the basic objective of the 6 to 12 miles coastal zone regime was to protect fishery resources by reserving access to small scale coastal fishery activities. in general, this puts less pressure on stocks in these zones which often harbour nurseries in juveniles. it also contributed to protecting the traditional fishing activities of coastal communities, thereby helping to maintain their economic and social fabric. the current critical situation of many stocks makes it more urgent now than ever, not merely to roll out the 6 to 12 mile access regime which is totally inadequate, but rather to roll out the exclusive zone to 24 miles if we are serious about conserving stocks. i ask you to support my amendments to extend the exclusive coastal fishing zone to 24 miles. i have no doubt that the greater majority of your fishermen would ask you to do the same thing. because i regret the present unsatisfactory state of fish stocks and because i am in favour of conservation, i am adamant that highly sensitive areas must be protected. the irish box is one such area of very great sensitivity. waters in this zone are important spawning grounds, which is why there has been a derogation from free access in these waters. regrettably, this did not prevent the illegal plunder of stocks in the irish box over the years by some community fishermen flying flags of convenience. this plunder must stop. these waters must be protected. existing arrangements for access to the irish box must be retained permanently in the reform process. there is no bureaucratic replacement for the knowledge and experience of fishermen. for this reason, and for many years, my group has been calling for a greater involvement of fishermen in the ways the common fishery policy is run. the commission has now adopted this idea, which i welcome, by proposing the creation of regional advisory councils which will include fishermen and their organisations for the very first time. if these councils are to play a meaningful role in the future, fishermen must be involved in all phases of the management process. fishermen must also be more involved in the work of scientists in order to establish mutual confidence. only in this way can fishermen contribute to and influence community policy. i congratulate mr varela for both of his balanced reports. i agree with his analysis. i agree with his criticism. i agree with his proposed changes to the commission's proposals. i will be supporting his reports. in conclusion, let me say unequivocally, as i did during the debate on the stevenson report, that the common fisheries policy is not only about fish, it is also, and more importantly, about fishermen. it is about their families and their families' future. it is about their way of life, the only one possible in many areas.

the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i too am very pleased that these two important directives have now finally reached the final stage of the decision-making process. the fastest growing type of waste today is waste from electrical or electronic products. the average european produces about 14 kg of this kind of waste every year. most of it ends up in landfills or in incinerators. these new directives are important milestones which mean that it will be easier to deal with the future environmental problems that our waste may cause, by allowing us to sort out this type of equipment for reuse and recovery, and thus also reduce its potentially dangerous effects. the new directives will oblige member states to ensure that waste electrical and electronic equipment is collected separately from other waste. the directives also set binding collection targets of 4 kg per inhabitant per year from private households. this collection objective will be based on individual responsibility, as proposed by the european parliament. a number of hazardous substances will be phased out throughout the community from 1 july 2006, which means that many problems in the waste chain can be avoided before they arise. i consider these solutions to be a great success for the european parliament and for cooperation with the council in the conciliation committee. i would like to return the courtesy and thank the rapporteur, mr karl-heinz florenz, and all the members of the european parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee for their contribution to the constructive agreement which will be put to the vote on wednesday. this is an important step for environmental policy. once again, i would like to thank florenz, who is always easy to work with.
madam president, i would also like to thank the conciliation committee for its constructive work. it has been a very good success for parliament and indeed for the european citizens. waste from electronic and electrical equipment is now one of the fastest growing waste streams in the european union. as the commissioner has said, it constitutes almost 14 kilograms per head and is growing by at least 3% to 5% every year. electronic and electrical equipment is one of the largest known sources of heavy metals and organic pollutants in the waste stream. without proper pre-treatment the highly toxic components can contaminate soil and ground water, as well as polluting the air. the directive can be seen as one of the basic instruments for an integrated product policy, where the whole life cycle of a product will be taken into consideration and eco-design can be promoted. the need for business to adapt to a changing agenda, taking more account of environmental concerns, is becoming more widely accepted. indeed business and the environmental ngos have been on the same wavelength during this process, which is not always the case. it is also accepted that countries and industries which innovate more quickly will end up being more competitive than those which delay. the adoption of this directive will be a signal in that regard. the guiding principle behind the directive is the extent of producers' responsibility. the objective of the epr is to make producers financially responsible for their products when these become waste so an upstream effect is created which leads to design for the environment, taking account of the durability, repairability or upgrading, disassembly or recycling of the product. in addition there is reuse of resources and separate collection, and hazardous substances contained in the weee are prevented from entering the environment. the directive also applies the principle of internalisation of external costs. costs of disposal, which up to now have been borne by local authorities, usually as part of waste disposal, are now to be internalised and provision made for the reuse, recycling and demanufacture of this equipment. hence the ultimate aim is waste prevention, thus sustainability.
madam president, i wish to join with the others in complimenting all involved, particularly on bringing this through conciliation successfully. in particular, i congratulate my colleague, the rapporteur, mr florenz, on the passion he has sustained on this issue, despite all the various problems he faced from industry and the different political groups in this house, not least his own group. i thank him for his commitment and belief in both these directives. the restriction on the use of certain hazardous substances, on the one hand, and the prevention of waste electrical and electronic equipment on the other is what we are talking about here in the two directives before us. colleagues have indicated the rate at which weee is growing. it is interesting to know that it will grow three times faster than the average municipal waste by 2010 – quite a frightening concept. because of its hazardous content, electrical and electronic equipment causes environmental problems during the waste management process if it is not properly treated, sorted, separated, recycled, reused, contaminants removed etc. we can insist on improved product design, and that will facilitate recycling and the disposal of products at the end of their life. it is against this background that the two directives must be reviewed. i noticed that at conciliation the views concerned were unanimous – and that includes views from ireland, portugal, greece and other countries whose waste network and recycling systems are much less developed than in some countries in the eu. i hope our officials, ministers and others who agreed to the targets and timetables did so realistically, because we should not commit ourselves to something we cannot deliver. if it is only a matter of time before countries are dragged before the ecj for non-compliance or non-transposition of a particular regulation, this brings into disrepute legislation passed through this house. i am glad, but slightly concerned, that they were unanimous because they might not be taking seriously what is being required of them. knowing the state of 'underdevelopment' of recycling and waste management in my own country, ireland, for example, i sincerely hope they mean what they say in agreeing to this directive and i fully support the fact that they have done so. in relation to the weee directive, one of the issues that caused most angst among industry was the handling of historic waste: who would pay for it and so on. it is still a concern, as i understand from industry, even though they have accepted – perhaps somewhat reluctantly – that the only way to pay is collectively and fairly. each manufacturer of new products should cover its own costs, and the collection and treatment of all new products can be done collectively. the manufacturers will have to provide a guarantee prior to placing their products on the market to ensure the financing of subsequent disposal of the products – through insurance perhaps or a blocked bank account. in the event of the disappearance from the market of a manufacturer, such a guarantee would ensure that the costs do not have to be borne by society or by other manufacturers. finally, we should be realistic in terms of targets for and timetabling of the abolition of the dangerous substances, in particular lead and lead solder, and the concerns that have been expressed by industry. let us be sure that technologically we are able to replace with a safer product, as far as the environment is concerned, what we are about to ban.

mr president, the danish presidency set itself an extremely ambitious agenda for the copenhagen summit. as a result, two fraught days were spent in copenhagen negotiating a financial package, with divisions at one stage threatening to stall proceedings. however, once this had been resolved, the eu formally invited eight countries from central and eastern europe, plus cyprus and malta, to join in 2004. this was a momentous occasion in european history, finally bringing to an end the divisions created by the cold war. however, it must be said that enlargement is not yet complete. negotiations have still to be concluded with bulgaria and romania and have yet to begin with turkey. i endorse the commitment given at the copenhagen summit to start the negotiations with turkey in 2004, subject, of course, to a review on progress on human rights and rule of law issues. i have consistently argued that the accession of turkey could form an important bridgehead between east and west and help consolidate turkey as a secular democracy and a calming force in an otherwise unstable region. as a result of these momentous decisions, our new neighbours will be ukraine, belarus and moldova. now is the time to consider what sort of relationship we want to develop with these countries and how far we want it to go. in conclusion, i am pleased that the recent uncertainty regarding the timetable for enlargement, which was partly due to our rejection of the treaty of nice in the first irish referendum, has been removed. it will now proceed in may 2004, ironically under the irish presidency and indeed, mr president, during your final six months as president of this parliament. i look forward to welcoming the new accession countries into the eu family on that historic occasion.

mr president, i am deeply disappointed by the commission's statement here today. we have had more lip service to the principle of services of general interest. we were told that the commission was going to produce a framework for services of general interest before the end of this year, now we get a promise of a green paper. we urgently need the framework directive, not a green paper. we urgently need a change in competition law which enables services of general interest, public services, to survive and to prosper, and we need a clause in our new constitution which guarantees public services right across europe. solidarity and citizenship are at the heart of the whole notion of the european union. i would argue that, having taken a major step this week towards the political and geographical unity of europe, if we are to create european citizens, we must have services of general interest universally available, accessible, affordable and of high quality. properly understood, services of general interest are for all citizens, not just for those who are excluded, or poor or indeed disadvantaged – though obviously they are of key importance to people in that situation. services of general interest support and sustain growth. they sustain environmental sustainability. they are a key component of any serious spatial strategy which will enable us to have sustainable rural communities and indeed liveable cities. they will provide us with healthy citizens who do not fear illness. they will enable citizens to commute and to communicate. they will enable citizens to be well-informed, to be well-educated, not only in terms of technological education, but also politically literate. all of these things are necessary if we are to create a europe of which we can be proud and which citizens will feel they own.

mr president, this is the international year of mountains, and i am glad that mrs frassoni, our co-chairman, managed to have this put on the agenda, as it is an essential issue. mountains are areas that contain some of the few remaining wildlife sanctuaries left in europe. they need special status as sensitive areas. there is a clause in the treaty for ultra-peripheral regions that provides for flexibility in adopting eu policies for special needs. this is what the commission should be doing. it should declare mountains to be sensitive regions and then adopt legislation accordingly. it is disappointing that the commission had no initiatives this year concerning mountains – not even a communication or a white paper. that would have been very welcome. the commission, whilst pushing for the international convention on the protection of the alps, states that the protocols have been ratified, but not everyone has ratified the transport protocol. it is essential, in relation to the threat that highways and the trans-european networks are having on mountain regions, that these protocols are properly implemented, not just in relation to the alpine regions but also in other regions such as the pyrenees which are in danger. we also need conventions for those areas to protect them. in relation to priorities, there is a conflict between the trans-european networks and the needs and concerns of people. it is quite clear that the people who have opposed trans-european networks have voiced real and true concerns. their concerns have been ignored to prioritise the trans-european networks. this is a conflict. finally, i cannot understand why the commissioner is not putting pressure on member states to ensure that they comply with natura 2000 in the alpine regions or why we do not have officially adopted lists of sites of community interest. that is disgraceful. i urge the commissioner to put pressure on the member states.
madam president, since july 1997, the european parliament has been a staunch defender of the autonomy of hong kong under the 'one-country two-systems' policy. in pursuit of this policy, we have worked constructively with the hong kong administration, reflected by the attendance of the former chief secretary anson chan and her successor, donald tsang, at meetings of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy. it is therefore appropriate that we should continue to monitor developments which could in any way undermine the autonomy of hong kong and threaten fundamental freedoms. enactment of legislation under article 23 has raised such concerns. while i welcome the personal guarantee given by chief secretary donald tsang that he will not allow the freedoms enjoyed by hong kong citizens to be undermined, this must be reflected in the proposed legislation. last weekend, a large demonstration in hong kong illustrated the genuine concerns that article 23 laws could undermine existing human rights and civil and religious liberties. i share these concerns and i urge the hong kong sar government to address them in the final proposals that they bring forward. in particular, the new laws must not violate the provisions of the international covenant on civil and political rights, nor must they in any way undermine the independence of the hong kong courts and their right to exercise the power of final jurisdiction. the reinterpretation of the basic law by the standing committee of the national people's congress during the right-of-abode case is still fresh in many people's minds. there must not be a repeat of this with regard to article 23 issues. i would ask the hong kong authorities to take note of this debate, to take note of this resolution, especially our request for the publication of a draft bill which should be subject to further consultation.
